If there is any conflict between section 3 and section 23(5)(a) of 1922 Act, the latter provision should prevail for the reasons already mentioned. From this it follows that section 23(5)(a ) of 1922 Act cannot be held to be an invalid provision as being in conflict with section 3 of 1922 Act. As regards second contention that parliament had no legislative competence to enact section 23(5)(a) of 1922 Act, for finding out the source of the power of Parliament to enact the provision in question, one has to look to entry No. 82 in List I of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution which reads : "Taxes on income other than agricultural income". This entry is a legislative topic. Therefore, it must be read widely. The word "income" is not defined in the Constitution. Hence one has to fall back on its natural and grammatical meaning, which means, "a thing that comes in" and thus is a word of broadest "connotation". There is no gainsaying the fact that the fund that is subject to tax is a fund that comes into the chest of a firm and a portion of the fund flows into the hands of the partners of that firm. Therefore, in that sense, it is an income not only in the hands of the registered firm but also in the hands of its partners. Hence, there was no force in the contention that Parliament was incompetent to enact section 23(5)(a) of 1922 Act.

The assessee further contended that section 14(2)(aa) of 1922 Act is void as it conflicts with the equality clause found in article 14 of the Constitution.

The grievance of the assessee was that when a Hindu joint family is assessed to tax its members are exempt from tax, when an unregistered firm is subjected to tax, its partners are exempt from tax, but when it comes to the case of a registered firm, not only the firm is made liable to pay tax, but also its partners are made liable to pay tax. This, according to him, is a clear discrimination. But the assessee ignored the fact that while a registered firm is given considerable concessions in the matter of taxation, no such concessions are available either to a Hindu joint family or to an unregistered firm. The provisions of the 1922 Act have clearly differentiated a registered firm from other firms as well as from other associations of persons. A clear-cut-classification is made between the several units and that classification is made in pursuance of the object of the 1922 Act and, therefore, the differentiation made between the several units cannot be considered as a discrimination coming within the mischief of article 14 of the Constitution.

The petition was, thus, liable to be dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c)  of the income-tax act, 1961 - penalty - for concealment of income - assessment year 1977-78 - assessee-huf returned its share of income from a partnership firm amounting to rs. 35,469 - search of assessee’s house led to recovery of gold and silver ornaments and cash - while gold and some silver ornaments were treated as stridhan of lady members, cash of rs. 96,000 out of rs. 1,28,085 recovered on search was treated as concealed income in view of conflicting versions of karta m and his wife j - m’s statement that it was accumulation of income from money-lending business carried on with money belonging to j could not be believed because j was not found doing any money-lending business - j’s statement that she found said amount of money in a bag lying on banks of river ganges was apparently fantastic - both statements were sans corroborative evidence - m eventually offered said amount to be included in huf’s income with request that penalty proceedings be not initiated, although that amount had been shown in separate return of j filed after search - whether it could be said that statements of m and j were not bona fide and were not sufficient to discharge onus that lay upon them to bring their case within proviso to explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) and hence, assessee-huf was liable for penalty for concealment of income, having failed to prove its source - held, yes

FACT: The assessee-HUF returned an income of Rs. 35,460 representing its share of income from a partnership firm for the assessment year 1977-78. The HUF consisted of karta M, his wife J and the three unmarried daughters who were living in the ground floor of a building, the first floor of which was occupied by M’s three sons with their families. On a search of the strong room located in the ground floor, the income-tax personnel recovered gold and silver ornaments of the value of Rs. 2,06,500 and Rs. 46,380 respectively, and Rs. 1,28,085 in cash. The ITO and subsequently the IAC under section 144B, accepted the explanation of the assessee that the gold and part of silver ornaments belonged to J and three daughters-in-law of the family, and that a sum of Rs. 15,000 cash belonged to M’s married daughter. They rejected the explanation that out of Rs. 1,28,085, Rs. 9,000 belonged to the assessee’s mother-in-law and also discarded the conflicting versions of M and J in regard to the cash of Rs. 96,000. M had stated that the said amount represented the accumulation of income out of the money-lending business carried on by him with the money provided to his wife J by her father on the eve of his insolvency, while J asserted that she had found the money in bag lying on the banks of the river Ganges when she went there on a pilgrimage. J also filed a return after the search and showed the said sum of Rs. 96,000 as her income. But during the course of the present proceedings before the IAC, the assessee offered the amount to be treated as the HUFs income, allegedly for purchasing peace and on the understanding that no penalty proceedings would be initiated. The IAC denied having held out any such understanding and finally the ITO completed the assessment by adding to the assessee’s income the cash balance of Rs. 1,13,085, Rs. 4,100 as value of pawned ornaments and Rs. 28,500, i.e., half of the value of silver ornaments as income from undisclosed sources. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) sustained the additions made by the ITO except the addition of Rs. 4,100. He also reduced the value of unexplained silver ornaments by Rs. 2,000. On second appeal, the assessee challenged the additions of Rs. 9,000, Rs. 8,085 and addition of Rs. 20,500 on account of silver ornaments, but did not contest the addition of Rs. 96,000. The appeal was, however, dismissed by the Tribunal. The ITO had also initiated penalty proceedings against the assessee for concealment of income and imposed the maximum penalty of Rs. 2,30,170.

headnotes.text: Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1968-69 - Whether state has a wide discretion in selecting persons or objects it would tax, and a statute is not open to attack on ground that it taxes some persons and objects and not others - Held, yes - Whether it is only when within range of its selection, law operates unequally, and that can not be justified on basis of any valid classification, that it would be violative of article 14 of Constitution - Held, yes - Whether section 271(1)(c) can not be regarded as violative of article 14 of Constitution as there is nothing in said section pointing out any hostile discrimination against a particular type of taxpayer - Held, yes - Whether moreover, since object of section 271(1)(c) is not to provide for any confiscation but to provide a penalty for concealment of income and that too by providing a deterrent penalty, it can not be said that provisions of section 271(1)(c)(iii) infringe article 19(1)(f) Constitution - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Whether provisions of section 271(1)(c) are discriminatory and violative of article 14 and constitute unreasonable restriction on fundamental rights guaranteed under article 19(1)(f) of the constitution - Held, no

Section 271(1)(c) of Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1964-65 - Whether Explanation creates a presumption in certain circumstances to effect that assessee will be deemed to have concealed particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income for purpose of clause (c) of section 271(1) if certain conditions are satisfied, namely, where total income returned is less than 80% of total income as assessed reduced by expenditure bona fide incurred by assessee for purpose of making or earning any income included in total income but which has been disallowed as a deduction - Held, yes - Whether Explanation provides nothing more than a rule of evidence relating to raising of a rebuttable presumption in certain circumstances which neither creates nor negatives any substantial right of assessee and is well within competence of legislature to create - Held, yes - Whether class of persons to whom Explanation applies is a rational classification and has nexus with object intended to be achieved, namely, of discouraging concealment of particulars of one's income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of such income during course of assessment - Held, yes - Whether therefore, it cannot be said that Explanation violates provisions of article 14 of Constitution and is ultra vires - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Where non-inclusion of cash compensatory support in original return filed by assessee was based on a decision of Special Bench of Tribunal and subsequently, in view of amendment brought by Finance Act, 1990 with retrospective effect that cash assistance was taxable, assessee filed revised return and included cash compensatory support (CCS) therein, act of assessee of non inclusion of CCS in original return could not be held to amount to 'concealment'

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1964-65 - Whether Explanation to section 271(1) inserted with effect from 1-4-1964 would apply to income returned after it came into force irrespective of fact whether income related period prior to 1-4-1964 or thereafter - Held, yes - Whether by Explanation to section 271(1) classifying assessees in two varieties and in allocating burden of proof in one class of cases on assessee and in other on departmental authority, Parliament has adopted an intelligible differentia dictated by experience gathered in administering Act and, therefore, said Explanation does not offend article 14 of Constitution - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1974-75 - Whether where returned income was more than 80 per cent of assessed income, burden of proof to show that penalty was leviable on concealed income, would lie on department - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1981-82 - Assessee claimed exemption under section 80T in respect of certain long-term capital gains - Assessee stated that a sum of Rs. 22,500 had been set apart for daughter’s marriage in year relevant to assessment year 1975-76 and jewellery in question was purchased with that money in year relevant to assessment year in question and same was sold in that year itself - Later assessee took stand that it was not cash which was lying with her but jewellery which was purchased in 1973 - Whether assessee’s explanation was not bona fide and, thus, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was leviable - Held, yes.

Section 271(1)(c), read with sections 276C/277, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 28(1)(c), read with sections 51 and 52, of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1944-45 to 1947-48 - Whether expression 'taxes on income' in Entry 54 of Federal list in Schedule VII of Government of India Act, 1935, is of widest import and would include laws in relation to taxation of evaded income and, therefore, section 28 of 1922 Act is within competence of central legislature -Held, yes - Whether quantum of penalty is one for legislature to decide and is wholly irrelevant for determining constitutional validity of penalty provision - Held, yes - Whether if in their nature two remedies provided under section 28 and under sections 51 and 52 of 1922 Act are not mutually exclusive and are concurrent, grant of a concession to assessee in form of a provision in section 28(4) of 1922 Act does not alter situation and make, two provisions mutually exclusive for purpose of attracting vice of unequal protection of laws forbidden by article 14 of Constitution - Held, yes - Whether proceedings for levy of penalty must be initiated by authority when it is in seisin of assessment or other proceedings during course of which it is found that assessee has brought himself within mischief of section 28 of 1922 Act but when once notice has been issued, jurisdiction of that authority to continue proceedings is not dependent upon continuance of other proceedings in course of which penalty proceedings came to be initiated - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 226/227 of the Constitution of India - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1974-75 - Assessee's appeal against order under section 271(1)(c) was dismissed by Tribunal - Instead of making a reference application under section 256, assessee filed present writ petition - Whether, since assessee did not adopt procedure available under section 256, it was not a fit case for interference under article 226, especially when no perversity in order was pointed out -Held, yes

Section 104 of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 23A of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Additional income-tax on undistributed profits of certain companies - Whether section 23A of 1922 Act is neither confiscatory in character nor does it violate articles 14, 19(1)(f) and (g) and 265 of Constitution - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1970-71 - During search custom authorities recovered valuables and cash from premises of assessee-HUF - Pursuant to notice under section 139(2), assessee filed its return - However, ITO assessed assessee on a much higher amount than returned and initiated penalty proceedings - IAC imposed penalty - Tribunal confirmed assessment as well as penalty order - Whether refusal by IAC to adjourn assessee’s stay proceedings had nothing to do with hearing of penalty proceedings and, therefore, assessee could not have any grievance relating to non affording of reasonable opportunity insofar as penalty was concerned - Held, yes - Whether since assessee’s explanations were rejected both by IAC and Tribunal by giving good reasons, assessee failed to discharge its onus and, therefore, Tribunal was justified in confirming imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1980-81 - Department seized from assessee cash with confirmation letters of concerned parties having advanced cash for supply of jewels - Both parties denied in statement recorded by department - Assessee was not supplied with those confirmatory letters or copies of said statement - Commissioner dismissed his petition under section 273A - Later, assessee, under amnesty scheme, surrendered said amount, but Assessing Officer while completing assessment levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) on ground of assessee having declared additional income only after detection - Whether, where conditional offer for assessment of his income was made, department could not dissect that offer into two parts, and assess his income as offered but ignore his request from non-imposition of penalty - Held, yes - Whether documentary evidence must prevail over any oral statement made by concerned parties recorded behind assessee’s back, and, therefore, on facts assessee could not be said to have concealed his income and penalty levied was, thus, not sustainable - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1969-70 - Assessee’s returned income was less than 80 per cent of assessed income - He, however, did not discharge burden showing that no case for imposition of penalty was made out - Whether, in aforesaid circumstances, imposition of penalty was justified - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1984-85 - Assessee surrendered income when it found it difficult to explain non-disclosure earlier - Income-tax Officer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) but Tribunal cancelled penalty holding that there was no concealment of income - Whether question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1974-75 - penalty levied on assessee under section 271(1)(c) - Tribunal held that there was deemed concealment of income - Whether question as to whether Tribunal had erred in reaching conclusion about deemed concealment of income was question of law to be referred - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1970-71 to 1975-76 - Where in assessment years 1970-71 to 1975-76, assessee's declared income was less than limit of 80 per cent of assessed income and as such presumption arose under Explanation and it was required to be rebutted by assessee and Tribunal found that assessee's explanation was a concocted one, imposition of penalty by Assessing Officer was justified [In favour of revenue]

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1973-74 - Whether where assessee failed to explain discrepancies in his stocks and Tribunal in penalty proceedings, by appreciating material on record afresh, found that there was conscious concealment of income by assessee, levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c) was valid - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1971-72 - Whether where income assessed by ITO was more than 80 per cent of returned income and assessee by not giving any explanation, failed to discharge onus cast upon it, Tribunal was right in holding that provisions of Explanation to section 271(1)(c) were attracted and, therefore, was justified in upholding order of ITO imposing penalty - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Whether question as to whether Tribunal was justified in directing to restrict aggregate amount of penalty under sections 271(1)(a) and 271(1)(c) to extent of twice amount of tax sought to be evaded calculated on basis of tax payable by a registered firm and not on basis of tax payable as an unregistered firm as provided under section 271(2), was a question of law to be referred - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) read with section 277 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Whether proceedings resulting in levy of penalty against a delinquent assessee for violation of any of prescribed statutory provisions of Income-tax Act, cannot be equitable to a punishment inflicted on said assessee as if he has committed an offence which is triable by a criminal Court and, therefore, such penalties do not in any way violate article 20(1) of Constitution - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For conceal-
ment of income - Assessment year 1977-78 - In course of assessment proceedings of firm 'B' to whom assessee-firm had made cash sale of GCI sheets in addition to other goods on credit sales, concerned ITO confronted assessee on basis of a katcha slip about genuineness of cash sale,

cer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Whether, since assessee

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1974-75 - Assessment of assessee-firm was completed on a total income including an addition relating to hypothecation of stock of raw materials, stores, finished goods, etc., with bank - Assessee failed to offer satisfactory explanation regarding discrepancy in stock as disclosed to bank Assessing Officer assessed unexplained purchases as income from other sources as assessee did not maintain any stock register - Assessing Officer initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) and imposed penalty - Whether addition sustained was on estimate basis and no clear concealment of income had been established in order to justify levy of penalty for concealment under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes - Whether in assessment, addition can be made on basis of presumption, but, in penalty proceedings, Assessing Officer has to establish that there is conscious concealment - Held, yes - Whether penalty under section 271(1)(c) can be imposed on sole basis of discrepancy of figure given to bank for taking more loan from bank - Held, no - Whether imposition of penalty was unjustified - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1971-72 - While completing assessee's assessment, ITO included a sum of Rs. 1 lakh in total income of assessee - Assessee claimed that amount related to encashment of a raffle ticket, which secured first prize - On investigation and collection of independent evidence authorities concluded that price winning ticket actually belonged to S and that assessee bad purchased ticket after it won prize and, therefore, amount of prize represented assessee's secret income undisclosed to department - Thereupon beside adding Rs. 1 lakh in total income, penalty was also imposed on assessee - Whether imposition of penalty was justified - Held, on facts, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1965-66 - Whether where ITO initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) in December 1967, maximum penalty that could be imposed was one and half times of amount of tax which would have been avoided and ITO was not right in imposing penalty at rate of 150 per cent of concealed income - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 2000-01  2001-02 - Where assessee had surrendered certain gift to buy peace as donor had died and assessee could not produce donor, as assessee's explanation was bona fide levy of penalty on assessee on account of addition of gift was not justified [In favour of assessee]

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1994-95 - Whether Explanation 4 to section 271(1)(c) amended in year 2002 by Finance Act, 2002 with effect from 1-4-2003 is prospective in its application and is not explanatory - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1976-77 - Tribunal upheld computation of income by recourse to well-established formula in accordance with proviso to section 145(1), but cancelled penalty under section 271(1)(c) on ground that concealment could not be attributed to assessee either under main provision or its Explanation - Whether presumption of concealment having been rebutted or not, was essentially a question of fact, and therefore, no referable question of law arose - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1)(c) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1949-50 - In respect of a house purchased during relevant year, assessee explained that he was merely a benamidar for his wife and purchase price of that property was gifted to his wife by her mother - ITO rejected said explanation and treated purchase price as income of assessee from undisclosed sources and levied penalty under section 28(1)(c) - Whether since sale deed was in name of assessee, it was for him to have disclosed in his return purchase of house with an explanation as to why income therefrom was not being returned and as assessee failed to discharge this burden, impugned penalty was rightly levied - Held, yes

Explanation to section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1969-70 - For relevant assessment year, assessee-firm's trading account disclosed total sales of Rs. 12.77 lakhs with a gross profit of 10.62 per cent - ITO found it low and estimated assessee's sales at Rs. 13 lakhs and gross profit at 18 per cent - On second appeal, Tribunal reduced percentage of gross profit to 15 per cent - Penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were initiated and penalty was imposed - Tribunal held that assessee had discharged the burden lying upon him to rebut the presumption arising from the fact that the returned income was less than 80 per cent of the assessed income -Whether Tribunal's finding was essentially one of fact and could not be interfered with as it was neither based on no evidence nor perverse - Held, yes

Explanation to section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1964-65 to 1967-68 - Whether concealment could be said to have been established where assessee had voluntarily disclosed income under Voluntary Disclosure Act, 1976 without paying tax thereon - Held, yes - Whether where difference between income originally assessed and income returned was more than 20 per cent, onus of proof lay on assessee, and Tribunal erred in casting onus of proof on department while cancelling penalty imposed under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessing Officer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) on value of excess stock of paints detected during course of survey operation under section 133A which assessee agreed to surrender and which it included in its return of income for assessment year in question and filed return on due date - Whether once income declared by assessee in its return filed under section 139(1) on due date, was accepted, it could not be said that assessee had concealed any particulars or had furnished any inaccurate particulars of its income and, hence, impugned penalty being unjustified had to be cancelled - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1977-78 - Whether where Tribunal had cancelled penalty after considering facts and circumstances of case, its order was justified and did not give rise to any referable question of law - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with sections 148 and 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1969-70 - Whether questions as to whether Tribunal was right in holding that assessee family did not conceal particulars of its income by confirming order of AAC and whether Tribunal was right in annulling proceedings of assessment initiated under section 148 by confirming order of AAC, were referable questions of law - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1978-79 - Whether initial burden under Explanation (1)(A) to section 271(1)(c) is on Department to prima facie record that there was concealment of income - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with  section 68, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income (Burden of proof) - Assessment year 2000-01 - Whether in penalty proceedings burden of proof varies from that in assessment proceedings and any finding in assessment proceedings would not automatically be adopted in penalty proceedings; thus, in penalty proceedings authorities have to independently arrive at a finding regarding 'concealment of income' or 'inaccurate particular' - Held, yes - Assessee disclosed fact of gift in his return of income for relevant assessment year - Assessing Officer in assessment order treated said exempted gifts as income from other sources and made additions - Assessment order was upheld by Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal - Subsequently, penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were also initiated against assessee by Assessing Officer, on ground that assessee had furnished inaccurate particulars and had concealed particulars of its income - According to Assessing Officer, assessment order clearly demonstrated gift to be a sham transaction designed to avoid payment of tax and such findings were relevant evidence in penalty proceedings - Whether since Assessing Officer did not record any findings as to incorrect, erroneous or false return of income filed by assessee and only doubted genuineness of gifts on ground of human probabilities, penalty imposed under section 271(1)(c) was not justified - Held, yes [Paras 25, 26 and 27] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Burden of proof in penalty proceedings vary from that in assessment proceedings and findings in assessment proceedings would not automatically be adopted in penalty proceedings; in penalty proceedings revenue authorities have to arrive at independent finding related to 'concealment of income' or 'inaccurate particular'

III. Section 271(1)(c), read with section 68, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income (Disallowance of claim, effect of) - Assessment year 2002-03 - Whether in view of facts stated under head 'cash credit', authorities below were justified in passing penalty order under section 271(1)(c) in respect of addition made towards bogus gift - Held, yes [Para 20] [In favour of revenue]

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Whether grant of imposition of penalty on assessee is essentially a question of discussion and if proper explanation is offered and same is accepted by Tribunal, High Court would not disturb such finding in exercise of its jurisdiction conferred under section 256(1) - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1974-75 - Whether since difference between income returned by assessee and income finally assessed was more than 20 per cent, Explanation to section 271(1)(c) would be attracted and onus would be on assessee to prove that failure to return correct income was not due to fraud or wilful neglect - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1970-71 to 1979-80 and 1981-82 - Assessee did not return income from a property as his income claiming to have thrown said property into HUF’s hotchpot by a declaration duly attested by a Notary Public - After making certain enquiries, ITO rejected assessee’s claim, added income from said property to his income and also imposed penalty - Whether penalty was not imposable since assessee’s claim was contestable one and based on material, even though such material was not considered sufficient - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1)(c) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1960-61 - ITO levied penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Tribunal held that assessment year being 1960-61, provisions of 1922 Act applied and as under relevant provision no minimum penalty had been prescribed, application of provisions of 1961 Act would offend provisions of article 20 of Constitution - Tribunal, therefore, applying section 28(1)(c) of 1922 Act restricted penalty to sum which was less than minimum penalty provided for under section 271(1)(c) of 1961 Act - Whether when penalty proceedings were initiated in 1965, those proceedings would be governed by provisions of 1961 Act - Held, yes - Whether article 20(1) of Constitution is not applicable to proceedings imposing penalty under Act - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, levy of penalty of amount which was less than minimum prescribed under section 271(1)(c) of 1961 Act was not justified - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1969-70 - Assessee was a partner in a firm and had filed a return declaring share income from firm - Assessing Officer held that firm was not a genuine firm and income earned in name of firm was assessee’s income and, therefore, included entire income from firm in assessee’s income - For concealment of income, Assessing Officer also imposed penalty upon assessee under section 271(1)(c), which was upheld by appellate authorities - Whether penalty imposed upon assessee was justified - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74 - Partners of assessee-firm constituted another partnership firm in name of ‘G’ - They filed separate returns of income for ‘G’ and also claimed for its registration - Assessing Officer granted registration and continued same in next year - Subsequently, Assessing Officer cancelled registration of ‘G’ observing that it was not a genuine firm and was only a branch of assessee-firm that was created with a view to evade tax liability of assessee - Assessment of assessee-firm was reopened and certain amounts were added to income of assessee - Assessing Officer also imposed penalty on assessee under section 271(1)(c) - Tribunal, however, on basis of appreciation of evidence recorded a finding that assessee had not concealed income or made mis-statement about its income, and, accordingly, cancelled penalty - Whether any question of law arose from order passed by Tribunal - Held, no

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1979-80 - During search conducted at business premises of assessee-firm, certain purchase vouchers were found which were not recorded in regular books of account of assessee - Similarly, certain papers were found which showed that some sales had also not been recorded - ITO took recourse to proviso to section 145 and by applying GP rate of 10 per cent, estimated assessee’s income - Income so assessed was more than double than income returned by assessee and, thus, ITO imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Whether since assessed income, which was more than double returned income, was on account of suppression of purchases and concealment of sales on part of assessee, Explanation to section 271(1)(c) was attracted - Held, yes - Whether therefore, penalty levied by Assessing Officer was justified - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1968-69 - Whether explanation appended to section 271(1)(c) does not constitute an ingredient of offence and it lays down a rule of evidence - Held, yes - Whether for imposing penalty, a charge sheet need not be drawn and it is not necessary to inform person sought to be penalised of exact charge against him - Held, yes - Whether in cases covered by Explanation to section 271(1)(c), revenue does not have to prove anything other than that returned income was less than 80 per cent of assessed income and thereafter, burden is on assessee to affirmatively establish lack of fraud, etc. - Held, yes - Assessee-firm filed its return of income- ITO included certain amount as income from other sources - Tribunal upheld inclusion in relation to two cash credit items and inclusion of an amount on account of bonus received by assessee as a result of devaluation of Indian currency - IAC initiated penalty proceedings and levied penalty - However, Tribunal cancelled penalty on a finding that in respect of two items there was no case of fraud or of wilful negligence and, in respect of third item relating to bonus, it observed that assessability of such a receipt was highly debatable matter - Whether since finding that assessee was not guilty of fraud or gross or wilful negligence was based on a consideration of relevant material and circumstances of case, Tribunal was justified in cancelling penalty - Held, yes
Section 297(2)(g) , read with section 271 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Repeals and savings - Whether provisions of section 297(2)(g) were violative of article 14 of Constitution of India - Held, yes

Section 276(1)(c), read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1985-86 - Whether question as to whether Tribunal was right in holding that assessee was liable to penalty under section 271(1)(c) for assessment year in question was a referable question of law - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c), read with section 115JB, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 2001-02 - Assessee filed its return of income declaring certain loss - While making assessment, Assessing Officer made disallowances on account of PF contribution made belatedly, deduction claimed under section 80HHC and depreciation claimed on machinery purchased on last day of year - However, as income so computed under normal procedure was less than income determined under section 115JB, assessee was assessed under section 115JB - Thereafter, Assessing Officer imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) in respect of aforesaid three additions holding that assessee had furnished inaccurate particulars of income - Whether, though there was concealment, yet that would have repercussions only when assessment would have been done under normal procedure - Held, yes - Whether when assessment was made on income computed under section 115JB and tax had been paid on income so computed, aforesaid concealment did not lead to tax evasion and, therefore, no penalty could have been imposed on assessee - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concalment of income (Nature of income received) - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee had set up a new unit which started its commercial production - In terms of section 41 of West Bengal Sales Tax Act, unit was allowed remission of sales tax for a period of 12 years upto 100 per cent of gross capital investment - Assessee claimed deduction on account of 'sales tax exemption in nature of capital subsidy' - Assessing Officer held that incentive in form of sale tax exemption was a revenue receipt and made addition to income of assessee - Thereafter, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was also imposed upon assessee - Whether since main issue involved while framing assessment was only with respect to interpretation as to whether sales tax subsidy taken by assessee was to be treated as a revenue or capital receipt, it did not amount to non-disclosure of any source of income which was liable for imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned penalty levied upon assessee was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where incentive in form of sales tax exemption received by assessee was treated as revenue receipt and further penalty under section 271(1)(c) was also imposed upon assessee, since main issue involved while framing assessment was only with respect to interpretation as to whether sales tax subsidy taken by assessee was to be treated as revenue or capital receipt, it did not amount to non-disclosure of any source of income which was liable for imposition of penalty and thus, impugned penalty was to be deleted

facts.text:
For the assessment year 1968-69, the assessee filed his original return without showing the income from sale of land, but when required to produce the sale deed in respect of the land sold by him, the assessee filed a revised return showing therein capital gains and business income on estimate basis. The ITO passed the assessment order and also issued notice under section 274 read with section 271 for failure to furnish the return within the stipulated time and also for concealment of income. Later, he levied penalty only under section 271(1)(c) of an amount equal to 100 per cent of the concealed income.

On writ, the assessee challenged the constitutional validity of section 271(1)(c) on two grounds: (1) that section 271(1)(c) is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as there is no classification at all even though there is a difference between various types of tax evasions; and (2) that the impugned provisions are a colourable exercise of legislative power inasmuch as in the guise of levying penalty the legislature had enacted for expropriation of the whole of the property of the citizen.

The petitioners, some of whom had been imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) of the 1961 Act and others under section 18(1)(a) of the 1957 Act, challenged the constitutional validity of these provisions on the ground that they are discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution of India besides being unreasonable restriction on the fundamental rights guaranteed under article 19(1)(f ) thereof. They further urged that the penalty based on the concealed income on wealth prescribed under the impugned sections is arbitrary and unjust and cannot be regarded as incidental to the levy of tax.

On writ :

The assessee, a jeweller, was detained in Bangalore on 7-9-1979 and cash of Rs. 1,20,000 was recovered from him along with 2 letters dated 6-9-1979 of two other jewellers stating that they had paid the sum as advance for supply of jewels. However, both the parties before the department denied having advanced any money to the assessee but their statements were not supplied to the assessee. Those letters were also returned to the assessee much after the completion of the assessment and passing of the penalty order at the instance of the Tribunal. The assessee filed his return for the assessment year 1980-81. The Assessing Officer included the cash amount in his income. The assessee filed an appeal against such clubbing. He also filed a petition before the Commissioner offering the said amount for assessment on the condition that no penalty or interest would be levied. While the Commissioner (Appeals) directed fresh assessment as per the Commissioner’s decision under section 273A, the Commissioner dismissed the petition as being not voluntary. Meanwhile with the introduction of amnesty scheme, the assessee filed a return by including the said amount in his total income. The Assessing Officer completed assessment and maintained that the assessee declared the amount only after it was detected; hence, it was a concealed income. He imposed penalty under section 271(1)( c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the penalty.

On second appeal:

The assessment of the petitioner for the assessment year 1960-61 was completed under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act on 27-2-1965, and thereafter a show cause notice under section 274/271 of the 1961 Act proposing to levy penalty for concealment of income was issued to the petitioner.

On writ, the petitioner contended (1) that the provisions of section 297(2)( g) were ultra vires, being violative of article 14 of the Constitution, and (2) that, in any event, even assuming that the 1961 Act was applicable, no penalty could be imposed under section 271 as the Income-tax Officer could not have been satisfied that there had been any non-disclosure by the assessee in the course of any proceedings under that Act.

The assessees filed writ petitions challenging the validity of the provisions of section 271(1B), which was brought on the statute book by the Finance Act, 2008 with retrospective effect from 1-4-1989, on the ground that it is ultra vires the Constitution of India inasmuch as apropos to its insertion in the Act, the salutary requirement of the Assessing Officer arriving at his own satisfaction during the course of assessment proceedings that the assessee has concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars of income before initiating penalty proceedings had been done away with, by a deeming fiction encapsulated therein. The assessees prayed that the impugned sub-section (1B) of section 271 may be struck down as constitutionally invalid or alternatively, it may be read down to the effect that the satisfaction should be deemed to have been recorded only where reasons are specified with respect to specific items of additions or disallowances leading to the initiation of penalty proceedings.

During the assessment year 1967-68, relevant to the accounting year ending 31-3-1967, the ITO found in the assessee's books cash credits of Rs. 11,000 in G's name. Although the assessee filed a copy of G's account, it failed to furnish his confirmation letter. The ITO, therefore, treated the aforementioned amounts as his concealed income and imposed a penalty of Rs. 11,225 under section 271(1)(c ). While the AAC sustained the same, the Tribunal deleted it, holding, inter alia, ( i) that even though G had denied the advancement of credit to the assessee in his own assessment proceedings, the ITO did not summon his representative as a witness ; and (ii) that there was no other cogent material or evidence to show that the impugned amounts represented the concealed income. The Tribunal also rejected revenue's application under section 256(1).

On application under section 256(2):

The assessee was assessed by the ITO at an income higher than that declared in the return filed. The ITO held that the assessee had certain concealed income which could be determined from the fact that household expenses had been underestimated and travelling expenses of family and club expenses as well as medical expenses which had been reimbursed, had not been shown properly. The ITO also imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the penalty was cancelled on the ground that the basis of the penalty proceedings had not been disclosed to the assessee who was put in a difficult position to defend the matter under section 274(1) and was not granted a reasonable opportunity of being heard. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the order cancelling the penalty and rejected the application for reference under section 256(1), holding that the finding regarding lack of reasonable opportunity was a finding of fact.

On application for reference under section 256(2):

The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of section 18(1)( a), as it stood for the assessment year 1969-70, on the following grounds: (i) that this provision permitted the levy of minimum penalty of ½ per cent of the net wealth assessed per month for each month of delay in filing the return and, therefore, it was in contravention of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution as in ah appropriate case the penalty may be equal to the value of total wealth assessed, that is, the maximum limit of the penalty permissible, and was, therefore, confiscatory; (ii) that section 18(1)(a)( i) permitted the imposition of penalty for delay of each month whereas the wealth-tax was assessed on the net wealth per year and this was in contravention of article 19(1)(f); (iii )that the penalty should be co-related with the duty and not with the net wealth assessed and, thus, the penalty being leviable at ½per cent of the net wealth was unreasonable and was hit by article 19(1)(f); (iv)that as this provision conferred jurisdiction on the WTO to impose minimum penalty which was 2 per cent of the assessed wealth up to the maximum which was equal to the total value of the assessed wealth and thereby gave a wide discretion to the WTO without any guidelines, this discretion violated article 14 of the Constitution; and (v) that levy of penalty at the rate of ½ per cent was discriminatory because the assessee, who was a smaller assessee and whose wealth-tax was assessed at ½ per cent. also will suffer a penalty of ½ per cent whereas the other who may be a substantial assessee and paid wealth-tax at a higher rate still the penalty which could be imposed was only ½ per cent and in this manner so far as a smaller assessee was concerned it was harsh, whereas for a substantial assessee it was rather lenient and, thus, was discriminatory and, therefore, contrary to the provisions contained in article 14 of the Constitution.

The petitioners were engaged in the business of sale of liquor in the States of Punjab and Haryana. The Excise and Taxation Commissioner auctioned country made liquor vends and the petitioners being the highest bidder, were sold these vends. As per the terms and conditions and the prevalent practice, the liquor contractor who intended to purchase country liquor for sale at his vend was required to deposit excise duty payable in respect of the quota of the country liquor he sought to purchase. On proof of this deposit of excise duty, the excise duty authority would issue a permit to the liquor contractor to purchase country liquor from the distillery and to transport and sell it at his vend. The distillery charges for the liquor sold by them were regulated by the Government and they included the price of the liquor and the expenses on bottling, labelling, etc. The Parliament introduced sections 44AC and 206C, 276BB with effect from 1-4-1989. In terms of section 44AC, 40 per cent of the purchase price of such liquor was deemed to be profit of the vendor and under section 206C income-tax at the rate of 15 per cent was to be deducted at source by the original seller.

On writ the petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of these provisions by contending that entry 82 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution empowers the Parliament to frame laws in relation to taxes on income other than agricultural income. Constitution does not authorize the Parliament to make laws for levy of income-tax on notional, deemed or presumptive incomes. The impugned provisions are violative of article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution as they impose an unreasonable restriction on the carrying on of trade and business by the petitioners. Income-tax is sought to be levied on the whole of the purchase price of the country liquor purchased by the liquor contractors though this purchase price cannot logically be termed as income of the liquor contractor, who has paid the purchase price of the country liquor. No income has accrued to him in this transaction. The equivalent of this purchase price paid shall not convert itself into profits or gains. At best, only a percentage thereof can come to the contractor as profit. The tax imposed is confiscatory in nature. The provisions are arbitrary, whimsical and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The contractors who deal in country liquor have been made liable to pay income-tax under the impugned provisions. However, the contractors who are engaged in the business of sale of Indian-made foreign liquor have been left off. Mostly, the liquor contractors who obtain vend licence for the sale of Indian-made foreign liquor and liquor contractor of country made liquor from a single and homogenous class and an invidious discrimination has been made against the country liquor contractors. There are different purchase prices fixed in different States for the country liquor. The same contractor, who has his business in more than two States, may have to pay income-tax at different rates in relation to his business in the country liquor in different States. This again is indefensible discrimination having no relationship with the objects achieved, i.e., the collection of revenue. The quantum of profit/income has been fixed arbitrarily and without any relationship to the ground realities.

The assessee had submitted his return of income for the assessment year 1974-75 showing a total income of Rs. 3,113 in response to a notice issued under section 143(2). Thereafter a search was made by the customs authorities of the assessee's residence from where a total of 565 wrist watches of foreign make valued at Rs. 87,455 were seized. The ITO included this sum in the income of the assessee for the assessment year 1974-75. The ITO also issued a notice under section 271(1)(c) and imposed penalty on the assessee. On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the ITO's order. Thereafter, there was a reference to the High Court and the High Court also held that the value of the wrist watches was the income of the assessee.

On appeal:

During the accounting years relevant to the assessment years 1974-75 and 1975- 76, the customs authorities seized certain foreign watches from the assessee’s premises. The customs authorities held that the aforesaid foreign watches seized belonged to the assessee only and accordingly levied penalty with regard to smuggled wrist watches and this penalty was confirmed by the magistrate. On the basis of the aforesaid material the ITO initiated reassessment proceedings for the assessment years in question. The ITO held that the assessee was the real owner of the foreign smuggled watches which were subsequently seized by the customs authorities and also held that the amount invested in the above watches came from sources undisclosed to the department. Therefore, he treated the investment in the watches seized by the customs department as income form undisclosed sources and assessed it as income from other sources. On appeal, the AAC upheld the aforesaid additions made in the reassessment which became final as there were no further appeals against it. However, the assessee filed application under section 154 stating that the loss arising on account of confiscation of watches by the customs authorities should have been allowed following the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Piara Singh [1980] 124 ITR 40. The ITO rejected the assessee’s application on the ground that he reassessment was upheld by the AAC and that as the assessee could not explain the sources for acquisition of watches which were found in his possession, the assessment of their value under the provisions of section 69A was correct. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO rejecting the application under section 154. While making the reassessments for the years in question, penalty proceedings were also initiated under section 271(1)(c) against the assessee. The ITO finally imposed penalty for the concealment of income. On appeal, the AAC upheld the imposition of penalties.

On further appeal:

For the assessment year 1968-69, the petitioners filed their respective returns declaring total income, but did not pay the tax payable thereon within the specified period, as required under section 140A(1), on the plea that their funds were locked up in the business. The ITO levied penalty under Section 140A(3) on the ground that they had large cash balance according to Wealth-tax returns, and that,’ therefore, there was no proper explanation for non-payment of tax under section 140A. Subsequently, regular assessments were completed and the tax payable thereon were determined. On appeal, the AAC had reduced the quantum of penalty, while the Writ Petitiions were pending.

On writ, the petitioner contended that (1) Section 140A(3) is confiscatory in nature and unreasonable and offends Article 19(1)(f); (2) while the Government pays interest only at 9 per cent (now 12 per cent) per annum for failure to refund within the specified time, any excess paid, assessee like the petitioner are liable to pay penalty under section 140A(3) for failure to pay tax in time, which amounts to an invidious and hostile discrimination against the petitioners, violating Article 14; this section also confers on the ITO an arbitrary and unguided power in the matter of imposition of penalty for non-payment of the tax and, therefore, is discriminatory violating for non-payment of the tax and, therefore, is discriminatory violating Article 14; and (3) the power to levy a penalty for non-payment of tax which has become payable is not incidental or ancillary to the power to ‘tax income’ and, therefore, Section 140A(3) is beyond the legislative competence of parliament.

For the assessment year 1954-55, the ITO initiated assessment proceedings under section 34(1)(a) of the Act of 1922, and completed the assessment under section 23(3) read with section 34(1)(a) of the Act of 1922. Under section 274(2) read with section 271(1) of the Act of 1961, penal proceedings were commenced and penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c) read with section 297(2)(g) of the Act of 1961 for deliberate concealment of income.

Appeal against penalty order was pending before the Tribunal.

On writ petition, the petitioner assessee sought quashing of penalty on the ground of violation of article 20(1) of the Constitution and also on the ground that no proceedings could have been started under section 271 of the 1961 Act (new Act,) as, under section 297 of the new Act, proceedings for the imposition of penalty could only be initiated under the repealed Act of 1922.

The ITO noticed that the assessee firm had advanced a sum of Rs. 50,000 to a sister concern in October 1983 and that there was a credit entry of Rs. 15000 in its cash book in May 1983. The assessee was asked to prove availability and source of those amounts. The assessee surrendered the amount as unexplained credit of Rs. 65,000. Treating this as concealment of income, penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c). Eventually, the penalty was cancelled by the Tribunal. Dissatisfied the Department filed the application under section 256(1) which was rejected.

On application under section 256(2) :

The assessee claimed that he had earned taxable income in assessment years 1981-82 to 1985-86 which was disclosed in good faith under the Amnesty scheme and requested that his return be accepted under the said scheme. The Assessing Officer was of the view that following the search and survey conducted in the cases of concerned parties, enquiries were directly made in the case of the assessee and the concealment was detected by the department before filing of the returns in question. Consequently the Assessing Officer added the impugned amount treating the same as his concealed income and charged interest under sections 139(8) and 217. He further initiated penalty proceedings under sections 271(1)(a), 271(1)(c) and 273(1)( b).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed such addition, holding the return of income furnished by the assessee as not covered by Amnesty scheme and, hence, not entitled to immunities declared under this scheme. He also confirmed charging of interest under sections 139(8) and 217.

On second appeal :

For the year 1964-65 the petitioner submitted a return of its income on 21-10-1964, showing its total income at Rs. 28,270. The ITO, however, assessed the income of the petitioner at Rs. 47,273 for that year and a penalty under section 271(1)(c) was imposed.

The assessee filed the writ petition challenging the penalty contending that the penalty having been imposed by the aid of the Explanation appended to sub-section (1) of section 271, which Explanation had come into force with effect 1-4-1964, the Explanation did not apply as the return in question related to the year which had concluded on 31-3-1964. The assessee further contended that the aforesaid Explanation offends article 14 of the Constitution.

The assessee-company filed a return declaring income of Rs. 11,049 for the assessment year 1984-85 and the same was the first year of the company. The assessment completed under section 144 was, however, set aside by the Commissioner (Appeals) with direction for being redone. While the fresh assessment proceedings were taken up, the assessee filed a petition before the Commissioner offering additional income consisting of 25 per cent of paid-up share capital and loss on share dealing, on the condition that the offer had been made to buy peace and to avoid unnecessary and prolonged litigation, and that there should be no penalty or prosecution. The ITO, accepting the offer of additional income, initiated penalty proceedings for concealment of income under section 271(1)(c) as well as for not furnishing any statement or estimate of advance tax under section 273(2)(b). The assessee contended that the offer of additional income was made only due to the difficulties experienced by the assessee in furnishing fool-proof evidence in support of the receipt of share capital because of the shifting of its registered office. The Assessing Officer imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) as also under section 273(2)(b). On appeal, the assessee placed reliance on the letter issued by the Member (Inv.) CBDT on the question of extending immunity under the Amnesty Scheme to the case of investment companies such as the assessee who came forward with an offer for tax in respect of at least 25 per cent of the share capital in the first year of assessment. Subsequently, during the course of the search under section 132, the revenue discovered certain slips which indicated suppression of sales and interest receipts. The ITO, therefore, held that the assessee was guilty of concealment of income. The assessee again filed a return of income on 13-1-1987 disclosing the suppressed sales and suppressed interest as its income. The ITO was not satisfied with the revised return and he was of the view that the assessee was guilty of concealing the particulars of income and filing inaccurate particulars and, thus, levied penalty under section 271(1)(c). It was, however, explained by the assessee (1) that the return filed by the assessee on 13-1-1978 was voluntarily filed before any receipt of notice under section 148 from the department (2) that the return was accepted by the department. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the ITO’s order.

On second appeal, the assessee contended that since the return was filed under the Amnesty Scheme, the revenue was not justified in levying the penalty.

violate article 14 of the Constitution. As regards the challenge on the grounds of article 19(1)(f ), it could not be said that the provisions are expropriatory. After all, all kinds of punishment and penalties can be said to be ex-proprietary in the sense that some part of the property of the delinquent concerned goes to the State. But, the power to impose punishment and penalties is incidental to the power for vindicating the main purpose of that power. The power to levy tax on income is vested in Parliament and, as incidental thereto, the power to impose penalties to vindicate that particular power of imposition of tax must also be given to the legislature.

The object of the legislature in the impugned provision is not to provide for any confiscation but to provide a penalty for concealment of income and that too by providing a deterrent penalty. Deterrence is the main theme or object behind the imposition of penalty and the whole object as shown by the history to this scheme of provisions is to provide gradually more and more deterrent penalties with a view to see that tax evasion does not take place and result in detriment to society as a whole. Therefore, it was not possible to say that the provisions of section 271(1)(c)( iii) infringe article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. Therefore, each of the special civil applications was dismissed.

Note: The case was decided in favour of revenue.

As regards the challenge on the basis of Article 14 of the Constitution, it is well-settled that while article 14 forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purposes of legislation. In order, however, to pass the test of permissible classification, two conditions must be fulfilled, namely : (i) that the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group ; and (ii ) that that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question.

In deciding whether a taxation law is discriminatory or not it is necessary to bear in mind that the State has a wide discretion in selecting the persons or objects it would tax, and that a statute is not open to attack on the ground that it taxes some persons and objects and not others. It is only when within the range of its selection, the law operates unequally, and that cannot be justified on the basis of any valid classification, that it would be violative of article 14. It is for the person who assails a legislation as discriminatory to establish that it is not based on a valid classification and it is well-settled that this burden is all the heavier when the legislation under attack is a taxing statute. In taxation even more than in other fields, legislatures possess the greatest freedom in classification. The burden is on the one attacking the legislative arrangement to negative every conceivable basis which might support it. Thus, unless the petitioner succeeds in establishing that there was a clear and hostile discrimination by virtue of the impugned legislation, the challenge on the ground of article 14 can not be sustained.

In the instant case, the challenge of the assessee, on the ground of article 14 must fail because in this piece of taxing statute he had not been able to point out any hostile discrimination against a particular type of taxpayer. The fact that the penalty with effect from 1-4-1968, is linked up with the income concealed rather than with the tax evaded shows the gravity which the legislature attaches to such tax evasions. The fact that under section 27l(1)(a)(i ) the penalty for not filing a return is correlated to the amount of the tax evaded as against the correlation of penalty to concealed income under the impugned provisions of section 271(1)(c)( iii) is totally beside the point because, so far as concealed income is concerned, the penalty for concealed income proceeds on altogether a different footing from penalty for omission to file a return in time. The history of legislation shows that Parliament has progressively moved more and more stringent measures of penalty obviously with a view to deter people from evading tax by concealing their income.

The object of the legislation behind all these penalty provisions, whether in section 28 of the 1922 Act or in section 271(1) of the 1961 Act is to provide a deterrent against tax evasion and the provisions are intended to be by way of an effective deterrent to put a stop to the practice which the legislature considers to be against the public interest.

The penalties imposed by the legislature to enforce the tax laws embrace both civil and criminal sanctions. Invocation of one does not exclude resort to the other. Thus, merely because a penalty is provided for concealing income and that penalty is correlated to the income concealed rather than to the tax evaded, it cannot be said that the provision is a piece of hostile legislation or hostile discrimination. The apparent harshness of the provision in the case of evaders of small income arises merely because at the lower levels of taxation the tax imposed is on a much lesser basis than on the higher slabs of income. Therefore, the higher the slab and the greater the extent of the income concealed, the lesser will be the ratio of the penalty, maximum and minimum, to the tax actually evaded as a result of concealment of such income. But this result has been brought about by the higher rates of taxation in the upper brackets of income. In any particular case the actual proportion between the penalty imposed and the tax evaded will depend upon the rate of tax applicable to the assessee concerned and again the penalty is to be levied on the basis of the concealed income and not on the basis of the entire income.

Under these circumstances it was obvious that the impugned provisions of section 271(1)(c)(iii ) could not be said to violate article 14 of the Constitution. As regards the challenge on the grounds of article 19(1)(f ), it could not be said that the provisions are expropriatory. After all, all kinds of punishment and penalties can be said to be ex-proprietary in the sense that some part of the property of the delinquent concerned goes to the State. But, the power to impose punishment and penalties is incidental to the power for vindicating the main purpose of that power.

Chapter XIV-B consists of sections 158B to 158BH which was inserted by the Finance Act, 1995 so as to provide for an assessment of the undisclosed income detected as a result of search, and devised to operate in the separate field of undisclosed income and in addition to the regular assessments covering previous years in the block period. In the instant case, the contention of the assessee that sub-section (2) of section 158BFA was oppressive or in any way violative of any article of the Constitution of India could not be accepted. There was no basis in that contention. [Para 7]

Section 158BFA has been introduced in Chapter XIV-B which deals with special procedure for assessment of search cases. The said provision is intended to act as an effective deterrent against evasion of tax and to put a stop to that practice which the Legislature considers to be against public interest. Merely, because heavy penalty is provided for concealing income and also disclosing of undisclosed and unexplained investment during search conducted, it cannot be said that such a provision is a piece of hostile legislation. Assuming that the provision is harsh since it is a deterrent against tax evaders, provision is not expropriatory. Power to levy tax on income is vested in the Parliament and power to impose penalties to vindicate that particular power of imposition of tax is also with the Parliament. Object and purpose of section 158BFA is to provide penalty for concealment of income and act as a deterrent against tax evaders. Heavy penalty is prescribed to check tax evasion. If Legislature in its wisdom felt that in the matter of search cases such a penalty should be imposed, it cannot be canvassed in a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution of India. [Para 8]

Therefore, there is no infirmity in the said provision. The prayer of the assessee to declare such provision as oppressive and violative of fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution could not be sustained.

The grounds on which a statute or a provision in a statute can be challenged are limited. In State of AP v. McDowell & Co. AIR 1996 SC 1627, the Supreme Court held that a law made by the Parliament or the Legislature can be struck down by courts only on two grounds, that is, (i ) lack of legislative competence, and (ii) violation of any of the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution or of any other constitutional provision. It was further held that no enactment can be struck down by just saying that it is arbitrary or unreasonable, or because the Court thinks it is unjustified. The Parliament and Legislatures, composed as they are, of the representatives of the people, are supposed to know and be aware of the needs of the people and what is good and bad for them and the Courts will not sit in judgment over their wisdom.

The constitutional validity of the entire scheme was considered and upheld by a Division Bench of the Bombay High Court in All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India [1997] 228 ITR 68/ 93 Taxman 737. The said decision of the Bombay High Court was affirmed by the Supreme Court in All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India [1998] 231 ITR 24/ 98 Taxman 446 .

With regard to the discrimination against persons who have been searched, the persons referred to in section 64(2)(ii) form a distinct class and are different from others. The three categories refer to or relate to a class in respect of which there was some kind of detection of concealed income or some action related to detection of concealed income. Section 132 enables search and seizure of documents, money, etc., which are not disclosed; section 132A enables requisition of books of account, etc., relating to undisclosed income; and section 133A enables survey and making of inventory which may lead to discovery of undisclosed income. These three categories are matters in regard to which notices can be issued under section 142 or section 148. Search under section 132 is followed by assessment under Chapter XIV-B. A requisition under section 132A is initiation of process to discover material related to concealed income. A survey under section 133A will lead to discovery of available assets and discovery of concealed income. Thus, all the three categories which are excluded from the benefit of section 64(1) are persons in regard to whom there is initiation or some kind of action relating to discovery of concealed income. Such persons are different and distinct from those in regard to whom no proceedings, process or action have been initiated to find out concealed income. In fact, initiation of action for search under section 132 or requisition under section 132A is authorised by the respective empowered authority, only where, in consequence of information in his possession, he has reasons to believe that there is some concealment or existence of other conditions stipulated in the said section.

As observed by the Supreme Court in the decisions in R.K. Garg v. Union of India [1982] 133 ITR 239/[1981] 7 Taxman 53 and Secretary to Government of Madras v. P.R. Sriramulu AIR 1996 SC 676, a large discretion in the Legislature is recognised by courts in making such laws. It cannot be said that there is no rationale in differentiating between the persons who have been searched on the basis of some information regarding concealment of income and persons who have not been searched. To find out whether the classification has any nexus to the object sought to be achieved, not only the object of framing the VDI Scheme, but also the object of introducing sections 132, 132A and 133A should also be kept in view. It is obvious that section 64(2)(ii) is intended to maintain the deterrent effect of sections 132, 132A and 133A on tax evaders. The intention of the VDI Scheme is not to nullify any provision of the Income-tax Act, but to achieve the stated object of the VDI Scheme within the framework of that Act without jeopardising the effect of the existing provisions of the Act.
