While making the reassessments for the years in question, penalty proceedings were also initiated under section 271(1)(c) against the assessee. The ITO finally imposed penalty for the concealment of income. On appeal, the AAC upheld the imposition of penalties.

On further appeal:

For the assessment year 1968-69, the petitioners filed their respective returns declaring total income, but did not pay the tax payable thereon within the specified period, as required under section 140A(1), on the plea that their funds were locked up in the business. The ITO levied penalty under Section 140A(3) on the ground that they had large cash balance according to Wealth-tax returns, and that,’ therefore, there was no proper explanation for non-payment of tax under section 140A. Subsequently, regular assessments were completed and the tax payable thereon were determined. On appeal, the AAC had reduced the quantum of penalty, while the Writ Petitiions were pending.

On writ, the petitioner contended that (1) Section 140A(3) is confiscatory in nature and unreasonable and offends Article 19(1)(f); (2) while the Government pays interest only at 9 per cent (now 12 per cent) per annum for failure to refund within the specified time, any excess paid, assessee like the petitioner are liable to pay penalty under section 140A(3) for failure to pay tax in time, which amounts to an invidious and hostile discrimination against the petitioners, violating Article 14; this section also confers on the ITO an arbitrary and unguided power in the matter of imposition of penalty for non-payment of the tax and, therefore, is discriminatory violating for non-payment of the tax and, therefore, is discriminatory violating Article 14; and (3) the power to levy a penalty for non-payment of tax which has become payable is not incidental or ancillary to the power to ‘tax income’ and, therefore, Section 140A(3) is beyond the legislative competence of parliament.

For the assessment year 1954-55, the ITO initiated assessment proceedings under section 34(1)(a) of the Act of 1922, and completed the assessment under section 23(3) read with section 34(1)(a) of the Act of 1922. Under section 274(2) read with section 271(1) of the Act of 1961, penal proceedings were commenced and penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c) read with section 297(2)(g) of the Act of 1961 for deliberate concealment of income.

Appeal against penalty order was pending before the Tribunal.

On writ petition, the petitioner assessee sought quashing of penalty on the ground of violation of article 20(1) of the Constitution and also on the ground that no proceedings could have been started under section 271 of the 1961 Act (new Act,) as, under section 297 of the new Act, proceedings for the imposition of penalty could only be initiated under the repealed Act of 1922.

The ITO noticed that the assessee firm had advanced a sum of Rs. 50,000 to a sister concern in October 1983 and that there was a credit entry of Rs. 15000 in its cash book in May 1983. The assessee was asked to prove availability and source of those amounts. The assessee surrendered the amount as unexplained credit of Rs. 65,000. Treating this as concealment of income, penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c). Eventually, the penalty was cancelled by the Tribunal. Dissatisfied the Department filed the application under section 256(1) which was rejected.

On application under section 256(2) :

The assessee claimed that he had earned taxable income in assessment years 1981-82 to 1985-86 which was disclosed in good faith under the Amnesty scheme and requested that his return be accepted under the said scheme. The Assessing Officer was of the view that following the search and survey conducted in the cases of concerned parties, enquiries were directly made in the case of the assessee and the concealment was detected by the department before filing of the returns in question. Consequently the Assessing Officer added the impugned amount treating the same as his concealed income and charged interest under sections 139(8) and 217. He further initiated penalty proceedings under sections 271(1)(a), 271(1)(c) and 273(1)( b).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed such addition, holding the return of income furnished by the assessee as not covered by Amnesty scheme and, hence, not entitled to immunities declared under this scheme. He also confirmed charging of interest under sections 139(8) and 217.

On second appeal :

For the year 1964-65 the petitioner submitted a return of its income on 21-10-1964, showing its total income at Rs. 28,270. The ITO, however, assessed the income of the petitioner at Rs. 47,273 for that year and a penalty under section 271(1)(c) was imposed.

The assessee filed the writ petition challenging the penalty contending that the penalty having been imposed by the aid of the Explanation appended to sub-section (1) of section 271, which Explanation had come into force with effect 1-4-1964, the Explanation did not apply as the return in question related to the year which had concluded on 31-3-1964. The assessee further contended that the aforesaid Explanation offends article 14 of the Constitution.

The assessee-company filed a return declaring income of Rs. 11,049 for the assessment year 1984-85 and the same was the first year of the company. The assessment completed under section 144 was, however, set aside by the Commissioner (Appeals) with direction for being redone. While the fresh assessment proceedings were taken up, the assessee filed a petition before the Commissioner offering additional income consisting of 25 per cent of paid-up share capital and loss on share dealing, on the condition that the offer had been made to buy peace and to avoid unnecessary and prolonged litigation, and that there should be no penalty or prosecution. The ITO, accepting the offer of additional income, initiated penalty proceedings for concealment of income under section 271(1)(c) as well as for not furnishing any statement or estimate of advance tax under section 273(2)(b). The assessee contended that the offer of additional income was made only due to the difficulties experienced by the assessee in furnishing fool-proof evidence in support of the receipt of share capital because of the shifting of its registered office. The Assessing Officer imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) as also under section 273(2)(b). On appeal, the assessee placed reliance on the letter issued by the Member (Inv.) CBDT on the question of extending immunity under the Amnesty Scheme to the case of investment companies such as the assessee who came forward with an offer for tax in respect of at least 25 per cent of the share capital in the first year of assessment. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, confirmed the penalties as, according to him, the disclosure of additional income was not voluntary or bona fide and the filing of the revised petition declaring additional income amounted to an admission by the assessee of concealing income in the original return and the letter of CBDT was not applicable to the assessee’s case.

On second appeal :

The assessee-firm was a dealer of cigarettes manufactured by GPIL. During search of GPIL’s premises, certain circulars were collected which instructed its dealers to charge ‘on-money’ on certain brands and to remit major portion of it to GPIL. The assessee-firm confessed that such ‘on-money’ charged so far was not accounted for in their books of account and they confirmed additional income. The Assessing Officer imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelled the penalty. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that though the dealers like the assessee concealed income, penalty could not be imposed as they were forced to charge ‘on-money’ for the benefit of the principal and other purposes in the interest of business. As a result, the Tribunal affirmed the deletion of penalty. The Tribunal refused to refer the issue to the High Court on the ground that the finding recorded by it was based on appreciation of materials available on record which gave rise to no question of law.

On an application under section 256(2) :

By virtue of section 44AC inserted by the Finance Act, 1988, a person dealing in alcohol meant for human consumption, timber, and forest produce, who obtained such goods by way of auction, tender or any other mode from specified sellers such as the Central or State Government, local authority, etc., was deemed to earn profits thereon at the rate of specified percentage of the purchase price and tax was to be collected from him by the seller at the time of sale and credited to the Government in terms of section 206C, also inserted by the Finance Act, 1988. These two provisions were enacted with a view to curbing tax evasion. By way of writ petitions this presumptive and pre-emptive levy of tax had been challenged by the petitioners on the grounds, (i) that what was sought to be taxed by force of section 44AC was not income and as such, the Parliament lacked legislative competence to enact it as well as section 206C, (ii)that section 44AC was discriminatory and arbitrary and hence violative of article 14, and (iii) that the rates fixed by section 44AC were confiscatory and the same had imposed unreasonable restrictions on the freedom to carry on trade or business and as such this section was violative of article 19(1)(g).

As a result of inspection by the sales tax authorities of the assessee’s business premises on 15-11-1985, certain stocks were found suppressed, and the CTO, on the basis of material found, determined the value of suppressed stock as also the gross turnover and levied and collected compounding fees from the assessee-firm. For the assessment year 1986- 87, the assessee-firm filed its original return after the aforesaid inspection was conducted. On the basis that the sales-tax authorities had estimated the unaccounted for sale, the profit on such unaccounted for sale was estimated at 25 per cent. In view of this and other factors, the ITO determined the assessee’s gross income at a figure higher than the originally returned income. However, before the assessment was made on 31-3-1987, the assessee filed a revised return disclosing a slightly higher income than that originally returned and sought the benefits of the Amnesty Scheme. The ITO rejected it on the ground that it was filed only after detection of the omission by the department. Penalty proceedings were initiated under section 271(1)(c). The assessee filed a written explanation, but the ITO held that inspection by the sales tax authorities was done before the close of the accounts on 31-3-1986 and the CTO had passed the assessment order dated 8-8-1986, determining a higher turnover of the assessee. According to the ITO, by the date of return filed on 18-9-1986. All the above facts were known, but the assessee had concealed particulars of its income or furnished inaccurate particulars of its income. The ITO, therefore, levied penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that penalty was levied on the basis of observations made in the assessment order. He also observed that the penalty was levied under the main section and the Explanation under section 271(1)(c) was never invoked nor the penalty justified on that basis. In such an event, he held that the burden of proving concealment lay entirely upon the department, but it had not been discharged.

On the revenue’s appeal:

For the assessment year 1985-86, the Tribunal determined the concealed income of the assessee at Rs. 70,000 and held that the assessee was liable to pay penalty under section 271(1)(c) on this amount. The reference application of the assessee was also rejected.

On application under section 256(2):

On search of the assessee’s premises under section 132 conducted on 14-10-1976 the revenue authorities recovered gold ornaments weighing about 183 tolas. At the time of the search, the assessee stated that she owned jewellery weighing 60 tolas only but subsequently she stated that she had received 183 tolas of gold ornaments at the time of her marriage. The ITO accepted the explanation only partly and made an addition of Rs. 92,902 to her income for the assessment year 1975-76. The Tribunal upheld the addition though with a reduced quantum, holding that the source of acquisition of the jewellery to the extent of 60 tolas only stood explained. The assessee did not challenge the finding of the Tribunal in reference. Thus, the returned income of the assessee remained less than 80 per cent of the income finally assessed. Also for the assessment year 1975-76 the assessee had filed her return for wealth-tax purposes on 16-1-1976 but had not disclosed the value of jewellery therein. In penalty proceedings initiated under section 271(1)(c ) the ITO imposed a penalty of Rs. 92,902 upon the assessee for concealment of income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) as a result of the order of the Tribunal in the quantum appeal, reduced the penalty to Rs. 27,812.

On second appeal :

The assessee-firm dealt in foodgrains. For the assessment year 1969-70, the ITO added a sum of Rs. 45,000 to the assessee's returned income on account of concealed income from undisclosed sources. The AAC and the Tribunal upheld the addition to the extent of Rs. 28,000. The ITO also levied penalty on the assessee under section 271(1)(c), but the Tribunal cancelled the same on the ground that there was no material to establish that the addition made to the assessee's income represented income which the assessee had consciously concealed. The Tribunal also dismissed the revenue's application for reference under section 256(1) on the ground that the Tribunal's aforementioned finding was a finding of fact so that no reference lay to the High Court.

On application under section 256(2):

The petitioner, assessee took forest contracts. It ran a saw-mill and also manufactured and sold furniture. It also did stone quarrying business. For the assessment year 1959-60 the petitioner filed a return of its income under section 22(2) of Act, 1922, on 21-10-1959, showing an income of Rs. 7,896. In the assessment proceedings the ITO noticed some discrepancies in the accounts and registers maintained by the assessee of its business and called upon the assessee to explain the discrepancies and furnish certain particulars. Thereupon, the assessee filed a revised return of its income on 17-1-1964, disclosing its total income as Rs. 50,605. The ITO finalized the assessment on 19-3-1964, after taking into consideration the revised return and issued a notice to the petitioner under section 271(1)(c) for concealment of income. The ITO referred the matter to the AAC as penalty intended to imposed by him exceeded Rs. 1,000.

The Inspecting Assistant Commissioner, finding that the assessee had concealed the particular of its income, made the impugned order imposing a penalty of Rs. 25,000 on the petitioner. The petitioner then preferred an appeal before the Tribunal which was dismissed. In the instant writ petition. It was contended by the petitioner that section 297(2)(g) being violative of article 14 of the Constitution is invalid and, therefore, no penalty could be imposed on the petitioner under section 271 and, that under section 271(1) a penalty can be imposed by the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner only if he, in the course of any proceedings under the Act of 1961, is satisfied that any person has committed any of the acts enumerated in clauses (a), (b) or (c) of section 271(1); that, as the assessment against the petitioner was made under the Act of 1922, and not under the Act of 1961, the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had no jurisdiction to impose any penalty under section 271(1).

For the assessment year 1974-75, the assessee-company returned an income of Rs. 1,39,180. But assessment was made on an income of Rs. 2,80,060. The additions were made on account of (i) certain purchases of raw materials and other items for which payments were not shown or bills not produced, (ii ) low inadequate and unsatisfactory G.P. rate, (iii) cessation of certain liabilities under section 41(1), and (iv) under-statement of profit and short-term capital gains on sale of certain machines, etc. In all these cases, the assessee opted to surrender the respective amounts. The Assessing Officer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c ) on the ground that additions represented a clear case of concealment of particulars of income by the assessee.

On appeal, the first appellate authority cancelled the penalty on the ground that there was no case of conscious concealment and additions were made simply on account of lack of opportunity to the assessee, that addition made on account of low G.P. rate did not make out a case for concealment, that books of account were in possession of the department and assessment was being finalised in March and that the surrenders were made with a view to buy peace and to avoid penalty.

On revenue’s appeal :

For the relevant assessment year, the Tribunal upheld penalty levied under section 271(1)(c) and held that sum of Rs. 1,00,000 added in the assessment of assessee-firm constituted the concealed income of the assessee.

On application under section 256(2), assessee contended that Tribunal's findings were based on irrelevant evidence.

The assessee concealed part of his income which was brought to tax subsequently by way of reassessment under section 147. Penalty for concealment was also imposed on the assessee under section 271 (1)( c) which was upheld by the AAC and the Tribunal with reduced quantum. The Tribunal also rejected the assessee's application for reference under section 256(1).

On application under section 256(2):

The assessee derived income from commission earned by booking goods for transportation. A search operation resulted in seizure of incriminating documents on the basis of which the Assessing Officer found (a) variation between the figures shown in a seized paper and those shown in the commission receipt book, and (b) income generated from gitti business, and (c) commission income from transportation of gitti. He accordingly made addition in respect of all the three sources of income even though the assessee disclaimed any such income from gitti business or from the gitti transportation and furnished confirmation letters from the truck owners and purchasers to the effect that no commission was being paid to the assessee. On the same basis, the Assessing Officer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c). The assessee took the plea that as once a truck was going with gitti, on return trip it was getting commission for transportation of goods of others and not from transportation of gitti. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee’s further plea that no penalty was leviable since income determined from various sources was on estimate, and observed that the fact stood proved on record that the assessee had concealed bare facts by which it could be easily inferred that it was concealing the sources of income as well as the real income from commission. He, thus, upheld the penalty.

On second appeal :

In the course of the assessment proceedings, it was found that the assessee had concealed particulars of his income to certain extent and proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were initiated. The amount represented the purchase price of raw materials for which no explanation was offered. Pursuant thereto, the IAC imposed a penalty which was reduced by Tribunal.

On reference, the High Court held that the Tribunal was not right in reducing the penalty imposed.

On application under section 261:

The ITO added Rs. 17,200 to the assessee's returned income under section 68 because of certain cash credits appearing in the assessee's account books after the assessee had failed to produce the alleged creditors and after the summons sent to them at the addresses furnished by the assessee had been returned un-served. The ITO also imposed penalty on the assessee under section 271(1)(c) on account of concealment of income. The AAC upheld the penalty but the Tribunal cancelled it, holding that the burden was on the department to establish that the amount received by the assessee constituted its income which it had concealed. The Tribunal relied upon the decisions of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Anwar Ali [1970] 76 ITR 696 and CIT v. Khoday Eswarsa & Sons [1972] 83 ITR 369 in arriving at its decision and also rejected the revenue's application under section 256(1).

On application under section 256(2), the revenue invoked the provisions of the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) to support its case.

In course of raid at the residence of the assessee, certain cash was found. The Assessing Officer rejected the explanation of the assessee and treated the said amount as unexplained income of assessee. The first appellate authority deleted the additions but on revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal set aside the orders of first appellate authority and restored the orders of the Assessing Officer. The assessee’s appeal was pending before the High Court. The Assessing Officer thereafter imposed penalty on the assessee under section 271(1)(c) which was confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals) but deleted by the Tribunal on the ground that there was no concealment. On reference, while the department challenged the orders of Tribunal with regard to deletion of penalty, the assessee raised preliminary objection relating to maintainability of the second appeal placing reliance on policy decision taken by the CBDT circulated under Circular F. No. 279/126/98-ITJ, dated 27-3-2000 (Instruction No. 1979) wherein the revenue was directed not to raise questions of law where the tax effect was less than the amount prescribed therein.

While completing the assessment for the assessment year in question, the ITO noticed certain cash credits in the names of different parties. On scrutiny, the ITO did not accept these cash credits as genuine and assessed certain amount being the overall peak credit of the entire transactions as the assessee's income from undisclosed sources. Simultaneously, he disallowed the interest claimed to have been paid to the creditors. These additions were upheld in appeal before the AAC. For such concealment of income, proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were initiated. But, in spite of the service of notice, the assessee did not attend the hearing of the penalty proceedings. The IAC held that the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) as introduced with effect from 1-4-1964, applied as the return was filed after the said date. As the assessee failed to discharge the onus reposed on him, the IAC held the assessee had concealed the income added by the ITO and accordingly imposed penalty. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) did not apply to the assessment year in appeal and that the department had failed to prove that the amount in question constituted the assessee's taxable income. In this view of the matter, the Tribunal cancelled the penalty imposed by the IAC. On reference, the High Court held that for imposition of the penalty law applicable would be law operating on the date of filing return and thus, remanded the matter to the Tribunal to determine whether the penalty was imposable bearing in mind the applicability of section 271(1)(c) on the date of filing return. The Tribunal then disposed of the appeal holding that the assessee did not adduce any evidence to show that the concealment was not due to any fraud, gross or wilful neglect on its part and as such, the IAC was justified in drawing the presumption in accordance with the Explanation of section 271(1)(c) that amounts in question represented the concealed income of the assessee.

On reference:

The assessee filed writ petition against levy of additional wealth-tax on urban land owned by him on ground that no income was being derived therefrom. He also submitted that the rate of additional wealth-tax imposed on urban land was discriminatory, confiscatory and thus, violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the constitution.

During the relevant accounting period the assessee constructed two floor of a house and claimed that the cost of such construction was met out of his saving of earlier years. This was not accepted by the ITO, who estimated the cost at higher figure and added the same to the income of the assessee as income from undisclosed sources. On appeal, the AAC reduced the addition which was further revised by the Tribunal. In the meantime, the ITO had initiated penalty proceedings and had referred the matter to the IAC. The IAC noted that the assessee had filed his return on 11-10-1965, by which date the Explanation to section 271 had come into operation, therefore, the onus was on the assessee to prove that he did not conceal particulars of his income. The assessee not having produced any evidence to show what was the real cost of construction, it was inferred that he had concealed the real cost and the IAC accordingly, imposed a penalty.

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the final addition to the income of the assessee sustained as income from undisclosed source could not be treated to be the concealed income of the assessee and the guilt of the assessee was not conclusively established and, held that no case was made out for imposition of penalty. The Tribunal further held that the Explanation to section 271(1)(c), which was promulagated in 1964 did not apply to the relevant assessment year.

On reference:

During a search in case of one 'G', a safe deposit vault was found, which belonged to the assessee, and contained cash of Rs. 60 lakhs, Indira Vikas Patras worth Rs. 50 lakhs and jewellery and bullion worth Rs. 17,84,865 as per registered valuer's report. The Tribunal followed the decision of the Madras High Court in the case of A.M. Sali Maricar v. ITO [1973] 90 ITR 116 and held that section 140A(3) was confiscatory and violative of article 19(1) of the Constitution.

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the penalty had been levied on the basis of estimated income, which could not lead to conclusion that there was conscious concealment on the part of the assessee and, therefore, it was not a fit case for levy of penalty, more so, when the assessee discharged the initial onus cast upon it in view of the application of the provisions of the Explanation to section 271(1)(c). The Commissioner (Appeal) confirmed the penalty order which was further affirmed by the Tribunal.

The assessee-company had made a disclosure under section 68 of the Finance Act, 1965 disclosing thereby that the amounts shown as hundi loans in its books of account represented its own income. section 271AAB before the Commissioner (Appeals) and it was submitted that penalty under this provision was not leviable as the assessment year 2014-15 was not covered under the definition of 'specified year' as due date for filing return of income for assessment year under appeal had already been expired before the date of search. The assessee writ petitioner challenged constitutional validity of proviso to section 10(34) along with provisions of section 115BBDA on grounds that section 115BBDA does not have any 'base', and that the provision makes hostile discrimination between a resident assessee and a non-resident assessee, as the provision only applies to a resident assessee. Another prayer made in the writ petition is for staying operation of the aforesaid provisions generally and in particular in relation to the assessment year 2017-18. It is submitted that the provisions under challenge are arbitrary, ultra vires and violative of article 14.

For the assessment year 1975-76, the ITO required the assessee-firm to explain the nature and source of certain cash credits appearing in its accounts as loans received from one S. The assessee failed to produce S before the ITO. On S being summoned and examined on oath, he flatly denied having given any loan to the assessee. The ITO held that the theory of loan advanced by S was a cooked up story and the, theory of payment of interest to S was also not genuine. Consequently, he included the sum of the cash credits and interest as income of the assessee from undisclosed sources, the returned income thereby falling short of 80 per cent of the assessed income. He also initiated penalty proceedings under sec- tion 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) sustained the ITO’s order. The Tribunal, while deciding the quantum appeal, held that the loans in question were bogus and that S never advanced the loans. The assessee did not offer any fresh explanation in penalty proceedings.

On second appeal, the assessee contended (i) that the ITO had erroneously invoked Explanation 1( A) to section 271(1)(c), which came into effect only from 1-4-1976 and was, therefore, not applicable for assessment year 1975-76, and (ii) that it was not established by the department that the impugned sum was the income of the assessee in the relevant year which the assessee had consciously concealed.

The petitioners, who were facing prosecution for the offence under section 276CC, for their failure to file return of income despite several notices, filed writ petitions challenging the constitutional validity of section 278E. The case of the petitioners was that the expression 'wilfully' occurring in section 276CC indicates the mens rea element and this being the basis for the prosecution, the prosecution was bound to prove the existence of mens rea on the part of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt; however, by introduction of section 278E, which gives rise to a presumption as to the culpable mental state of the accused, the entire basis of accusatorial jurisprudence, as accepted and recognized in India, has been shifted. The petitioners contended that while having to defend wholly baseless and vexatious criminal proceedings, they were also expected to discharge the burden of not possessing the criminal intent and proving it beyond a reasonable doubt. According to the petitioner, the impugned provision violated article 21 of the Constitution of India and their right to pray for discharge from the criminal proceedings had been negated merely on the basis of the impugned provision. According to the petitioner, by the said provision, the guarantee against self-incrimination protected by article 20(3) of the Constitution had also been taken away from them.

On 26-5-1960, a notice under section 22(2) of the 1922 Act was served on the assessee-firm calling upon it to submit a return of its income for the assessment year 1960-61 within 35 days of the service of the notice. If filed a return on 18-11-1961. The Income-tax Officer completed the assessment on 23-11-1964. In view of the amendment made by the Finance Act of 1956, in section 23(5) of the Act of 1922 the tax payable by the firm as also the amount to be included in the income of each partner was determined.

On the same date, the Income-tax Officer issued a notice under section 271, read with section 274, of the Act 1961, calling upon the firm to show cause why an order imposing a penalty should not be passed on account of late filing of return. After considering the explanation of the assessee, the Income-tax Officer made an order on 19th November, 1966, under section 271(1)(a) of the Act of 1961, imposing a penalty by treating the firm as unregistered for non-compliance with the notice under section 22(2) of the 1922 Act. The assessee took the matter in appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner challenging the imposition of penalty. Although those proceedings were still pending, a writ petition was filed on August 26, 1966, in the High Court challenging, inter alia, the validity and the constitutionality of section 23(5) of the Act of 1922 and section 297(2)(g) and section 271(2) of the Act of 1961, respectively. The High Court did not accede to any of the contentions of the assessee and the petition was dismissed.

On appeal to the Supreme Court.

During the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1971-72, the assessee stated that the cash of Rs. 22,070 introduced in his books of account represented his past savings from agricultural income. The ITO rejected the explanation and added the said sum to the assessee's total income under income from undisclosed sources. On rejection of appeal by the AAC, the assessee appealed to the Tribunal. The Tribunal, after giving a maximum possible allowance for savings from agricultural income, held that the assessee was unable to explain the credit to the extent of Rs. 10,000. Addition of Rs. 10,000 was finally maintained. Then the ITO initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c). The assessee had returned income of Rs. 4,760, while the income finally assessed was Rs. 16,160 after giving effect to the relief allowed by the Tribunal. As, according to the ITO, the income returned was less than 80 per cent of the income assessed, provisions of the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) were applicable. The ITO further observed that failure of the assessee to return the correct income did arise from fraud or gross or wilful neglect and the assessee would be deemed to have concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. The AAC as well as the Tribunal confirmed this finding and the quantum of penalty imposed by the ITO. The Tribunal also rejected the assessee's reference application under section 256(1).

On application under section 256(2):

For the assessment year 1985-86, the assessee had originally filed the return of income disclosing an income which was accepted by the ITO under section 143(1) on 10-9-1985. Subsequently, during the course of the search under section 132, the revenue discovered certain slips which indicated suppression of sales and interest receipts. The ITO, therefore, held that the assessee was guilty of concealment of income. The assessee again filed a return of income on 13-1-1987 disclosing the suppressed sales and suppressed interest as its income. The ITO was not satisfied with the revised return and he was of the view that the assessee was guilty of concealing the particulars of income and filing inaccurate particulars and, thus, levied penalty under section 271(1)(c). It was, however, explained by the assessee (1) that the return filed by the assessee on 13-1-1978 was voluntarily filed before any receipt of notice under section 148 from the department (2) that the return was accepted by the department. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the ITO’s order.

On second appeal, the assessee contended that since the return was filed under the Amnesty Scheme, the revenue was not justified in levying the penalty.

violate article 14 of the Constitution. As regards the challenge on the grounds of article 19(1)(f ), it could not be said that the provisions are expropriatory. After all, all kinds of punishment and penalties can be said to be ex-proprietary in the sense that some part of the property of the delinquent concerned goes to the State. But, the power to impose punishment and penalties is incidental to the power for vindicating the main purpose of that power. The power to levy tax on income is vested in Parliament and, as incidental thereto, the power to impose penalties to vindicate that particular power of imposition of tax must also be given to the legislature.

The object of the legislature in the impugned provision is not to provide for any confiscation but to provide a penalty for concealment of income and that too by providing a deterrent penalty. Deterrence is the main theme or object behind the imposition of penalty and the whole object as shown by the history to this scheme of provisions is to provide gradually more and more deterrent penalties with a view to see that tax evasion does not take place and result in detriment to society as a whole. Therefore, it was not possible to say that the provisions of section 271(1)(c)( iii) infringe article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. Therefore, each of the special civil applications was dismissed.

Note: The case was decided in favour of revenue.

As regards the challenge on the basis of Article 14 of the Constitution, it is well-settled that while article 14 forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purposes of legislation. In order, however, to pass the test of permissible classification, two conditions must be fulfilled, namely : (i) that the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group ; and (ii ) that that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question.

In deciding whether a taxation law is discriminatory or not it is necessary to bear in mind that the State has a wide discretion in selecting the persons or objects it would tax, and that a statute is not open to attack on the ground that it taxes some persons and objects and not others. It is only when within the range of its selection, the law operates unequally, and that cannot be justified on the basis of any valid classification, that it would be violative of article 14. It is for the person who assails a legislation as discriminatory to establish that it is not based on a valid classification and it is well-settled that this burden is all the heavier when the legislation under attack is a taxing statute. In taxation even more than in other fields, legislatures possess the greatest freedom in classification. The burden is on the one attacking the legislative arrangement to negative every conceivable basis which might support it. Thus, unless the petitioner succeeds in establishing that there was a clear and hostile discrimination by virtue of the impugned legislation, the challenge on the ground of article 14 can not be sustained.

In the instant case, the challenge of the assessee, on the ground of article 14 must fail because in this piece of taxing statute he had not been able to point out any hostile discrimination against a particular type of taxpayer. The fact that the penalty with effect from 1-4-1968, is linked up with the income concealed rather than with the tax evaded shows the gravity which the legislature attaches to such tax evasions. The fact that under section 27l(1)(a)(i ) the penalty for not filing a return is correlated to the amount of the tax evaded as against the correlation of penalty to concealed income under the impugned provisions of section 271(1)(c)( iii) is totally beside the point because, so far as concealed income is concerned, the penalty for concealed income proceeds on altogether a different footing from penalty for omission to file a return in time. The history of legislation shows that Parliament has progressively moved more and more stringent measures of penalty obviously with a view to deter people from evading tax by concealing their income.

The object of the legislation behind all these penalty provisions, whether in section 28 of the 1922 Act or in section 271(1) of the 1961 Act is to provide a deterrent against tax evasion and the provisions are intended to be by way of an effective deterrent to put a stop to the practice which the legislature considers to be against the public interest.

The penalties imposed by the legislature to enforce the tax laws embrace both civil and criminal sanctions. Invocation of one does not exclude resort to the other. Thus, merely because a penalty is provided for concealing income and that penalty is correlated to the income concealed rather than to the tax evaded, it cannot be said that the provision is a piece of hostile legislation or hostile discrimination. The apparent harshness of the provision in the case of evaders of small income arises merely because at the lower levels of taxation the tax imposed is on a much lesser basis than on the higher slabs of income. Therefore, the higher the slab and the greater the extent of the income concealed, the lesser will be the ratio of the penalty, maximum and minimum, to the tax actually evaded as a result of concealment of such income. But this result has been brought about by the higher rates of taxation in the upper brackets of income. In any particular case the actual proportion between the penalty imposed and the tax evaded will depend upon the rate of tax applicable to the assessee concerned and again the penalty is to be levied on the basis of the concealed income and not on the basis of the entire income.

Under these circumstances it was obvious that the impugned provisions of section 271(1)(c)(iii ) could not be said to violate article 14 of the Constitution. As regards the challenge on the grounds of article 19(1)(f ), it could not be said that the provisions are expropriatory. After all, all kinds of punishment and penalties can be said to be ex-proprietary in the sense that some part of the property of the delinquent concerned goes to the State. But, the power to impose punishment and penalties is incidental to the power for vindicating the main purpose of that power.

Chapter XIV-B consists of sections 158B to 158BH which was inserted by the Finance Act, 1995 so as to provide for an assessment of the undisclosed income detected as a result of search, and devised to operate in the separate field of undisclosed income and in addition to the regular assessments covering previous years in the block period. In the instant case, the contention of the assessee that sub-section (2) of section 158BFA was oppressive or in any way violative of any article of the Constitution of India could not be accepted. There was no basis in that contention. [Para 7]

Section 158BFA has been introduced in Chapter XIV-B which deals with special procedure for assessment of search cases. The said provision is intended to act as an effective deterrent against evasion of tax and to put a stop to that practice which the Legislature considers to be against public interest. Merely, because heavy penalty is provided for concealing income and also disclosing of undisclosed and unexplained investment during search conducted, it cannot be said that such a provision is a piece of hostile legislation. Assuming that the provision is harsh since it is a deterrent against tax evaders, provision is not expropriatory. Power to levy tax on income is vested in the Parliament and power to impose penalties to vindicate that particular power of imposition of tax is also with the Parliament. Object and purpose of section 158BFA is to provide penalty for concealment of income and act as a deterrent against tax evaders. Heavy penalty is prescribed to check tax evasion. If Legislature in its wisdom felt that in the matter of search cases such a penalty should be imposed, it cannot be canvassed in a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution of India. [Para 8]

Therefore, there is no infirmity in the said provision. The prayer of the assessee to declare such provision as oppressive and violative of fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution could not be sustained.

The grounds on which a statute or a provision in a statute can be challenged are limited. In State of AP v. McDowell & Co. AIR 1996 SC 1627, the Supreme Court held that a law made by the Parliament or the Legislature can be struck down by courts only on two grounds, that is, (i ) lack of legislative competence, and (ii) violation of any of the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution or of any other constitutional provision. It was further held that no enactment can be struck down by just saying that it is arbitrary or unreasonable, or because the Court thinks it is unjustified. The Parliament and Legislatures, composed as they are, of the representatives of the people, are supposed to know and be aware of the needs of the people and what is good and bad for them and the Courts will not sit in judgment over their wisdom.

The constitutional validity of the entire scheme was considered and upheld by a Division Bench of the Bombay High Court in All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India [1997] 228 ITR 68/ 93 Taxman 737. The said decision of the Bombay High Court was affirmed by the Supreme Court in All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India [1998] 231 ITR 24/ 98 Taxman 446 .

With regard to the discrimination against persons who have been searched, the persons referred to in section 64(2)(ii) form a distinct class and are different from others. The three categories refer to or relate to a class in respect of which there was some kind of detection of concealed income or some action related to detection of concealed income. Section 132 enables search and seizure of documents, money, etc., which are not disclosed; section 132A enables requisition of books of account, etc., relating to undisclosed income; and section 133A enables survey and making of inventory which may lead to discovery of undisclosed income. These three categories are matters in regard to which notices can be issued under section 142 or section 148. Search under section 132 is followed by assessment under Chapter XIV-B. A requisition under section 132A is initiation of process to discover material related to concealed income. A survey under section 133A will lead to discovery of available assets and discovery of concealed income. Thus, all the three categories which are excluded from the benefit of section 64(1) are persons in regard to whom there is initiation or some kind of action relating to discovery of concealed income. Such persons are different and distinct from those in regard to whom no proceedings, process or action have been initiated to find out concealed income. In fact, initiation of action for search under section 132 or requisition under section 132A is authorised by the respective empowered authority, only where, in consequence of information in his possession, he has reasons to believe that there is some concealment or existence of other conditions stipulated in the said section.

As observed by the Supreme Court in the decisions in R.K. Garg v. Union of India [1982] 133 ITR 239/[1981] 7 Taxman 53 and Secretary to Government of Madras v. P.R. Sriramulu AIR 1996 SC 676, a large discretion in the Legislature is recognised by courts in making such laws. It cannot be said that there is no rationale in differentiating between the persons who have been searched on the basis of some information regarding concealment of income and persons who have not been searched. To find out whether the classification has any nexus to the object sought to be achieved, not only the object of framing the VDI Scheme, but also the object of introducing sections 132, 132A and 133A should also be kept in view. It is obvious that section 64(2)(ii) is intended to maintain the deterrent effect of sections 132, 132A and 133A on tax evaders. The intention of the VDI Scheme is not to nullify any provision of the Income-tax Act, but to achieve the stated object of the VDI Scheme within the framework of that Act without jeopardising the effect of the existing provisions of the Act.

In the light of the above observations let us examined as to whether the rule contained in the Explanation can be said to be a rule of substantive law or a rule of procedural law, i.e., whether it is a rule for establishing or dis-establishing a specified substantive right or a rule of evidence merely. Clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 provides for the payment of certain penalty that may be directed by the ITO or the AAC if he is satisfied that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. Thus a person becomes liable to the penalty, how much that penalty should be we are not concerned with in connection with the enquiry, if he has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of the same. The Explanation only provides that, in certain circumstances, the assessee will be deemed to have concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars and the burden will then be on him to establish that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on his part. The condition which raises this presumption is that where the total income returned by the assessee is less than 80% of the total income as assessed under sections 143, 144 and 147 reduced by the expenditure incurred by him for the purpose of making or earning any income included in the total income but which has been disallowed as a deduction, the presumption will arise. Thus if an assessee makes a return and that return is disbelieved and he is assessed to a higher amount than he purports to show in the return and the total income that he has shown in his return is less than 80% of the income for which he is assessed, then the law thinks, as provided by this Explanation, that he has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars. Can it be said, in the circumstances, that the existence of the position of the return being less than 80 per cent of the total income assessed is not relevant to the concealment of the particulars of his income by the assessee or his furnishing inaccurate particulars of such income. Clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 contemplates a certain amount of penalty for concealment of the particulars of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars by an assessee. If the return of an assessee's income is found not to be correct and is less than 80 per cent of the income at which he is ultimately assessed, the Explanation in such a state of affairs provides for the raising of a presumption against the assessee for his having concealed the particulars of his income or having furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. Obviously, applying the test laid down in Izhar Ahmad Khan's case (supra ) the Explanation provides nothing more than a rule of evidence relating to the raising of a rebuttable presumption in certain circumstances. It is not a rule which creates or negatives any substantive right. Such a rule is within the competence of the legislature to create. The question, however, is as to whether by the creation of such a rule the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution have been violated.

Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees to every citizen equality before the law and for the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

An applicant pleading that article 14 has been violated must make out that not only he had been treated differently from others, but he has been so treated from persons similarly circumstances without any reasonable basis, and such differential treatment is unjustifiably made.

bypass a constitutional prohibition by employing indirect methods and, therefore, the court has to look behind the form and appearance to discover the true character and nature of legislation: vide Dwarkadas Shrinivas v. Sholapur Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd. [1954] 24 Comp. Cas 103; [1954] SCR 674; AIR 1954 SC 119 and Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India AIR 1960 SC 554. Looking at the substance of section 140A(3), there could be no doubt that it deprives or takes away the owner of his retained income and thus it is confiscatory in nature. That the penalty levied under section 140A(3) is not compensatory or interest for delayed payment of the tax or retention, is clear from the fact that it has no relation to the duration of the delay or the wilful or other nature of the violation to pay or the inability to pay the tax. There is not even a power to extend the time for payment. The moment thirty days given under sub-section (1) of section 140A is over, the liability for penalty is attracted. It is also not related to the quantum of the tax payable except that the penalty is attracted if the tax payable exceeds Rs. 500. Thus this section is not hedged in or circumscribed or limited by any condition other than the lapse of 30 days from the date of furnishing of the return and non-payment of the tax payable within those 30 days in order to attract the liability for penalty.

The revenue contended that, though a discretion is vested in the ITO to levy a penalty for failure to pay tax, having regard to the nature of the provisions, he is expected to exercise a judicial discretion and impose a penalty only in those cases where the failure to pay was wilful by a person who had enough resources to pay but deliberately and fraudulently fails to pay. He also relied on the proviso to sub-section (3) requiring the issue of notice and giving opportunity to the assessee of being heard. This will enable the assessee to bring to the notice of the assessing authority the mitigating circumstances which would have to be taken into account by the assessing authority. In this connection he also relied on a Circular No. 20(LXXVI) D of 1964 dated 7-7-1964, issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes. Apart from the doubt on the binding nature of this circular, inspite of Section 119, the authority of the ITO under section 140A(3) being quasi-judicial in nature. This instruction could not violate the provision if it is otherwise invalid.

The test is not what is actually done in exercise of the powers under section 140A(3) but what the section enables to be done by the assessing authority. The power to levy penalty under section 140A(3) is very wide and enables levy of penalty even in cases where the delay in payment was bona fide or due to inability or other good reasons and the amount of penalty is also not made dependent on the amount of tax payable or the length of time of the delay.

Though the Supreme Court, in the case of Check Post Officer v. K.P. Abdulla and Bros., [1971] 27 STC 1 (SC) was concerned with the legislative competency of a State legislature under entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, the ratio of that judgment, is that a provision for confiscation or levy of penalty is not a provision for enforcement of payment of tax. Thus, the provision for confisaction of property for non-payment of tax arrears could not be sustained as a provision ancilliary or incidental for enforcement of payment and, therefore, a reasonable restriction under clause (5) of article 19 of the Constitution. Even as a punishment for failure to pay the tax within time, the legislation could not be sustained from the attack of article 19(1)(f).

The provision of Section 140A(3) has no rationales or intelligent connection with the recovery of the tax itself. Actually, the Act itself does not provide for the issue of a demand notice under section 156 of the Act. If it is intended to be a coercive process it must be to recover the debt itself but not to enhance it. The provision, far from enabling to recover the debt imposes an additional burden. Far from effectuating recovery, the levy of penalty may even frustrate the very object.

Moreover, the liability for penalty arises because of the contumacious or fraudulent conduct of the assessee. Mere failure to pay tax is not an offence. Failure to pay even for long time per se does not prove fraudulent conduct. It is the intent to defraud that attracts liability to penalty. The fraudulent evasion creates a right to the Government to claim damages. But the tax payable under section 140A is a civil liability which could not attract any confiscation of property. Any provision enabling confiscation for failure to discharge that liability in time will be unreasonable and infringe article 19(1)(f).

Briefly put, if the gap between the returned and actual income is more than 20 per cent a presumption of law arises that the assessee's case is covered by clause (c) but that presumption being in rebuttal the assessee is given an opportunity to establish that it is not so. The classification of the assessees into two varieties as envisaged by the Explanation is founded on intelligible differentia. The two categories of assessee in legislature wisdom are; (1) who, in the opinion of parliament, have been guilty of gross and flagrant violation of ethics benefiting a citizen in the matter of submission of income-tax returns, and (2) the rest of the assessees falling in the category not answering such description. The Explanation is an instance of the legal adage res ipsa loquitur, meaning that the thing speaks for itself. In substance, Parliament wants the income tax authorities to assume if the gap between the returned income and the actual income is so glaring as to the extent of not less than 20 per cent that assessee in question has concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income, but in case the difference is less than twenty per cent., then such assumption would not arise and it shall be for the department to establish that the assessee has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. In allocating the burden of proof in one class of cases on the assessee and in the other on the departmental authority, think Parliament has adopted an intelligible differentia dictated by the experience gathered in administering the Act.

It is not for the courts to tell Parliament what sort of classification it should introduce. The function of the courts is only to find out whether the classification actually introduced by Parliament is hit by article 14 of the Constitution. There may be a variety of classifications which can be introduced for achieving a particular object, but if Parliament in its wisdom adopts one in preference to another, the courts cannot take exception to the classification chosen if it is not proved to be obnoxious to the constitutional provision. The classification introduced by the Explanation to section 271(1) does not offend article 14 of the Constitution.

Intelligible differentia deductible from the wording of the Explanation to section 271(1) has a rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved by the Explanation. If the assessees commit the excess of showing their incomes at figures so short as to attract the applicability of the Explanation, they shall be presumed to be guilty within the meaning of clause (c) and liable to penalty to the extent mentioned in sub-section (1)(iii ) of section 271 if they cannot prove that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on their part. The allocation of burden on the assessees in the circumstances mentioned in the Explanation will surely have a deterrent effect in the matter of submitting under-estimated or false returns with the consequence that the prospects of submitting true returns of the income or returns which are more close to actuality shall brighten up. Hence there is a rational nexus between the differentia introduced by the Explanation and the object which Parliament had in view in enacting that Explanation.

In the result, the writ petition failed and was dismissed.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The expression 'income' as used in section 69A has wide meaning and means anything which comes in or results in gain. Hence, in the facts of this case, a legitimate inference could be drawn that the assessee had income which was invested in purchasing the wrist watches and, as such, that income was subject to tax. The High Court was justified in affirming the Tribunal's order, holding that the assessee was the owner of wrist watches and, thus, including the value in the assessment of the income of the assessee by virtue of section 69A coupled with surrounding circumstances. Therefore, inclusion of the money in purchasing the wrist watches, i.e., Rs. 87,455 was correct and proper for the assessment year under reference.

As regards the penalty imposed, from the facts found by the revenue, the assessee had shown only a total income of Rs. 3,113 and subsequently the raiding party seised wrist watches worth Rs. 87,455. Thus, the value of that income was included in the assessable income of the assessee. 'Therefore, the total assessable income of the assessee came to Rs. 90,568 whereas the returned income was Rs. 3,113 which was certainly less than 80 per cent of the total income and, as such, the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) applied. Accordingly, the revenue had discharged the onus of proving concealment of income. Therefore, imposition of penalty was right.

There can be no dispute about the proposition that a taxing statute which is beyond the legislative competence or which violates any of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution of India would be void. A taxing statute can be scrutinised on the anvil of article 14 of the Constitution like any other law. As held by the Supreme Court in K.T. Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala AIR 1961 SC 552, a taxing statute is not wholly immune from attack on the ground that it infringes the equality clause in article 14, though the Courts are not concerned with the policy underlying a taxing statute or whether a particular tax could have been imposed in a different way or in a way that the Court might think more just and equitable. If the Legislature has classified persons or properties into different categories which are subjected to different rates of taxation with reference to income or property, such a classification would not be open to the attack of inequality on the ground that the total burden resulting from such a classification is unequal. Similarly, different kinds of property may be subjected to different rates of taxation, but so long as there is a rational basis for the classification, article 14 will not come in the way of such classification resulting in unequal burdens on different classes of properties.

To meet with the manifold ways that the tax evasion may take place, the taxing statutes may have to devise different means to meet with different situations. While uniformity may be a virtue, it may fail to answer a given situation. When the situation warrants a special procedure to be adopted, the Legislature is entirely within its domain to devise it to achieve the object of the law. Bringing to tax the income chargeable to tax is the paramount object of any taxing statute and for achieving such object it may prescribe a special procedure to more effectively deal with a given complex situation. The past experience in respect of search cases showed that valuable time was lost in trying to relate the undisclosed incomes to different previous years under section 132B and that by the time search related assets were computed, the effect of search was considerably diluted.

Chapter XIV-B devises a special procedure for assessing the undisclosed income. The persons whose undisclosed income is already detected in search procedure are treated differently than others. Since their undisclosed income is detected, they are justifiably asked to relate it to the relevant years of the block period. The fact that undisclosed income of a person is detected in search proceedings is a valid reason for asking him to declare in the return whether he had any other undisclosed income. The block period is only of ten years which is not more onerous than the upper period of ten years for initiating escaped assessment proceedings by issuing notice under section 148 read with section 149. The block period assessment was required to be done in such cases because relating the undisclosed income detected in search would have otherwise entailed re-opening of the past assessments of several previous years over a period of time and an extensive search for the previous years to which the undis-closed income related. The assessee whose undisclosed income is detected and would, therefore, know to which year it belonged is now put under an obligation to disclose any other undisclosed income and to relate all his undisclosed income for the block period to the relevant previous years in the returns filed by him under Form 2B. In the inquiry under section 143(3) which is made applicable to the block assessment of undisclosed income, the Assessing Officer can go into the matter and detect the undisclosed income in respect of the block period in such search cases. This special procedure cannot be termed as an arbitrary discrimination against the per-sons whose undisclosed income is detected in the search proceedings. Treating the persons whose undisclosed income is detected in search proceedings differently for the purpose of assessing their undisclosed income than others is, therefore, a classification based on an intelligible differentia having a reasonable nexus with the object of the law to effectively bring to tax the undisclosed income of the block period of such persons who did not and would not have disclosed it. Making of the special procedure for assessment of search cases by providing that there should be block assessment made in respect of the undisclosed income against the persons to whom it belongs, therefore, clearly passes the twin criteria of there being a valid classification on the basis of intelligible differentia between those for whom the special provisions are made and others who fall outside that class and a reasonable nexus of such classification with the object sought to be achieved by such statutory provisions.

It cannot be said that every country liquor contractor is evading income-tax or is running the business in benami names and has set up fictitious firms/associations. Still there are honest liquor contractors in the country. There is no basis for assessing the profits and gains of every liquor licensee at the rate of 40 per cent of the purchase price. In the very nature of things, there may be many persons who may actually earn less profits than specified or may incur losses. In the Finance Bill, the profits and gains were proposed to be assessed at the rate of 60 per cent of the purchase price. It has not been explained why it was reduced to 40 per cent in the Act. However, in social interest, instead of striking down section 44AC, it was thought better to read it down to make it consistent with the guarantees in articles 14 and 19(1)(g) and to read it as an adjunct to sections 28 to 43C. On this construction, section 44AC does not dispense with sections 28 to 43C absolutely. The non obstante clause in section 44AC(1), notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sections 28 to 43C, would be confined to the limited purpose of sustaining the deductions provided for in section 206C. The level of profits and gains would be relevant only as explaining and justifying the level of deductions provided for in section 206C. So far as the percentages of collection at source maintained in section 206C are concerned, they cannot be said to be unreasonable or excessive since they would be only tentative collections subject to a final assessment. After the tax is collected in the manner provided by section 206C, a regular assessment will be made in accordance with sections 28 to 43C. Read down in this manner, section 44AC does not suffer from any constitutional infirmity.

Following the aforesaid judgment of the Andhra Pradesh High Court, sections 44AC and 206C, when read down in the manner suggested therein can be declared constitutionally valid.

The provision concerned is a provision in a taxing statute. It is open to the Parliament to classify the taxpayers on any rational basis and also treat the different classes of taxpayers differently. It is also permissible for the Parliament to further classify in a rational and non-arbitrary manner the assessees in relation to their conduct. The Parliament can legislate with respect to the assessees who comply with the requirements of law and extend such concessions as it deems fit to such assessees, which concessions it may choose to deny to those who have violated the law and such violations have been established by reason of the action taken by the authorities. It is in that background and with the object of laying down a special procedure for the assessment of the assessees who fail to comply with the law by not disclosing in full their taxable income and by not paying the taxes properly due from them that Chapter XIV-B consisting of sections 158B to 158BH was inserted in the Act.

The assumption made in the Scheme of the Act that a person who comes forward with the return or with further information after a search, does so only on account of the detection already made under the search and the likelihood of further exposure is a reasonable assumption and it can in no way be regarded as arbitrary. The special procedure provided in Chapter XIV-B is meant to apply to all such cases notwithstanding anything contained in any other provisions of the Act as provided in section 158BA(1) and other provisions of the Act, therefore, cannot control the contents of this Chapter except to the extent provided for in Chapter XIV-B.

There is no fundamental right in an assessee to commit breaches of the law. The right that can be asserted by one who has chosen to violate the law is the right to be treated in a manner similar to that in which other similar offenders are treated. Chapter XIV-B accords similar treatment to all persons belonging to the class to whom that Chapter is to apply. There is no discrimination therein among those who suffer such searches.

The petitioner’s argument that in cases where the assessee had paid advance tax, such payment would clearly indicate his intention to disclose his income and it could not be said that such person would not have disclosed his income, cannot be accepted for the payment of advance tax by itself does not establish an intent to disclose the income. The disclosure is to be made by filing the return. Even in search cases, where the time for filing the return under section 139(1) has not expired, income disclosed in the books of account is not treated as undisclosed income. All that is denied to the assessee in search cases is the opportunity to file a return after the period specified in section 139(1) and to claim that the income that he would have disclosed in a belated return is not to be regarded as undisclosed income. The reason for denying such opportunity in search cases is obvious. After having suffered a search, the assessee is not to be enabled to escape the consequences of his failure to disclose all his income by filing a return after the search and after the expiry of the time prescribed under section 139(1) and by disclosing therein income which had remained undisclosed up to the date of the search. Therefore, section 158BB(1)(c ) is not in any way unconstitutional.

The Indian Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1954 has no extra-territorial operation. Even if that law had extra-territorial operation, by the express words of article 245(2) of the Constitution, the law cannot be pronounced to be invalid on the ground that it would have extra-territorial operation. The Parliament was competent to enact the Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1954 which introduced sub-sections (1A) to (1D) in section 34 of the 1922 Act. The competence to the Constitution and not by reference to fanciful arguments. The Act 33 of 1954 is not rendered invalid by any provision of the Constitution. That Act is a valid piece of legislation.

The ITO is entitled to initiate proceedings under section 34(1A), of the 1922 Act if he in good faith has reason to believe the matters specified in section 34(1A)(i) and (ii ). He is not bound to disclose to the assessee the source of the information upon which he came to entertain that belief. The working of section 34(1A) of the 1922 Act will be wholly impossible if one is to hold that the ITO is bound to disclose the source of his confidential information or the name of the informant. The notice under section 34(1A) of the 1922 Act commences a quasi-judicial enquiry in which the assessee is entitled to appear and produce his evidence. In that enquiry the ITO will be bound to disclose to the assessee the material on the basis of which is seeks to find that the assessee's income to the extent of rupees one lakh or more has escaped assessment during the relevant years. Natural justice demands full disclosure of all the materials which the ITO seeks to use against the assessee in course of that enquiry, so that the assessee has sufficient opportunity to meet the case made against him. That stage of the enquiry will arise in this case after the assessee files its return and produces its account books. It is not desirable that the assessee should be informed of those materials at this stage. If the assessee is dishonest, the disclosure of the materials to this stage will be likely to lead to the manipulation of the books of account and other records. An honest trader who has not concealed his income has nothing to fear by submitting a fresh return and producing his account books pursuant to the notices issued by the ITO. If the assessee is an honest trader, there is no likelihood of its incurring fresh penalties by filing a fresh return and by producing its account books. There had been no violation of natural justice in this case and the proceedings under section 34(1A) of the 1922 Act upto this stage could not be quashed on the ground of any alleged violation of natural justice.

There was no merit in the appeal the same dismissed accordingly.

Note: The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

Every person earning taxable income has to provide for payment of taxes. However, certain situations may arise where the assessee may not be able to pay the taxes within 30 days as required by section 140A. But in such cases, if he properly explains the circumstances to the satisfaction of the ITO, he would not levy the penalty. Chapter 22 provides for criminal prosecutions in case of several matters and not only for concealment and evasion of taxes. Penalties are also provided by Chapter 21 in the case of failure to furnish information regarding securities, etc., failure to furnish returns or to comply with notices, failure to give notice of discontinuance as required by section 176(3), for filing a false estimate or failure to pay advance tax, etc. The said provision could not be held to be confiscatory. What is due towards tax cannot be said to be the "property" of the assessee since it is a debt due to the State towards tax, even as per his own return. The mere fact that it is not quantified by the department on that date would not make it any the less the tax due under section 140A(1). It is not necessary that every provision conceived in the interest of the revenue, i.e., made to ensure proper payment of taxes should be compensatory only and that no penalties can be provided therefore. The impugned provisions, therefore, squarely come within the ambit of article 31-C of the Constitution and even if petitioner's contention, that the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property conferred under clause (f) of sub-article (1) of article 19 is affected, was to be accepted, he was not entitled to raise any challenge. These two contentions of the petitioner must, therefore, fail. As to the contention of impugned provision being beyond the legislative competence; Entry 82 of List I of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution authorises legislation relating to taxes on income other than agricultural income. The contention was that it was under this entry that the impugned provisions have been enacted, the true purpose of Chapter XX-A is beyond the purview of the entry and, therefore, Parliament had no legislative competence to enact the Amending Act of 1972. Legislative power has been distributed between the Union and the States and some heads of legislation had been kept in the concurrent list under Schedule VII. The ambit of each entry is of the widest amplitude and law is settled beyond doubt that if by the pith and substance test the legislative entry supports legislation, a statute is not open to attack on the ground of want of competence. Undoubtedly, the Income-tax Act is a legislation in exercise of legislative powers under entry 82. So is the impugned provision. The impugned Chapter makes provision for imposition of penalty and for checking evasion of tax, because such a position is concomitant to the power to raise taxes. Such supplementary provisions are necessary for administering the statute effectively and for meeting the purpose for which the law is made. The scheme under the impugned provision for compulsory buying of the property at the stated consideration together with fifteen per cent thereof in the event of a clandestine deal to evade tax is not foreign to the law of income-tax. Parliament was initially satisfied with levy of penalty. By experience it appeared that that was not sufficient to meet the growing evil. The background of the legislation clearly indicates that as evasion of tax and black money became a growing menace, a high-power commission had to be appointed and, after probing into the matter, some of its recommendations were laid before Parliament and emerged in the shape of the Amending Act of 1972. The Amending Act in these circumstances cannot be held to be beyond the range of legislative competence.

The writ application failed and was accordingly dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.
