Attribution of income taxable under section 67(10)87 to capital assets remaining with the specified entity, under section 7288.

[R. 8AB of the 1962 Rules]

50. (1) For the purposes of section 72(5)89, the amount chargeable to income-tax as income of specified entity under section 67(10)87, shall be attributed to capital asset remaining with the specified entity in the manner provided in this rule.

(2) Where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, in excess of balance in his capital account, chargeable to tax under section 67(10)87 relates to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, the amount attributable to the capital asset remaining with the specified entity for purpose of section 72(5)90 shall be—

A= B×(C/D).

Where,—

A= the amount attributable to the capital asset remaining with the specified entity for purpose of section 72(5)90;

B= amount charged under section 67(10)91;

C= increase in, or recognition of, value of the asset remaining with the specified entity, because of revaluation or valuation; and

D= aggregate of increase in, or recognition of, value of all assets because of the revaluation or valuation.

(3) Where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, is in excess of the balance in his capital account, charged to tax under section 67(10)91 does not relates to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, the amount charged to tax under section 67(10)91 shall not be attributed to any capital asset for the purposes of section 72(5)90.

(4) Irrespective of anything contained in sub-rule (2) or sub-rule (3), where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, in excess of balance in his capital account, charged to tax under section 67(10)91 relate only to the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, the amount charged to tax under section 67(10)91 shall not be attributed to any capital asset for the purposes of section 72(5)90.

(5) The specified entity shall furnish the details of amount attributed to capital asset remaining with the specified entity in Form No. 2792.

(6) The person who is authorised to verify the return of income of the specified entity under section 26593 shall verify Form No. 2792.

(7) Form No. 2792 shall be furnished on or before the due date referred to in section 263(1)(c)94 for the tax year in which the amount is chargeable to tax under section 67(10)91.

(8) For the purposes of this rule,—

(a)

the amount chargeable to tax under section 67(10)91 shall relate to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, if the revaluation is based on a valuation report obtained from a registered valuer as defined in rule 56(f)95;

(b)

the specified entity shall not be entitled for the depreciation on—

(i)

the increase in value of an asset on account of its revaluation; or

(ii)

the recognition of the value of a self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, due to its valuation; and

(c)

the expressions "self-generated asset" and "self-generated goodwill" shall have the meanings respectively assigned to them in section 67(11)(b)96.

INCOME TAX INFORMANTS REWARDS SCHEME, 2018

LETTER [F.NO.292/62/2012-IT (INV.III)/26]., DATED 23-4-2018

The undersigned is directed to say that the reward scheme for informants, named 'Guidelines for grant of rewards to Informants, 2007', as was issued in 2007 vide Board's letter referred above, has been revised and "Income Tax Informants Rewards Scheme, 2018" has been issued in supersession of it with effect from date of issue. Further, guidelines containing procedure to be followed by Departmental officers for implementation of the Reward Scheme is issued separately. While the "Income Tax Informants Rewards Scheme, 2018" is for public circulation, the "Guidelines for Departmental officers" is for departmental use. Copy of the revised reward scheme is enclosed herewith.

Introduction

1. In supersession of the 'Guidelines for grant of rewards to Informants, 2007' and other existing guidelines on the subject, the following new reward scheme is hereby introduced for regulating grant and payment of reward to a person who is an informant under this scheme. A person can get reward up to Rs. Five crore by giving specific information about evasion of Income tax on income and assets in India and abroad. Identity of the informant shall be kept confidential.

Short Title

1.1. This scheme shall be called "Income Tax Informants Reward Scheme 2018".

Commencement

1.2. This scheme comes into effect on the date of issue.

Scope

1.3.This scheme shall regulate the grant and payment of reward to informants in cases where information is received by a JDIT (Inv) from the informant on or after the date of issue of this Scheme that leads to detection of substantial tax evasion under the provisions of Income Tax Act, 1961 and/or the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income & Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015. This scheme shall not be applicable to information regarding recovery of irrecoverable taxes as the Central Board of Direct Taxes has issued separate Guidelines for the same vide F. No. 385/21/2015-IT (B) dated 26-8-2015.

1.3.1. However, the 'Guidelines for grant of rewards to Informants, 2007' shall continue to be applicable in cases where information was received before the date of issue of this Scheme.

Where a resident of a Contracting State considers that the actions of one or both of the Contracting States result or will result for him in taxation not in accordance with this Agreement, he may, notwithstanding the remedies provided by the taxation laws of those States, present his case to the competent authority of the State of which he is a resident or, if his case comes under paragraph 1 of article 24, to that of the State of which he is a national. The case must be presented within three years from the first notification of the action resulting in taxation not in accordance with the provisions of this Agreement.

2. The competent authority shall endeavour, if the objection appears to it to be justified and if it is not itself able to arrive at an appropriate solution, to resolve the case by mutual agreement with the competent authority of the other Contracting State, with a view to the avoidance of taxation which is not in accordance with the Agreement notwithstanding any time limits in the domestic laws of the Contracting States.

3. The competent authorities of the Contracting States shall endeavour to resolve by mutual agreement any difficulties or doubts arising as to the interpretation or application of this Agreement. They may also consult together for the elimination of double taxation in cases not provided for in this Agreement.

4. The competent authorities of the Contracting States may communicate with each other directly for the purposes of reaching an agreement in the preceding paragraphs.

ARTICLE 26 : EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION - 1. The competent authorities of the Contracting States shall exchange such information including documents as is necessary for carrying out the provisions of this Agreement or of the domestic laws of the Contracting States concerning taxes covered by this Agreement, or for the prevention or detection of evasion or avoidance of taxes covered by this Agreement. Any information so exchanged shall be treated as secret and shall be disclosed only to persons or authorities (including a court, an administrative body or reviewing authority) involved in the assessment, collection, enforcement or prosecution in respect of, or the determination of appeals in relation to, the taxes which are the subject of this Agreement. Such persons or authorities shall use the information only for such purposes, but may disclose the information in public court proceedings or in judicial decisions.

2. In no case shall the provisions of paragraph 1 be construed so as to impose on a Contracting State the obligation :

(a) to carry out administrative measures at variance with the laws or the administrative practice of that or of the other Contracting State;

(b) to supply particulars which are not obtainable under the laws or in the normal course of the administration of that or of the other Contracting State;

(c) to supply information which would disclose any trade, business, industrial, commercial or professional secret or trade process, or information, the disclosure of which would be contrary to public policy.

ARTICLE 27 : DIPLOMATIC AND CONSULAR OFFICERS - Nothing in this Agreement shall affect the fiscal privileges of diplomatic or consular officers under the general rules of international law or under the provisions of special agreements.

ARTICLE 28 : ENTRY INTO FORCE - 1. The Contracting States shall notify each other in writing, through diplomatic channels, of the completion of the procedures required by the respective laws for the entry into force of this Agreement.

2. This Agreement shall enter into force thirty days after the receipt of the latter of the notifications referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article.

3. The provisions of this Agreement shall have effect :

(a) in Malaysia :

(i) in respect of Malaysian tax, other than petroleum income-tax, to tax chargeable for any year of assessment beginning on or after the first day of January in the calendar year following the year in which this Agreement enters into force;

(ii) in respect of petroleum income-tax, to tax chargeable for any year of assessment beginning on or after the first day of January of the second calendar year following the year in which this Agreement enters into force; and

(b) in India;

in respect of income in any fiscal year beginning on or after the first day of April next following the calendar year in which the Agreement enters into force.

Seizure and confiscation of goods

55. (1) If any officer authorised under section 55 of the Act, finds any goods in any office, shop, godown, vehicle, vessel or any place of business or any other building or place of a dealer which have not been accounted for in the accounts, registers, or other documents maintained in the course of his business, the officer may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, seize such goods. The order of seizure on Form-LL shall specify the description, the quantity and the value of the goods seized. A copy of it shall be served on the dealer or the person-in-charge of the goods.

(2) Any officer may, if security in cash is furnished to his satisfaction, order release of goods seized to the owner, and if he is not present, to the person-in-charge of the goods pending further enquiry, if necessary. The order of release on Form-OO shall be subject to the condition that if the goods in question are finally confiscated under sub-rule (4), they shall be produced within such time as may be required, failing which, the cash security furnished shall stand forfeited to the State Government without further notice.

(3) In cases not falling under sub-rule (2), if the whole or any part of the goods, seized under sub-rule (1) are of a perishable nature, the officer may sell them or get them sold, in public auction as laid down in sub-rules (8) to (17):

Provided that the notice of fifteen days laid down in sub-rule (9) below shall not apply to the public auction of goods of perishable nature and in lieu of the same, the officer shall cause adequate publicity through displaying a notice on the notice board of his office.

(4) Any such officer, after making such enquiry as he deems fit and after giving the owner of the goods, if he is ascertained, an opportunity of being heard, may confiscate the whole or any part of the goods seized, if he is satisfied that there is evasion or an attempt to evade tax thereon in any manner whatsoever. If the owner is not ascertainable even after the enquiry, the officer shall order for confiscation of such goods. A copy of the order of confiscation on Form-UU shall be served to the owner of the goods if he is ascertainable.

(5) The goods confiscated under sub-rule (4) shall be sold in public auction as laid down in sub-rules (8) to (17).

(6) If, on enquiry, under sub-rule (4), it is considered by the officer who seized the goods that confiscation is not warranted in regard to any of the goods seized, or if any order of confiscation is set aside or modified in regard to any goods, on appeal or revision, such goods shall be returned to the owner or any other person authorised by him if they had not been sold in public auction under sub-rule (3) or (5). If they had already been sold in public auction, the proceeds of the same less the expenses incurred in the sale, if any, by the Government, shall be refunded to the owner of the goods or any other person authorised by him.

(7) In case wherein a confiscation order has been passed in respect of any goods, the owner of which was not ascertainable before the order is passed, such owner of the goods, or any other person on his behalf may appear before the officer who ordered the confiscation and satisfy him with relevant records regarding the bonafides of the goods in question and regarding the reasons for his non-appearance earlier. If the officer is satisfied that there has been no evasion or attempt at evasion of tax he may order, for reasons to be recorded in writing, the release of the goods confiscated or if such goods had already been sold and delivered, the refund of the sale proceeds of the goods, less the expenses incurred for safe custody of the goods and other incidental charges. If the officer is not so satisfied, he may after recording reasons therefor, order that the sale under sub-rule (5) shall be proceeded with or that the proceeds of the sale already conducted shall not be refunded, as the case may be.

(9) A notice of fifteen days shall be given before the auction is conducted.

(10) Intending bidders shall deposit as earnest money a sum equal to five percent (5%) of the estimated value of the goods.

Decision of Income-tax Appellate Tribunal interpretating Dharamendra Textile Processors’ case 6.3 Based on the interpretation of Dharamendra Textile Processors’ case, department officials are of the view that the penalty is mandatory in each and every case of default. So the taxpayers were at the receiving end for some time. But taxpayers got some relief from some of the decisions of Income-tax Appellate Tribunals. In the case of Kanbay Software v. Dy. CIT [2009] 122 TTJ (Pune) 721 and ACIT v. VIP Industries [2009] 30 SOT 254 (Mum.), it was held that the judgment of the Supreme Court in Dharamendra Textiles Processors which holds that penalty under section 271(1)( c) is a civil liability and that wilful concealment and mens rea are not essential ingredients for imposing penalty cannot be read to mean that in all cases where addition is confirmed, penalty shall mechanically follow. In order to attract section 271(1)(c), there must be concealment the fact that the same is wilful or unintentional is irrelevant. But where an assessee genuinely claims a deduction after disclosing necessary facts, there is no concealment even if the claim is rejected. If penalty is imposed under such circumstances also there will remain no course open to an assessee to raise disputed claims and such proposition is beyond recognized canons of law. Similar types of decisions were also given under indirect taxes also.

Decision of Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Rajasthan Spg. & Wvg. Mills [2009] 20 STT 481

6.4 Proceedings were initiated against the assessees for non-payment and short-payment of excise duty. The demand for duty was confirmed on the assessees and penalty under section 11AC was also imposed. However, the Tribunal in its impugned orders had taken a view that there was no warrant for levy of penalty since the assessees had deposited the duty even before the show-cause notice was issued. In the instant appeal, the revenue relying upon the decision in Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2008] 306 ITR 277/174 Taxman 571 (SC), contended that mere non-payment or short payment of duty would inevitably lead to imposition of penalty equal to the amount by which duty was short paid.

The Hon’ble Supreme Court held that payment of differential duty, whether before or after the show-cause notice is issued, cannot alter liability for penalty, the conditions for which are clearly spelled out in section 11AC. From section 11A(1) read with its proviso, it is clear that in case the short-payment, non-payment or erroneous refund of duty is unintended and not attributable to fraud, collusion or any wilful mis-statement or suppression of facts, or contravention of any of the provisions of the Act or of the rules made under it, with an intent to evade payment of duty then the revenue can give notice for recovery of the duty to the person in default within one year from the relevant date. In other words, in the absence of any element of deception or malpractice, the recovery of duty can only be for a period not exceeding one year but in case the non-payment, etc., of duty is intentional and by adopting any means as indicated in the proviso, then the period of notice and the period for which duty can be demanded, gets extended to five years.

The Supreme Court further held that sub-section (2B) of section 11A provides that in case the person-in-default makes payment of the escaped amount of duty before the service of notice, then the revenue will not give him the notice under sub-section (1). This, perhaps, is the basis of the common, though erroneous view that no penalty would be leviable if the escaped amount of duty is paid before the service of notice. It, however, overlooks the two Explanations qualifying the main provision. Explanation 1 makes it clear that the payment would, nevertheless, be subject to imposition of interest under section 11AB. Explanation 2 makes it further clear that in case the escapement of duty is intentional and by reason of deception, the main provision of sub-section (2B) will have no application.

19. Excess share premium not taxable in hands of closely held co. if its shareholders are relatives: ITAT

[Vaani Estates (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2018] 98 taxmann.com 92 (Chennai - Trib.)] The assessee-company had only two shareholders 'S' and her husband. On passing away of husband, his shares devolved on their daughter 'V'. The assessee proposed to acquire an immovable property at approximately Rs. 23.09 crores. 'S' brought in money into the company in lieu of allotment of fresh 10,100 shares with a share premium of Rs. 23.31 crores.

The Assessing Officer opined that company had received excess price/share premium for the shares allotted to 'S' over and above the face value of shares. Accordingly, he brought Rs. 23.31 crores to tax in the hands of the company under Section 56(2)(viib).

The ITAT held in favour of assessee as under:

When 'S' introduced money into the company for allotment of shares at an exorbitant premium in contrast to its intrinsic value of just Rs. 10 per share, the benefit of such investment had only passed on to her daughter because there were only two shareholders in the company at that point of time. Had 'S' gifted the money to her daughter 'V' and thereafter if daughter had brought the same into the company for allotment of equity shares at face value, question of invoking of the provisions of section 56(2)(viib) would not have arisen.

Provisions of section 56(2)(viib) couldn't be invoked in the case of the assessee-co. because by virtue of introducing cash in the company by 'S' for allotment of equity shares with unrealistic premium the benefit had only passed on to her daughter 'V' and there was no scope in the Act to tax when cash or asset was transferred by a mother to her daughter.

20. No concealment penalty if assessee has bona fide belief that notional income isn't taxable: ITAT

[DCIT v. Shah Rukh Khan [2018] 93 taxmann.com 320 (Mumbai - Trib.)]

The assessee, Mr. Shah Rukh Khan, had received a villa at Dubai as gift and offered an amount of Rs. 14 lakhs as the notional income of the villa for tax in his return of income for the year under consideration. During the course of assessment proceedings, assessee claimed that Article 6 of India-UAE tax treaty doesn't expressly recognize the right of the resident State to tax the income from immovable property situated in the source State. Therefore, the notional income of the villa owned by him in Dubai could not be subjected to tax in India.

The ITAT held that claim raised by the assessee being clearly backed up by a bonafide belief on his part that the notional income of the villa was not liable to be taxed in India, no penalty for concealment of income could be validly imposed on the assessee.

21. Australia has taxing rights under Australia-India DTAA even if there is no provision in its domestic law: Australian Court

[Satyam Computer Services Ltd. (Now Tech Mahindra Limited) v. Commissioner of Taxation [2018] 98 taxmann.com 358 (FC-Australia)]

The Applicant, Tech Mahindra, had offices in Sydney and Melbourne through which it provided software products and information technology services to entities in Australia. Payments received by applicant for the services provided in Australia by the employees located in India were treated as 'Royalties' as per Article 12(3)(g) of the Australia-India DTAA .

Applicant argued that, though Australia was allocated the right to tax the 'Royalties' by the Indian Agreement but it could only exercise that right if it had the right to impose tax on those amounts under Australia's domestic law. As of now, the domestic law does not give any right to Australia to tax such income.

The Federal Court of Australia held as under:

The language of Article 23 should be given effect to according to its terms and the context. Article 23 provides that that income derived by a resident of one contracting States may be deemed to be income from sources in other contracting state for purpose of law of that other State. Therefore, royalty income was to be included in the applicant's assessable income because it was income from an Australian source by reason of Article 23 of the Australia-India DTAA. The Court rejected the argument that the tax treaties can only be used as shields not swords. It held that the tax treaties also provide standalone taxing power and independent imposing of tax to a particular income.

. Where the transaction was reported at a price lower than the market price by more than 15 per cent, Government had acquired powers to acquire the property at the declared price.

Constitutional validity of this provision was challenged in C.B. Gautam v. Union of India [1993] 199 ITR 530/[1992] 65 Taxman 440. The Honour-able Supreme Court gave well reasoned decision. In my submission, the ratio of that decision is as under: 1.Where there is an attempt at tax evasion, it should be curbed.

2.Law does not confer arbitrary or unfettered discretion to the authorities.

3.Where a provision in law causes natural injustice, Courts would read down the provision causing injustice; and read in provisions granting justice. Where this is not possible, the law has to be held to be invalid.

Now apply this ratio to TP provisions and see whether the TP provisions would pass the test of natural justice!

We may consider following steps for improving the quality of justice under TP. These are only brief outlines. Each thought can invite full length discussion.

Just as we have Double Tax Avoidance Agreements; there should be TP Adjustment agreements.

Corresponding adjustments

10. Present Indian law does not permit "Corresponding Adjustments". These adjustments can be of two kinds.

1. Where the Indian AE as well as the foreign AE - both are taxable in India. For example, interest or royalty payment. If there is an allegation of payment at prices other than ALP; adjustment in price for both the assessees should be allowed. Indian law permits the adjustment where Indian tax revenue is increased; and not the corresponding adjustment where tax revenue is reduced.

Is it natural justice? Is it decency and dignity that one expects from such a large and prominent Government like the Indian Government?

2. In an international transaction, one Government alleges under pricing by its assessee - AE. Consequently it collects higher tax.

Natural Justice demands that the AE of the other country should get a higher price as deductible expenditure. Its tax should be reduced.

Just as we have Double Tax Avoidance Agreements; there should be TP Adjustment agreements. These may look ‘absurd’ today; and "essential good tax law practice" tomorrow.

‘Corresponding adjustment’ is a different term from the ‘Subjective adjustments’ required to compensate for differences between the circumstances of two different companies.

Safe harbours

11. It is well known that TP compliance imposes a very heavy cost on the assessee. Not imposing all procedures for small assessees is one kind of safe harbour.

When both AEs are residents of normal tax countries - like say India and USA; the incidence to transfer taxable profits may be rare. (If one of the AEs has substantial losses; or if it is entitled to tax exemption; there is room for suspicion) When two normal assessees from two normal tax countries are AEs doing international transaction; much greater discretion may be used in making ‘Subjective adjustments’ in prices. In other words, there may be less scrutiny of the assessee and more liberties to him.

Red signals

12. When we call for ‘safe harbours’, it is equally justifiable to have ‘Red Signals’. For example, when an AE is dealing with another AE situated in a tax haven, the tax Commissioner would be justified in more investigative scrutiny. Here also, he may not draw any conclusions before investigation. But deep investigation may be justified.

Penalty - Three Levels

13. There can be a full paper on the concept that: ‘The adjustments between the price charged by the assessee and the market price is subjective. By definition there can be no final word on something that is subjective. Each person is entitled to his own view. And yet frauds cannot be tolerated.’

If we accept the above statement; on TP assessment, where the Assessing Officer makes an addition, there can be three alternative situations.

1. In genuine cases like Gillette and Pepsi in the initial years - where one established AE is subsidising another AE; the TP provisions should not be applied. No additional tax and no penalty.

2. There is no cause for subsidy. And there is a genuine difference of opinion between: (i) Assessee on one side - whose opinion is approved by the TP auditor; and (ii) The Assessing Officer on the other side.

The assessee recognises that he may be wrong; and pays up additional tax. The Assessing Officer recognises that he may be wrong. So no penalty. This position is accepted in some countries like Spain. No penalty under TP.

3. The assessee has committed an outright fraud. Deterrent penalty may be levied.

Such approach calls for discretion. And it should be allowed in TP. The present Indian legal provisions on TP fall short of natural justice. Introduction of adequate ‘Safe Harbours’; ‘Red Signals’ and reasonableness in penalty provisions can bring more justice in the Indian Law.

It is hoped that the Indian tax department and professional will sit together and evolve a TP code which in letter and in administration passes the test of natural justice.

Sri Jagatbandhu Mohanty, [1961] 12 STC 706, the Orissa High Court said that there are two important points of difference between the Bihar Sales Tax Act and the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. (1) Whereas income-tax for the assessment year is assessed on the income of the previous year, sales tax becomes liable to be paid immediately after each sale is effected though, for facility of computation and payment of tax, provision has been made for the filing of returns at the. expiry of each quarter. (2) Whereas rates of income-tax vary in accordance with the amount of income and therefore no one can be certain of what income-tax he has to pay at least until the accounting year expires, the rate of sales tax does not vary on the amount of taxable turnover and a dealer, therefore, can always be certain of what sales tax he has to pay as soon as he effects a sale. In other words, sales tax becomes payable immediately after a sale is transacted. It said further that the words 'due' and 'payable' are separate. Eventually, honourable high court came to the conclusion that it is, therefore, clear that to the extent of liability admitted in a return the amount of tax is payable before the dealer submits that return. FACTS

The writ petition was filed in the high court of Delhi by the petitioner. The petitioner challenged the section 145(2) of the income tax Act which notify us to follow the ICDS, empowered by the central government for computing the income chargeable using mercantile system of accounting under the head "Profit and gains of business or profession" or "income from other sources". The petitioner challenged the notification no. 87/2016 and circular no. 10/2017 demanding to follow 10 ICDS.

ISSUSE

Is part of ICDS which override the laws as mentioned in judicial precedents are need to be struck down or not?

HELD

The Delhi High Court held the updated ICDS and its specific provisions and also CBDT for issuing clarification as to be ultra vires the Act. And the section 145(2) has been read down by restricting the central government powers to only notify if the provisions made do not contradict the judicial precedents. The court also held that, under Articles 141 and 1447 of the Constitution, when there is a binding judicial precedent, the executive cannot supersede it unless the Act is amended by way of a validation statute.

ANALYSIS

As ICDS is mandatory to follow it was no longer possible for an Assessee to measure taxable income in accordance with the Act, as elucidated by Supreme Court and High Court judgments. Also many provisions in the ICDS were in conflict with the act or judicial precedents which in result becomes prevailing over the judicial precedents. So, accordingly there is a need to resist the powers of central government in notifying the ICDS in such a way that no override situation occurs. The decision taken by Delhi High Court to read down the section 145(2) of the Act is in accordance with the constitution. Further, CBDT clarified that in the event of a conflict between the provisions of the ICDS and the Act, the provisions of the act will take precedence.

PART II - TRANSFER PRICING

Need for transfer pricing provisions

7. At the outset it may be stated that Indian direct tax laws as a package are much better than most packages in similar countries.’ We cannot talk of ‘city countries’ or tax havens. For a proper industrial country, the Indian tax package is good. As stated in the beginning of this article - Part I; ‘good’ can always be improved. Our legal system is in the process of continuous evolution. Some specific attention needs to be paid to transfer pricing.

It is known that multinational corporations (MNCs) and even small business enterprises would like to reduce their tax liabilities by transferring their taxable income out of India to a country where they would face lower or ‘nil’ tax. This may be easily accomplished by under pricing taxable exports & over pricing imports of goods & services. This is called transfer pricing. Income earned in India is Indian tax base. Transfer of income to another jurisdiction is erosion of the tax base. Hence it is the right of Indian tax department to prevent erosion of its tax base through proper transfer pricing provisions.

India is following OECD and scores of other countries who have already introduced similar provisions. We are learning from the experiences of all these countries and making a better law.

However, the very system of transfer pricing presents severe complications.

The essence of transfer pricing (TP) is that:

‘whenever ‘Associated Enterprises’ (AE) enter into ‘International Transactions’, they have to justify that the price charged is an Arm’s Length Price (ALP). The concept of ALP involves a comparison with price charged by others. Now the Indian Income-tax Act and Rules made for TP have a built-in mechanism for adjustment of differences between the assessee and the other enterprises. This is a fundamental requirement. Every assessee is different from the others. Every assessee will have his own reasons to charge a higher or a lower price. These reasons may be bona fide reasons not involving any concealment of income.’

Each assessee will claim that there is no concealment of income. And yet there will be some assessees who have actually transferred their taxable profits out of the country purely with a view to avoiding Indian tax.

‘How to find out the difference between the two! How to deter the fraudulent and how not to harass the honest’ - is the issue.

The adjustment process involves considerable subjectivity. Let us see some illustrations.

When an Indian AE sells goods to another AE it knows that there is no risk of non-payment of price. It also has a perfect relationship and understanding. There is no sales and marketing cost involved. The demand is assured for a long period; ensuring capacity utilisation. Hence the seller will be prepared to charge a lower price. What should be the adjustment for all these factors! Whatever figures or percentages one person may give, can be challenged by another.

Pepsi & Gillette opened up subsidiaries in India. Their subsidiaries incurred continuous losses for the initial years. Throughout this period, the holding companies subsidised the Indian subsidiaries in several different ways. By its very nature, several products and services were either not charged or were under charged. And yet there was no question of an intention to conceal income. Legitimately, neither the U.S. nor the Indian Government can allege concealment of income.

Implementation of transfer pricing provisions - Need for discretion

8. It is essential that the Commissioner making the TP assessment recognises that he is dealing with several subjective factors. In subjective business matters, the business decision by the businessman cannot be challenged. A person who is not a businessman (This phrase includes auditor as well as tax Commissioner) is not competent to challenge the business decision of the businessman. Hence the TP provisions should be implemented with a lot of discretion and restrain.

Does our law permit non-application of TP provisions in the bona fide cases of Pepsi, Gillette and several similar cases? The Indian tax administration does not give room for discretion. In fact, the profession, the department and even corporate institutions are all unanimous that discretion should be removed and flat provision should be made in the law. Most of the penalties which were discretionary have now been made compulsory and flat with little discretion for the tax Commissioners. We have gone to the extreme where in somecases we do not even trust our judges. Even the Courts’ discretion has been done away with.

Indian Income-tax Act had another drastic provision. Compulsory acquisition of property under Chapter XXC. Capital gains tax payable on transfer of immovable property could be evaded by undervaluing the transaction. Where the transaction was reported at a price lower than the market price by more than 15 per cent, Government had acquired powers to acquire the property at the declared price.

Constitutional validity of this provision was challenged in C.B. Gautam v. Union of India [1993] 199 ITR 530/[1992] 65 Taxman 440. The Honour-able Supreme Court gave well reasoned decision. In my submission, the ratio of that decision is as under:

Act disallows a FEO from putting forward or defending any civil claim. Further, any individual filing a claim on behalf of a company or LLP among other things, wherein the FEO has a controlling interest shall also be disallowed from filing or defending claims. Section 14 violates the right of access to justice under Article 21 as there is no rational nexus between the offence and the punishment, as some corporate interests of the FEO may not have any connection to the economic offences in question.8 Proportionality: The declaration of an individual as a FEO entitles the authorities to confiscate the properties owned by the individual even if the property owned by the FEO is not the proceeds from criminal activity, and has been legitimately acquired. It allows the authorities to confiscate property belonging to the perpetrator which is not directly or factually linked with the commission of a particular offence under investigation.9 Furthermore, the Act also allows the appropriate authorities to confiscate the property of a FEO in excess of the amount owed by them. For example, it has been claimed by Vijay Mallaya that the assets confiscated from his firm under the Act amount to Rs. 14000 crores, as opposed to the Rs. 9000 crores that he actually owes.10

Generally, such due process safeguards act as a balancing mediator between the excesses of State power, and the rights of the individual. In the case of FEOs, these safeguards have been put aside to enable the prosecution of individuals who cannot be brought before the justice system. That being said, how far is too far? Rights of an individual may be curtailed by a statute if they are proportionate to the goals sought by it. Therefore, there is a need for proportionality tests to ensure that such confiscation down not interfere with the rights of individuals thereby addressing the risks that the punishment meted out on the accused through the statute is not too harsh as compared to their crimes.11

Draconian Measures as a Deterrent: One of the primary objectives of the Act is to have a deterrent effect on economic offenders by imposing harsh penalties as a consequence of becoming a FEO. The act relies upon the reasoning that if the punishment for absconding is high, then the deterrent effect would also be higher. Consequently, instead of attaching the property of the fugitive economic offenders like other the PMLA act, or the attachment of benami property, the Act contemplates the confiscation of the property of the person after they are declared to be a fugitive economic offender. Furthermore, the Act also does not make a distinction between the properties of the fugitive economic offender, and contemplates the confiscation of their property irrespective of the fact that it may not be proceeds of the crime or benami property. The goal of providing for such excessive punishment is the maximization of the deterrent effect.12

However, this justification is not adequate due to the fact that an individual who is orchestrating economic offences that are above INR 100 crores in value is a legally literate person who knows how to circumvent the law. Therefore, if there is a possibility that the properties of a FEO will be confiscated without following due process safeguards, then they may try to commit a crime that yields higher value to offset the cost of the assets that would be lost through confiscation. Alternatively, a fugitive economic offender could liquidate their assets before absconding in order to take those assets with them.

In such cases, the draconian measures of the Act are economically inefficient because they do not deter a FEO from committing economic offences, while also justifying the commission of said offences in a more damaging manner which puts a lot more revenue on the black market and out of the reach of the confiscating authorities.13

In light of the above, it is contended that the present Act is a prime example of the excesses of state power, wherein the safeguards protecting individuals from wrongful prosecution have been set aside, and the constitutional validity of the provisions of the Act is bound to be challenged. Therefore, a different approach is the call of the hour, which does not infringe upon basic constitutional safeguards.

A mechanism that shifts the focus from the individual to the properties of the FEO would be a more justifiable method for implementing the objective of the Act. Generally, this is how pre-confiscation conviction models sidestep procedural safeguards. In the UK, Part V of the Proceeds of Crime Act, 2002 deal with the confiscation of properties that have been obtained through criminal activity. However, as discussed earlier, the Act follows a 'property centric'14 approach rather than an 'individual centric' approach. In such cases, when a particular property has been proved to be 'proceeds of crime', then the government may confiscate such properties after giving a reasonable opportunity to the 'owner' of the property to defend their claim. In this scenario, an ex parte order would only be against the property and its legitimacy as opposed to a determination of the guilt of the accused. Consequently, a higher quantum of procedural safeguards would not be necessary as it would be a 'civil forfeiture'.

Constitutionality of the levy

7. The constitutionality of the imposition of service tax on the services provided by the practising chartered accountants was challenged by the Chartered Accountants Association of Gujarat before the Gujarat High Court in Chartered Accountants’ Association v. Union of India [2001] 115 Taxman 543 = 252 ITR 53 on the following grounds—

(a)The levy of service tax is a ‘tax on profession’ within the meaning of entry 60 of List II (State List) in the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. Since profession is nothing but rendering services in the respective professional field, therefore, service tax on services rendered by professionals lacks legislative competence, as ‘tax on profession’ is a matter assigned to the States.

(b)The levy of service tax on services provided by ‘professionals’ and not on the similar services provided by ‘non-qualified accountants’ is discriminatory and, thus, violative of article 14 of the Constitution.

(c)The levy will cost the clients 5 per cent (now 10 per cent and 12 per cent after enactment of the Finance Bill, 2006) more than what it would cost when the same services are rendered by a non-qualified person who is not covered by the levy. As such the client would prefer such non-qualified persons. Therefore, the service tax levy violates the freedom of profession guaranteed under article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.

After evaluating the arguments of the petitioner-association in light of the various decisions of the Supreme Court and High Courts, the Gujarat High Court upheld the constitutionality of the levy of service tax, replying the contentions raised by the petitioner-association in the following manner—

(i)Tax on services rendered by a professional is different from the tax on profession itself. The former is a tax payable each time the professional renders services for remuneration, but the latter is payable even if no service is provided. In fact the professional tax is required to be paid for the privilege of having the right to exercise the profession whether or not the person chooses to exercise such profession. Thus, the two taxes being separate, the contention that ‘tax on services of professional’ is a ‘tax on profession’ is unsustainable.

[Note : After the enactment of the Constitution (88th Amendment) Act, 2003, still to come into force) there is no reason for doubting the Parliament’s legislative competence regarding levy of taxes on services. The said Act has inserted an entry 92C in List I (Union List) to the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution which reads as ’92C. Taxes on services.’ Thus, the said entry confers on the Parliament the exclusive power with regard to imposition of taxes on services.]

(ii)Professionals rendering services are not at par with non-qualified persons rendering similar services, the quality of services rendered by the two being different. Further, it is easier for the State to identify the qualified professional and tax services rendered by them as against the difficulty in tracing non-qualified persons rendering services in similar fields. There the classification between qualified professionals and non-qualified persons is not violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.

Introduction

1. GST is the flavour of the season in India. All and sundry have been holding forth on how the introduction of GST would add 1 -2% to the GDP and that it is the panacea for all our economic problems. Political parties and Governments of all hues have largely backed the introduction of GST – the differences between them being only in the details. The industry in particular has been a consistent supporter of GST, although they may demur on some of the specifics. It is only the consumer who ultimately bears the tax, whose voice is not heard – but that is another story.

In this piece, we attempt to address a couple of fundamental questions that many of us may be asking ourselves:

1.

Why did taxing jurisdictions including India allow the Indirect Tax landscape to be littered with a whole host of taxes in the first place?

2.

How GST is going to be the Panacea which addresses the concerns and challenges that led to the litany of indirect taxes?

To arrive at the answers to above questions, the tax, the basic premises on which taxes are levied and the reasons for having Direct and Indirect Taxes1, have to be analysed.

Tax, Multiple Tax and its justification

2. Well, then, what is tax? To put it simply, tax is the price that we pay for 'public goods'. And, what are 'public goods'? Public goods are those goods/services which emanate from the collective wants of the populace and are enjoyed by them collectively – typical examples are preservation of internal order and protection from external aggression and in modern times, it extends to such facilities as roads, dams, sanitation, water, healthcare, education etc; as against this: 'private goods' are goods/services that are rendered by one or more private parties to other private parties in pursuance to a contract. The crucial aspects which distinguish 'public goods' from 'private goods' are:

Public goods being unsolicited, its price cannot be collected contractually and hence the need for a legislation to extract the same by authority of law; and

The distribution of the price of public goods on the populace who are the consumers of such public goods would have to be based on some formula/proposition which is fair and equitable and thereby acceptable to such consumers.

The process of seeking answers or rather addressing the questions posed by the above mentioned distinguishing features of public goods and the need to minimize the risk of default by the consumers of public goods, has formed the bedrock of the theory of taxation over the centuries.

Without getting into the nitty-gritties of the reasons wherefore the assumptions underlying the framing of tax laws have come to be accepted, we outline the same below:

Consumption of public goods is directly proportional to the income earned by the citizen/user of public goods – in other words, more the income earned, more the amount of public goods consumed; and therefore the need to adopt a progressive form of taxation whereby a person with a higher income/earning pays tax which is proportionately more than the tax payable by a person with a lower income. Herein lies the reason why high income individuals are taxed at rates higher than those imposed on lesser earning folks.

The risk of evasion of collecting tax at source/on income is significant, given the nature of human beings especially the more resourceful amongst them; and therefore the risk of evasion has to be mitigated by taxing multiple events such as expenditure, property, consumption of luxury goods etc, rather than attempting to collect all the taxes due at source/income. The underlying assumption being: no person can successfully avoid/evade all events of taxation; and therefore, at least some of the taxes that are due to the government would get paid.

The reader may very well ask, shouldn't we then do away with Income Tax and resort only to transaction taxes as transaction taxes are much less prone to evasion? The answer to that is yes we can, but that would lead to a regressive form of taxation and would result in a poorer person paying more tax as a proportion of his income as against a richer/high income person, simply because a poorer person tends to spend more of his income vis-à-vis a richer/higher income earning person and thereby ends up paying a higher percentage of his income as tax as compared to a richer person. And, therefore the need to spread the taxes due on income as well as expenses – it may be noted that taxing income and expenses together is not double taxation; it is just that the total tax due is spread between the two streams and has proved to be more efficient and equitable in practice.

These then are reasons why we have multiple taxes – in India the need to have multiple taxing events also arises because of the federal structure which divides the taxing powers between the centre, the states and the local government.

In sum, taxes on multiple events were imposed to spread the risks posed to government revenue from the very real threat of evasion. This answers the first of the two questions that we posed.

35. Need clarity on the levy of multiple penalties under the ITA 2025

The ITA 2025 has omitted the expression "without prejudice" from several penalty provisions, e.g., Sections 440, 441, 443, 444, 460, 462, and 463 (corresponding to Section 271A, 271AA, 271AAD, 271AAE, 271H, 271J, and 271K of the ITA 1961). These sections deal with serious defaults, such as failure to maintain books, false entries, incorrect reporting, TDS/TCS statement defaults and incorrect certifications, etc. In the absence of this phrase, it has become unclear and ambiguous whether any other provisions of the ITA 2025 are still fully effective or whether these provisions will override or conflict with any other penalty provision of the ITA 2025.

This omission has created ambiguity, as taxpayers may contend that only one specific penalty should apply for a particular contravention, thereby precluding other penalties arising from the same transaction or its consequences. This is especially relevant where the same default can trigger dual penalties. The lack of explicit statutory guidance increases the risk of interpretational disputes, inconsistent enforcement, and litigation.

It is therefore recommended that the ITA 2025 be suitably amended or clarified to explicitly state the legislative intent on whether multiple penalties can be levied for the same default. Clear drafting will ensure certainty, uniform application of penalty provisions, and effective deterrence, while avoiding unnecessary litigation.

36. Start-ups may be penalised for not fulfilling conditions after claiming the deduction

Section 140 of ITA 2025 [Corresponds to Section 80-IAC of ITA 1961] does not contain any provision to withdraw the deduction if the start-up fails to fulfil the prescribed conditions. It is apprehended that an amendment could be made to Section 140 to withdraw the deduction if the assessee company fails to comply with the conditions prescribed in the DPIIT's notification.

37. Prosecution for wilful attempt to evade payment of tax should be contingent upon assessment

Section 478 of ITA 2025 [corresponding to Section 276C of ITA 1961] is widely used to initiate prosecution proceedings. The basic difference between sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of Section 478 is that the former is attracted in cases where there is a wilful attempt to evade any tax, penalty or interest, whereas the latter is attracted when there is a wilful attempt to evade the payment of tax, penalty or interest.

The logical corollary is that to attract the provision of Section 478(2), there should be an already determined tax, the payment of which is wilfully evaded by the assessee. However, the existence of a pre-determined tax is not a condition to be satisfied for attracting the provision of Section 478(1).

It is also stated that both sections use the word "wilfully". However, the word 'wilfully' is not defined and is thus left to the officer's discretion. Thus, to remove the ambiguity, the following changes should be proposed under Section 478.

(a)

A provision should be inserted that sub-section (2) of Section 478 shall not apply unless the assessment determining the tax demand is made.

(b)

A provision should be inserted that sub-section (2) of Section 478 shall not apply if the appellate authority has provided the relief to the assessee in regard to the alleged tax evaded as referred to in sub-section (1) of Section 478.

In other words, the prosecution under Section 478(2) should be linked with the assessment outcome.

38. Prosecution on failure to furnish the return of income should be launched only in proven cases

A prosecution is launched under Section 479 [Corresponds to Section 276CC of ITA 1961] if a person fails to furnish the return of income, which he is required to furnish under Section 263(1)(a) [Corresponds to Section 139(1) of ITA 1961] or in pursuance of a notice issued by the Income-tax authorities. Such an offence is punishable with rigorous imprisonment of 3 months to 7 years and with a fine.

However, if the same manufacturer sets-up a separate trading company within Gujarat and initially sells the same to the trading company and, subsequently, trading company makes inter-State sale, as trading company is covered by Section 15(b), full input tax credit will be allowed. Declared goods are truly goods of special importance.

5. Arguments against the amnesty schemes

5.1 These schemes may not withstand the judicial scrutiny - Any amnesty scheme, if floated, may not withstand the judicial scrutiny because of the decisions of the Supreme Court in the cases of (i) R.K. Garg v. Union of India [1982] 133 ITR 239/[1981] 7 Taxman 53 concerning Special Bearer Bonds Act, 1981; and (ii) All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India [1998] 231 ITR 24/98 Taxman 446 (SC), relating to VDIS, 1997. In these decisions, though the constitutional validity of voluntary disclosures with immunity from penal provisions has been upheld, yet a democratically elected government has not to take technical pleas in such matters. It has to assess the overall moral and social impact of such decisions. From these angles, the proposal of floating any Income-tax Amnesty Scheme or even interest-free bearer bonds would be objectionable for the following reasons:-

(a)

Any scheme for voluntary disclosure, prima facie, seems to be immoral in the sense that it would provide immunities and exemptions to dishonest taxpayers vis-à-vis those who have discharged their tax obligations honestly and religiously and on this count, it would be an unreasonable measure. In this context, it may be useful to quote from the dissenting observations of A.C. Gupta, J. in the R.K. Garg's case (supra) concerning special bearer bonds. He has said:-

"It has been held by this Court in E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu AIR 1974 SC 555 and Smt. Menaka Gandhi v. Union of India AIR 1978 SC 597, that the principle of reasonableness does not exclude notions of morality and ethics…."

(b)

Resorting to amnesty schemes with immunities from interest, penalties and prosecutions is clear acceptance from the Govt.'s side that it has lost heart and as no means to check tax evasion and black money. Hence, begging from the taxpayers on their terms is imperative to augment funds. Such an approach would project a very poor image of the Govt. amongst the taxpayers and would be a great setback for voluntary compliances.

(c)

It is time that tax evasion is considered as a crime against the society - not merely a civil offence - and should be dealt with on that basis. On this reasoning, no one would approve of immunity to a thief, who steals someone's money and makes it available to the Govt. for its use for sometime [like in the case of bearer bonds] and on that basis, gets the money back for his use without any punishment.

(d)

The issues that arise in the context of amnesty/disclosure schemes are: Can fair minded, reasonable, unbiased and resolute men, who are not swayed by emotion or prejudice regard such scheme with equanimity and call it reasonable, just and fair, regard it as providing equal treatment and protection in the defence of the rights of being treated equally, which is expected of a sovereign democratic republic? The answers to these queries had to be an obvious NO.

(e)

Any amnesty scheme in any form would have deleterious effect on the level of compliance among the taxpayers and on the morale of the tax administration.

(f)

The operation of special bearer bonds scheme in the past has shown that such bonds help in generating more black money and these get freely traded at a premium by unscrupulous taxpayers, giving an impression to the honest taxpayers that dishonest taxpayers have been given the liberty by the Govt. to openly flaunt their immunity and wealth. Should the Govt. permit them to openly flaunt their immunity and wealth?

LAW - SUPREME COURT’S DECISION

9. Let us see the Indian law on the issue of natural justice.

Indian Income-tax Act had another drastic provision. Compulsory acquisition of property under Chapter XXC. Capital gains tax payable on transfer of immovable property could be evaded by undervaluing the transaction. Where the transaction was reported at a price lower than the market price by more than 15 per cent, Government had acquired powers to acquire the property at the declared price. Constitutional validity of this provision was challenged in C.B. Gautam v. Union of India [1993] 199 ITR 530/[1992] 65 Taxman 440 . The Hon’ble Supreme Court gave well reasoned decision. In my submission, the ratio of that decision is as under:

1.Where there is an attempt at tax evasion, it should be curbed.

2.Law does not confer arbitrary or unfettered discretion to the authorities.

3.Where a provision in law causes natural injustice, Courts would read down the provision causing injustice; and read in provisions granting justice. Where this is not possible, the law has to be held to be invalid.

Now apply this ratio to TP provisions and see whether the TP provisions would pass the test of natural justice!

We may consider following steps for improving the quality of justice under TP. These are only brief outlines. Each thought can invite full length discussion.

CORRESPONDING ADJUSTMENTS

10. Present Indian law does not permit "Corresponding Adjustments". These adjustments can be of two kinds.

Just as we have Double Tax Avoidance Agreem-ents; there should be TP Adjustment agreements.

1.Where the Indian AE as well as the foreign AE - both are taxable in India. For example, interest or royalty payment. If there is an allegation of payment at prices other than ALP; adjustment in price for both the assessees should be allowed. Indian law permits the adjustment where Indian tax revenue is increased; and not the corresponding adjustment where tax revenue is reduced.

Is it natural justice? Is it decency and dignity that one expects from such a large and prominent Government like the Indian Government?

2. In an international transaction, one Government alleges under pricing by its assessee - AE. Consequently it collects higher tax.

Natural Justice demands that the AE of the other country should get a higher price as deductible expenditure. Its tax should be reduced.

Just as we have Double Tax Avoidance Agreements; there should be TP Adjustment agreements. These may look ‘absurd’ today; and "essential good tax law practice" tomorrow.

‘Corresponding adjustment’ is a different term from the ‘Subjective adjustments’ required to compensate for differences between the circumstances of two different companies.

SAFE HARBOURS

11. It is well known that TP compliance imposes a very heavy cost on the assessee. Not imposing all procedures for small assessees is one kind of safe harbour.

When both AEs are residents of normal tax countries - like say India and USA; the incidence to transfer taxable profits may be rare. (If one of the AEs has substantial losses; or if it is entitled to tax exemption; there is room for suspicion) When two normal assessees from two normal tax countries are AEs doing international transaction; much greater discretion may be used in making ‘Subjective adjustments’ in prices. In other words, there may be less scrutiny of the assessee and more liberties to him.

RED SIGNALS

12. When we call for ‘safe harbours’, it is equally justifiable to have ‘Red Signals’. For example, when an AE is dealing with another AE situated in a tax haven, the tax Commissioner would be justified in more investigative scrutiny. Here also, he may not draw any conclusions before investigation. But deep investigation may be justified.

PENALTY - THREE LEVELS

13. There can be a full paper on the concept that: ‘The adjustments between the price charged by the assessee and the market price is subjective. By definition there can be no final word on something that is subjective. Each person is entitled to his own view. And yet frauds cannot be tolerated.’

If we accept the above statement; on TP assessment, where the Assessing Officer makes an addition, there can be three alternative situations.

1. In genuine cases like Gillette and Pepsi in the initial years - where one established AE is subsidising another AE; the TP provisions should not be applied. No additional tax and no penalty.

2. There is no cause for subsidy. And there is a genuine difference of opinion between: (i) Assessee on one side - whose opinion is approved by the TP auditor; and (ii) The Assessing Officer on the other side.

The assessee recognises that he may be wrong; and pays up additional tax. The Assessing Officer recognises that he may be wrong. So no penalty. This position is accepted in some countries like Spain. No penalty under TP.

3. The assessee has committed an outright fraud. Deterrent penalty may be levied.

Such approach calls for discretion. And it should be allowed in TP. The present Indian legal provisions on TP fall short of natural justice. Introduction of adequate ‘Safe Harbours’; ‘Red Signals’ and reasonableness in penalty provisions can bring more justice in the Indian Law.

In the case of Shriram Properties Ltd. v. CST [2007] 7 STT 131 (Kar.), the petitioner was engaged in activity of construction of complexes. The Government issued an exemption Notification No. 1/2006-ST, dated 1-3-2006, under which certain concession is extended to various classes of service providers, including the service provider in construction of complexes activities. However, the proviso to that notification provides that the benefit of the notification will not be available in cases where CENVAT credit of duty on inputs or capital goods, or CENVAT credit of service tax on input services used for providing such taxable service, has been taken under provisions of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The petitioner being aggrieved by the said proviso to the notification filed petition, contending that the notification brought about artificial classifications, in the sense that those who have not availed of the CENVAT credit facilities are given the benefit of the notification but those who have availed of the same are deprived of the benefit of the notification and, thus, the notification is discriminatory and bad, in law. The High Court of Karnataka held that the notification has never the effect of either enhancing the tax liability of the petitioner, nor did it per se discriminate against the petitioner. A concession which is subject to a condition, as under the instant notification, in the sense that, a person claiming benefit under one particular provision is not entitled to benefit under the other, cannot be said to be a discriminatory provision. There is no scope for striking down a notification of this nature which, if at all, is to be examined and understood as a whole and not in piecemeal. The exemption notification always comes subject to the condition, to which the exemption is granted. There is no question of the Court dissecting the notification of this nature to extend the benefit and not to insist on compliance of the condition for a particular assessee. It is for the Legislature to take care of the class of persons to which certain benefits are to be extended and in what manner, etc. Thus, according to the High Court the notification does not create any discrimination which necessitates the notification itself to be quashed.

DR. YOGENDRA KR. VERMA*

SERVICE TAX - ITS CONSTITUTIONALITY AND ADMINISTRATIVE CHALLENGES

Each country evolved a taxation system on services adopting either comprehensive approach or selective approach, depending upon socio-economic compulsion. While most of the developed countries tax all the services with very few and limited exemption, some of the developing countries tax selected services only and India has also adopted a selective approach to taxation of services. The Finance Act, 1994 imposed service tax only on three subjects, but as on date almost hundred subjects have come under the net of service tax. Through this write-up, the author has explained constitutional validity of service tax and administrative challenges faced by it. He is of view that as service tax is important from the viewpoint of neutrality in taxation, well synchronized taxation on manufacturing, trade (domestic and international) and service without giving rise to cascading effect of taxation would be an ideal approach worth pursuing in the immediate future. He has also given a list of suggestions which according to him should be attended urgently to improve the administration of service tax in the country.

Introduction

1. The object of monetary policy is to establish equilibrium between the available resources and the Government expenditure by framing of fiscal policy that aims at growth of the economy and social prosperity, such an ideal condition, however, unfortunately, is hard to achieve. The countries that gained independence after the end of Second World War were poor and undeveloped countries. India also fell into this category. The priorities thrown open to our nation centered around faster and balanced growth of economy directed towards narrowing the gap in social and economic imbalance plaguing our country for centuries.

Services constitute a very heterogeneous spectrum of economic activities. The share of services sector in real GDP (Gross Domestic Product) in India has surpassed that of agriculture and industry at a relatively faster pace as compared to other industrialized nations. Service sector has become the main contributor to the GDP not merely in the developed economies like USA (71%), Japan (60%), UK (67%), but also in developing economies like China (33%), Indonesia (41%), Pakistan (50%) and Brazil (56%). Service sector not only occupies major chunk of the GDP that is around 52 per cent in India, but also the growth rate of economic activities in the service sector is faster. In any welfare State, it is the prime responsibility of the Government to fulfil the increasing developmental needs of the country and its people by way of public expenditure. India being developing economy is striving to fulfil the obligation of a welfare State within its limited resources. In developed economies, consumption of goods and services is treated alike. The Government’s prime sources of revenue are direct and indirect taxes. Collection of revenue through direct taxes is a problem in developing nations due to a narrow tax base with individual income disparities being high. Further, there is a persisting tendency to evade the direct taxes in India. On the other hand, indirect taxes are hidden in the cost of goods and services and it is more convenient to collect indirect taxes and the cost of collection is also comparatively less. Central excise duties on the goods manufactured in India and custom duties on imported goods constitute the two major sources of indirect taxes in India. But revenue receipt from custom and excise are on the decline due to WTO commitments and rationalization of commodities duty. This is one of the reasons of extending the tax base to the service sector to improve the revenue productivity and efficiency of our domestic tax system. It is also necessary from the point of view of evolving a coordinated system of domestic indirect taxation on goods and services.

It is also well-known that services institute a larger proportion of the consumption of rich rather than of the poor as the demand for services is income elastic. Each country evolved a taxation system on services adopting either a comprehensive approach or selective approach, depending upon the socio-economic compulsion. While most of the developed countries tax all the services with very few and limited exemption, some of the developing countries tax selected services only and India has also adopted a selective approach to taxation of services.

Legislative history

2. Dr. Manmohan Singh, the then Union Finance Minister, in his Budget speech for the year 1994-95 introduced the new concept of service tax and stated that "there is no sound reason for exempting services from taxation, therefore, I propose to make a modest effort in this direction by imposing a tax on services of telephones, non-life insurance and stock brokers." In Budget speech 1994, the Finance Minister, giving the reason behind imposition of service tax, said:

"87. Over the years, while attempts have been made to widen the base for domestic indirect taxes, the service sector has not been subjected to taxation. Yet this sector accounts for about 40 per cent of our GDP and is showing strong growth. There is no sound reason for exempting services from taxation, when goods are taxed and many countries treat good and services alike for tax purposes...."1

What is Entry Tax?

1. Entry tax is a tax on goods that enter a State by way of inter-State purchases, branch transfers, consignment sales, and/or imports from outside the country, for consumption, use or sale within the State.

It is imposed by a State Govt. in pursuance of powers conferred under Entry 52, List II of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India which provides as follows:

"Taxes on entry of goods into a local area for consumption, use or sale therein."

Many States currently levy an entry tax on select commodities. Most of the States give 100% set off against VAT for entry tax payment. There are a few States where set off is restricted which results in cascading effect.

Constitutional Validity

2. Constitutional validity of Entry Tax was always in question and was challenged before various Courts on the ground that tax was not compensatory in nature and levy violated clauses of article 301 of the Constitution. On the other hand government always defended by saying that entry tax was a differential tax and non-discriminatory in nature as per Article 304(a) of the Constitution and was compensatory in nature as per Article 304(b) of the Constitution and, hence, did not violate the provisions of Article 301 of the Constitution of India empowering free trade and commerce in the country.

2.1 Background - Validity of Entry Tax vis-à-vis Article 301 arose first when an appeal was filed in the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Atiabari Tea Co. Ltd. v. State of Assam AIR 1961 SC 48.

It was held that taxing laws are not excluded from the operation of Article 301, which means that tax laws can and do amount to restrictions on the freedom guaranteed to trade under Part XIII of the Constitution. However, the prohibition on free trade was not an absolute one. Statutes restrictive of trade can avoid invalidation if they comply with Article 304(a) or (b).

Hence, vide this judgment, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has confirmed that even tax legislation would have to bear the scrutiny of Part - XIII and in case the tax legislation infringes the Part XIII of the Constitution, then the same will be held invalid and unconstitutional.

In that case, it was held that the impugned Act had put a direct restriction on the freedom of trade, and since the State Legislature had not complied with the provisions of Article 304(b), the Act was declared void.

Part XIII of the Constitution deals with Trade and Commerce and Intercourse within the territory of India.

2.2 Relevant provisions of the Part - XIII - The relevant provisions are reproduced below:

"Article 301-Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse.

Subject to the other provisions of this Part, trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall be free.

Article 302-Power of Parliament to impose restrictions on trade

The Parliament may impose restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse between one State and another or within any part of the territory of India as may be required in the public interest.

Article 303-Restrictions on the legislative powers of the Union and of the States with regard to trade and commerce.

(1)

Notwithstanding anything in article 302, neither Parliament nor the Legislature of a State shall have power to make any law giving, or authorising the giving of, any preference to one State over another, or making, or authorising the making of, any discrimination between one State and another, by virtue of any entry relating to trade and commerce in any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule.

(2)

Nothing in clause (1) shall prevent Parliament from making any law giving, or authorising the giving of, any preference or making, or authorising the making of, any discrimination if it is declared by such law that it is necessary to do so for the purpose of dealing with a situation arising from scarcity of goods in any part of the territory of India.

Article 304:

Notwithstanding anything in article 301or article 303 the Legislature of a State may by law -

(a)

Impose on goods imported from other States or the Union territories any tax to which similar goods manufactured or produced in that State are subject, so, however, as not to discriminate between goods so imported and goods so manufactured or produced; and

(b)

Impose such reasonable restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse with or within that State as may be required in the public interest:

Provided that no Bill or Amendment for the purposes of clause (b) shall be introduced or moved in the Legislature of a State without the previous sanction of the President."

6. Section 271C penalty cannot be imposed for belated or non-payment of TDS: Supreme Court

[US Technologies International (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2023] 149 taxmann.com 144 (SC)]

The assessee, a private limited company, was engaged in a software development business. It deducted tax at source (TDS) in respect of salaries, contract payments, etc., for the relevant assessment year. The assessee deposited the amount of TDS in instalments with a delay ranging from 5 days to 10 months.

During the survey conducted by the AO, the delay in depositing the amount of TDS was noticed, and interest under Section 201(1A) was charged. The words used in Section 271C(1)(a) are very clear, and the relevant words used are "fails to deduct." It does not speak about the belated remittance of the TDS.

As per the settled position of law, the penal provisions are required to be construed strictly and literally. The cardinal principle of interpretation of the statute and, more particularly, the penal provision are needed to be read as they are. Nothing is to be added, or nothing is to be taken out of the penal provision.
