7. The responses gathered from the targeted dealers and manufacturers have been analysed and discussed hereunder. This will reflect the implication of entry tax on trade and commerce.

7.1 Implication of entry tax on the registered dealers and manufacturers - Survey conducted over hundred registered dealers and manufacturers in respect of six selected commodities, namely, cement, marble, biscuits, gamocha (handmade Towels), plant and machinery and ENA (Extra Natural Alcohol) reveals, some positive and some negative aspects of entry tax which are discussed below :

u Entry tax - some positive aspects :

(i )Purchase of commodities directly from other States for consumption like cement from Meghalaya, marble form Rajasthan, gamocha from Tamilnadu and Kerala at comparatively cheaper rate results in trade diversion. When cement is directly purchased from Meghalaya for final consumption in Assam or as an input for construction purpose in Assam, the eventual VAT on cement goes to the exchequer of Meghalaya State. Further, the local dealers in Assam lose their market share. In this place when entry tax is levied on entry of cement from Meghalaya into Assam, perhaps the consumers would not feel encouraged to buy cement from Maghalaya. Thus, the consumer would be forced to buy cement from a local dealer within Assam. This way entry tax can be a counter-veiling measure to check this trade diversion and can protect the local dealers of the State.

(ii )Purchase of commodities from outside the State directly for consumption and not for re-sale, does not attract VAT. So the State Government does not get any revenue on such commodities. Entry tax on such imports can become a source of revenue to the State Government.

(iii )The dealers from other States may open their new branches in Assam if people stop buying from them directly and this may expand the trade and business of the region.

(iv )The trade development fund created out of the revenue collection by way of entry tax, if utilized for infrastructural development and other developmental activities in connection with trade, commerce and industry of the State, as announced by the State Government, will definitely pave the way for farther industrialization of the State.

u Entry tax — Some negative aspects - Entry tax does not only have the positive side, it has some negative aspects as well which are discussed below :—

(i )An analysis of the responses reveals that entry tax on raw-materials purchased from outside the State for manufacturing purpose will definitely have harsh impact on manufacturing units of the State. The raw-materials required like chemicals and wrappers for biscuit manufacturing units, ENA (Extra Natural Alcohol) for the manufacturing of alchohol, etc. are either not available in the State or if available, then they are comparatively costlier or not of good quality. Entry tax on these raw-materials is going to increase the cost of production of the local manufacturers and so they may not be able to compete with the prices of the finished products imported from outside for re-sale.

(ii )Entry tax on plant and machinery may affect the local manufacturing units adversely as all the plant and machineries required for manufacturing purpose are imported from outside the State. This may increase the capital expenditure of the manufacturing units.

(iii )Manner of levy and collection of tax is also not simple for the small consumers. Even small purchasers need to obtain road-permit from transport department which is not practically feasible.

(iv )The commodities carried through buses, passenger trains, etc., are hardly checked. Hence, improper entry of good through buses and trains may increase in number.

(v )The number of check gates and officials required for tax administration are not sufficient in number.

(vi )All the abovesaid negative aspects may pave the way for evasion of tax to a great extent.

11. State is a secured creditor for tax purposes under GVAT Act; Section 53 of IBC doesn't override Section 48 of GVAT Act: SC

IBC | State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Ltd. [2022] 142 taxmann.com 157/174 SCL 250 (SC)

In the landmark ruling, the Supreme Court held that the State is a secured creditor for tax purposes under GVAT Act, and Section 53 of IBC doesnot override Section 48 of the GVAT Act.

In the instant case, the following questions were placed before the Supreme Court:

(a)

Is State a secured creditor under IBC for tax purposes under Gujarat VAT (GVAT Act)?

(b)

Whether Section 53 of IBC overrides Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT (GVAT Act) or not?

The Apex Court held that the State is a secured creditor under the GVAT Act. Section 3(30) of the IBC defines the secured creditor as "a creditor in favour of whom security interest is created".

The court further held that such security interest could be created by the operation of law. The definition of a secured creditor in the IBC does not exclude any Government or Governmental Authority. Therefore, the State will be treated as the secured creditor under IBC for tax purposes.

In view of the above, the Supreme Court concluded that State is a secured creditor for VAT under GVAT Act, and Section 53 of IBC doesnot override Section 48 of the GVAT Act.

With regard to the overriding effect of Section 53 of the IBC, it was held that Section 48 of the GVAT Act is not contrary to or inconsistent with Section 53 or any other provisions of the IBC. Section 53 of the IBC deals with the distributions of the asset. As per Section 53, proceeds from the sale of the liquidation assets shall be distributed in the order of priority and within such period as prescribed in the provision.

Under Section 53(1)(b)(ii), the debts owed to a secured creditor, which would include the State under the GVAT Act, shall rank equally with other specified debts, including debts on account of workman's dues for 24 months preceding the liquidation commencement date.

The term "Secured Creditor", as defined under the IBC, is comprehensive and wide enough to cover all types of security interests, namely, the right, title, interest or a claim to the property created in favour of or provided for a secured creditor by a transaction, which secures payment or performance of an obligation and includes mortgage, charge, hypothecation, assignment and encumbrance or any other agreement or arrangement securing payment or performance of any obligation of any person.

In view of the statutory charge in terms of Section 48 of the GVAT Act, the claim of the tax department of the State squarely falls within the definition of "Security Interest" under Section 3(31) of the IBC, and the State becomes a secured creditor under Section 3(30) of the Code.

Introduction

1. It is common in enforcement provisions in a statute like levy of penalties to prescribe the minimum and maximum amount, setting forth the limits within which penalties can be imposed at the discretion of the officers authorized for the same taking into account the facts and circumstances of the cases where penalties are called for. In fiscal enactments like those relating to levy of taxes such as income-tax, wealth tax, service tax, etc., penalties are attracted for various defaults such as for delays in furnishing the returns, non-compliance of notices, failure to pay tax in time or for concealments, frauds, misrepresentations, etc. The legal provisions prescribing penalties mention the minimum and maximum amounts of penalties that can be imposed. For example, in the I.T. Act, 1961, section 271(1)(c) provides that for concealment of particulars of income or for furnishing inaccurate particulars thereof, penalties that can be imposed shall not be less than, but which shall not exceed three times the amount of tax sought to be evaded for such defaults. In other words, the penalty to be imposed cannot be less than 100% of the tax sought to be evaded, but shall not exceed 300% of such tax. Similarly, u/s 76 of the Finance Act, 1994 (Act) relating to levy of service tax from 8-4-2011, the amount of penalty leviable u/s 76 is not less than Rs.100 per day during which the failure continues or 1% of such tax per month, whichever is higher. The total amount of penalty leviable u/s 76, however, cannot exceed 50% of the service tax payable.

2. Whether in exercise of discretion, penalty can be imposed even below the minimum amount prescribed?

This issue came up for consideration of the Gujarat High Court in the case of CCE&C v. Port Officer [Tax Appeal No. 1367 of 2009, dated 8-7-2010]. The year for which the proceedings came up before the High Court section 76 of the Act provided for levy of penalty at Rs.200 for every day of default or equal to 2% of such tax a month, whichever was higher, not exceeding the amount of tax due. Similarly, penalties were imposable in respect of defaults mentioned in sections 77 to 79 also. Section 80 stipulated that despite sections 76 to 79, no penalty might be levied if the taxpayer proved that there was reasonable cause for failure.

2.1 Facts of the case - In the case that came up before the High Court, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the penalty imposed as per section 76 of the Act and the matter was taken to Tribunal - CESTAT - by the Central Excise Department. The Tribunal decided the issue by saying that penalty could be reduced below the minimum prescribed in view of section 80 of the Act. The issue was then taken to the High Court contending that the penalty could not be reduced below the minimum prescribed.

2.2 Arguments before the High Court - It was claimed before the Court that when the Act gives discretion to the authority of levying the penalty, the penalty amount could as well be below the minimum prescribed by the statute. It was argued that when section 80 of the Act (supra) gives discretion to the authority not to levy the penalty at all in cases of reasonable cause, the provision (section 80) could as well be construed to give power even to levy the penalty below the minimum prescribed, if the facts and circumstances of the case warrant such a decision on 'reasonable cause' ground.

2.3 Court's decision - The High Court observed that a plain reading of section 76 of the Act indicates that a person, who is liable to pay service tax and who has failed to pay such tax, is under an obligation to pay, in addition to the tax so payable and interest on such tax, a penalty for such failure. The quantum of penalty has been specified in the provision by laying down the minimum and the maximum limits, with a further rider for the maximum limit. The discretion vested in the authority is to levy minimum penalty as laid down in the section.

From the discretion it is not possible to read a further discretion being vested so as to entitle the authority to levy a penalty below the stipulated limit. The moment one reads such further discretion in the provision, it would amount to re-writing the provision, which is not permissible. It is not as if the provision is couched in a manner so as to lead to absurdity if it is read in a plain manner.

CIT [2007] 291 ITR 519/161 Taxman 218 (SC). Object behind enactment of section 271(1)(c), read with the Explanations thereto, indicates that the said section has been enacted to provide for a remedy for loss of revenue. In para 136 of the Union Budget, reference has been made to the provision stating that the levy of penalty is mandatory. In the notes on clauses also, the similar indication has been given.

Thus the Supreme Court held that above being the position, the plea that the rules 96ZQ and 96ZO have a concept of discretion inbuilt could not be sustained. As per Supreme Court, Dilip N. Shroff’s case (supra) was not correctly decided but Chairman, SEBI v. Shriram Mutual Fund [2006] 5 SCC 361 has analysed the legal position in the correct perspectives.

The Supreme Court approved the following proposition of law :

u Mens rea is an essential or sine qua non for criminal offence. A straitjacket formula of mens rea cannot be blindly followed in each and every case. The scheme of a particular statute may be diluted in a given case. If from the scheme, object and words used in the statute, it appears that the proceedings for imposition of the penalty are adjudicatory in nature, in contradistinction to criminal or quasi-criminal proceedings, the determination is of the breach of the civil obligation by the offender. The word ‘penalty’ by itself will not be determinative to conclude the nature of proceedings being criminal or quasi-criminal; the relevant considerations being the nature of the functions being discharged by the authority and the determination of the liability of the contravenor and the delinquency.

Under the first principle a casus omissus cannot be supplied by the Court except in the case of clear necessity and when reason for it is found in the four corners of the statute itself but at the same time a casus omissus should not be readily inferred and for that purpose all the parts of a statute or section must be construed together and every clause of a section should be construed with reference to the context and other clauses thereof so that the construction to be put on a particular provision makes a consistent enactment of the whole statute. This would be more so if literal construction of a particular clause leads to manifestly absurd or anomalous results which could not have been intended by the Legislature.

The effective date of the above section from Assessment Year 2017-18.

The Faceless Assessing Officer, Jurisdictional Assessing officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner may during the course of any proceedings under the Act, direct that any person who has under-reported his income shall be liable to pay penalty in addition to tax, if any, on the under-reported income. 1. CHANGES PROPOSED IN SECTION 115BAB

1.1. Concessional rate of tax restricted to income derived from manufacturing activity

A new Section 115BAB has been inserted in Income-tax Act by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019. This provision provided an option to pay tax at the concessional rate of 15% to the newly incorporated domestic manufacturing companies. As a manufacturing company can earn income under the 4 heads of income, the Ordinance did not give any clarity on the nature of income which shall be subject to concessional tax rate. Thus, there was an ambiguity whether the reduced tax rate shall apply on total income of the company or only income derived from the manufacturing activities.

To bring clarity on the issue, the Amendment Bill proposes that the income which is neither derived from nor incidental to manufacturing or production of an article or thing shall be taxed at the rate of 22%. This higher rate of tax shall be applicable only in respect of those income for which no specific rate of tax has been provided seperately in Chapter XII and such tax shall be charged on the gross receipt without claiming any deduction or allowance in respect of any expenditure or allowance.

Thus, assessee would be able to claim deduction of expenditure or allowance while computing the short-term capital gain arising from non-depreciable assets.

The short-term capital gain from transfer of depreciable asset would continue to be taxed at normal rate of 15% if use of such depreciable assets was incidental to manufacturing or production of any article or thing.

7. The mooting of an amnesty scheme for service-tax evaders is totally misconceived one and a wrong strategy. Amnesties cannot be solutions to the problems of non-compliance. ii.

The view that such schemes permit errant taxpayers to continue on their wayward paths is not supported by the large number of "repeat" beneficiaries of these schemes;

iii.

When such schemes are launched after a few years, they reduce the incentives for voluntary compliance in the first place and weaken the morale of both, honest taxpayers and the tax administration.

The Finance Act, 2016 introduced section 270A applicable from the assessment year 2017-18 onwards and it is a disconnect / departure from section 271(1)(c) which was in vogue for more than 5 decades. Previously, the reasons such as concealment of income / furnishing inaccurate particulars of income were subjected to penal consequences. The deliberate act of furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income only being liable for penalty got omitted much earlier and except for a few court decisions holding that "mens rea" as a fundamental requirement for slapping penalty, the penal consequence for concealment of income significantly hinged on the Explanation 1 to section 271.

Both the tax administration and tax counsels were tired of interpreting the very same legal provisions or the scope of legal provisions in the backdrop of various court decisions justifying levy of penalty or providing relief from penalty. The Finance Act, 2016 therefore provided some change from the earlier legal requirements for levy of penalty relating to concealment of income chargeable to tax. However, how draconian these provisions would be, was not visualized fully when it was in literal form in the statute book. When inexorable tax assessments got completed the taxpayers have to fret and lament how harsh these legal provisions are by putting huge financial burden on their purse.

This write up takes a snapshot of the legal provisions per se and how it could be damaging in certain real-life situations.

1. Under-reporting of income: The Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner may during the course of any proceedings under the Act, direct that any person who has under-reported his income shall be liable to pay penalty in addition to tax, if any, on the under-reported income.

Thus, the Assessing Officer during the course of assessment can initiate proceedings for levy of penalty. The Commissioner (Appeals) when adjudicating the matter can initiate penalty proceedings afresh for levy of penalty. Where the Commissioner (Appeals) deviates from the proceedings (i.e. alters the base for penalty) initiated by the Assessing Officer then the Commissioner (Appeals) is the competent authority to initiate penal proceedings. Also, where the Commissioner (Appeals) enhances the assessment he can initiate consequent proceedings for levy of penalty due to such enhancement and since his order of enhancement supplants the assessment order of the Assessing Officer, he is the competent person to initiate penal proceedings. The Commissioner can initiate proceedings for levy of penalty under section 270A when he invokes section 263 i.e. revision of order prejudicial to the Revenue.

2. Instances of under-reported Income: Sub-section (2) to section 270A lists out the following instances for under-reported income:

(i)

Where the income assessed is greater than the income determined in the ITR processed under section 143(1)(a). However, after the ITR is processed when the income assessed is greater than the income determined under section 143(1)(a), it is treated as under-reporting of income.

(ii)

Where the assessee has not filed ITR and the income assessed is greater than the maximum amount not chargeable to tax it is treated as under-reported income. Also, where the ITR is furnished for the first time under section 148 and the income admitted is more than the maximum amount not chargeable to tax, it is treated as under-reported income.

(iii)

Where the income reassessed is greater than the income assessed or reassessed immediately before such reassessment it would be treated as under-reported income. The quantum being the amount so enhanced.

(iv)

The amount of deemed total income assessed or reassessed as per section 115JB or section 115JC when it is greater than the deemed total income determined under section 143(1)(a).

(v)

Where no ITR is filed, the amount of deemed total income assessed as per section 115JB or section 115JC which is greater than the maximum amount not chargeable to tax. Where the amount of deemed total income reassessed as per section 115JB or section 115JC is greater than the deemed total income assessed or reassessed before such reassessment.

Entering into single mortgage deed by consortium of banks is a colourable device to evade stamp duty: Supreme Court

T.V. GANESAN

CS

Supreme Court of India in its Judgment in Chief Controlling Revenue Authority v. Costal Gujarat Power Ltd. [Civil Appeal No. 6054 of 2015, dated 11-8-2015] held that a mortgage executed by a borrower in favour of a security trustee would not be treated as a single document for determining the liability under the Gujarat Stamp Act, in the event the Security Trustee holds the security for the benefit of multiple lenders. This judgment is a marked departure from the position that only the form of the instrument would be looked at for determination of stamp duty. The Supreme Court has also looked at collateral evidences such as inter-se agreements between the security trustee and the lenders. This article highlights the important provisions of the stamp duty, the implication and consequences of the Supreme Court's Judgment.

Introduction

1. Stamp duty is a State subject and each State Government has its own set of provisions relating to payment of stamp duty payable on various registered as well as on certain unregistered documents. Further, certain State Government Departments, Institutions of Local Self-Government, Semi-Government Organisations, Banks, Non-Banking Institutions etc. which have been notified by the State Government shall ensure that proper stamp duty is paid on the various instruments which are executed in the State. Change is the only constant in life and the law-makers of India are also following the said maxim especially when it comes to Fiscal Statutes like the Stamp Duty Act. Every year certain State Government would amend or change certain provisions of their State Stamp Act. But here is a case due to Supreme Court's landmark judgment and its interpretation of the provisions of the Act and taking into account the collateral documents on the transaction, the stamp duty payable on an instrument increases.

Usually, stamp duty is payable on the instrument and not on the transaction. And in case an instrument e.g. a Mortgage Deed is executed between a borrower (Mortgager) and a Security Trustee (Mortgagee) then the stamp duty is payable only on the instrument. Syndicated loans are very common in lending transactions and in case of large loans consortium of lenders (various bankers) lend the money. But the entire syndicate loan transaction is governed through a single agreement between all the parties. This article highlights the position of law whether in a mortgage deed with security trustee to secure loans of multiple banks would be treated as distinct transactions and would be liable for stamp duty as if separate mortgage deeds were recorded for each bank but in reality only one Mortgage Deed is to be executed covering the entire transaction. The article will also analyse the implication of the latest Supreme Court Judgment on the transaction as it will impact the cost of borrowing and will have far reaching consequences on the settled principle of not going beyond the corporate veil.

Facts of the case

2. A company named Coastal Gujarat Power Ltd [CGPL] secured assistance from few lenders for setting up an ultra mega power project in the area of Kutch-Bhuj in the State of Gujarat. The lenders, i.e., the financial institutions totalling to thirteen in number formed a consortium as a Trust and executed a Security Trustee Agreement [STA] inter se appointing one Banker viz., the State Bank of India [SBI] as the Lead Trustee, called the Security Trustee. CGPL executed an Indenture of Mortgage for Delayed After Assets Deed with SBI, being the Security Trustee, mortgaging its assets as mentioned in the Deed itself. The said document was presented for registration before the Sub-Registrar, Mudra, by paying stamp duty of Rs. 4,21,000 and the Deed was registered.

Contention of the Revenue Authority

3. According to the Revenue Authority, CGPL i.e. the borrower was liable to pay a total of Rs. 54,62,000 on the said Deed and, hence, demanded the balance amount of Rs. 50,41,000 from CGPL by issuing show cause notice dated 5-11-2009. The said issue was forwarded for consideration of the Dy. Collector, Stamp Duty Valuation Organisation, Bhuj-Kutch under section 33 of the Gujarat Stamp Act, 1958. CGPL was given an opportunity of hearing and vide order dated 3rd April, 2010, the Dy. Collector held that the company, i.e., CGPL was liable to pay the deficit stamp duty with the amount of penalty of Rs. 250.

Revision application by the Company

4. The revision application filed by the company under section 53(1) of the Gujarat Stamp Act was dismissed vide order dated 28th March, 2011.

Appeal before the Gujarat High Court in Coastal Gujarat Power Ltd. v. Chief Controlling Revenue Authority [Stamp Reference No. 1/2011]

Readers may draw solace from the Madras High Court decision in the case of CIT v. Gem Granites [2014] 42 taxmann.com 493 (Madras) taking note of the apex court decision in the case of MAK Data (Supra). The assessee in this case admitted seizure of cash consequent to search under section 132 and the case of the assessee as regards quantum of assessment was dismissed by the court. As regards penalty the tribunal held that the onus to prove concealment of income is on the Department and it is not automatic. The Madras High Court took note of the apex court decision in MAK Data (Supra) and held that the burden is on the assessee to offer an explanation for taking out the case from penal consequences. It held that if the assessee has discharged onus by giving a cogent and reliable explanation and if the Department did not agree with the explanation the onus would be on the Department to prove that there was concealment of particulars of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income.

Therefore in spite of the decision in the case of MAK Data (P) Ltd (Supra) if the assessee gives a cogent and proper explanation, the burden would be shifted on the Revenue for classifying the case as misreporting of income.

Conclusion

Presently, when the ITR is processed under section 143(1)(a) and there is enhancement of income no penalty is leviable. However, once the assessment is made under sections 143(3), 144 and 147 then any upward revision of income or reduction of loss would expose the taxpayers to penal consequence except in certain cases provided in section 270A(6). The penal consequence could be mitigated with regard to under-reporting of income simpliciter by having recourse to section 270AA. However, instance of under-reporting of income due to misreporting is a heavy burden cast on the taxpayers. The penal provisions are not only to penalize the errant assessees but also to have deterrent effect. The quantum of penalty seems to be too much and that would only pile up the cases for litigation. Section 270AA may have to be expanded by allowing misreporting also by limiting the relief for one or two times during the life time of the taxpayers so that the tax realization is quick to the exchequer and the tax disputes are also kept in check for better compliance and administration.

ization of public-revenue. The possible reasons for re-introduction of entry tax are as follows:

Rationality of the study

5. As a part of reform of the indirect tax structure in India, VAT (Value Added Tax) system has been introduced replacing the age-old sales tax system of the country. Para-2.16 of the white paper circulated by the Empowered Committee of Finance Ministers suggesting to introduce VAT system was as follows:

"As mentioned earlier, all other existing taxes such as turnover tax, surcharge, additional surcharge and Special Additional Tax (SAT) would be abolished. There will not be any reference these taxes in the VAT Bills. The States that have already introduced entry tax and intend to continue with this tax should make it vatable. If not made vatable, entry tax will need to be abolished."

But entry tax has not been abolished in many States even after the implementation of VAT system specially in the consuming States like Assam, Orissa, Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh, etc.

The Assam Entry Tax Act, 2001 came into force with effect from October 1, 2001 but later on it was declared null and void in the judgment given by the High Court on November 16, 2006. Now with necessary amendments, the new Assam Entry Tax Act, 2008, has again came into force on and from June 1, 2008.

Imposition of entry tax in Assam when the talks are going on to reform the existing indirect tax structure making it more simple and transparent, is a matter of great concern. The taxing authority claims the entry tax as a measure to protect the local dealers and to check the diversion of trade whereas the manufacturers protest it on the ground that this will lead to an increase in their cost of production. Again lack of proper checking at check gates may pave the way for tax evasion to a great extent.

Hence, it is necessary to conduct a research investigation to ascertain the factual position and to see the genesis and rationality of introducing entry tax in Assam and also to see its impact on manufacturers, dealers, consumers and public at large.

Genesis of Entry Tax in Assam

6. Article 265 of the Indian Constitution has empowered the States to levy tax and as per article 267(2) the State Legislature by making a law can establish a new Act levying tax in the State.

The Assam Entry Tax Act came into force with effect from October 1, 2001 vide Notification No. FTX/146/2001/3, dated September 28, 2001. At the beginning the entry tax was levied only on 8 items. But later on, the No. of items on which the entry tax was levied gradually increased and reached up to 58 by December, 2005. No Presidential assent was taken for the levy of entry tax on these subsequent items. The aggrieved dealers and manufacturers filed a law suit in the Gauhati High Court. On this, the Single Bench Decision given on November 16, 2006 by the Hon’ble Gauhati High Court Judge, Mr. Anshari declared the Assam Entry Tax Act, 2001 as ultra vires since the original Act was in violation of article 304(a) of the Indian Constitution and further it amounted to violation of article 301 read with article 304(b) which says that no bill or amendment shall be introduced or moved in the Legislature of a State without the previous sanction of the President.

3.6-4 Constitutional validity of the Gujarat Tax Luxuries (Hotels and Lodging Houses) Act, 1977 and other similar Acts - Not violative of Article 19(1)(g) - Writ petitions were filed before the Supreme Court challenging the constitutional validity of legislations of different States, viz., the State of Gujarat, State of Tamil Nadu, the State of Karnataka and the State of West Bengal imposing a tax on ‘luxuries’ under entry 62 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India.

These relate to the challenge to the legislation by the State of Gujarat, viz., the Gujarat Tax on Luxuries (Hotel and Lodging Houses) Act, 1977, to the corresponding legislation of the State of Tamil Nadu, viz., the Tamil Nadu Tax on Luxuries in Hotels and Lodging Houses Act, 1981, to the corresponding Karnataka legislation, viz., the Karnataka Tax on Luxuries (Hotel and Lodging Houses) Act, 1979, to the West Bengal Entertainments and Luxuries (Hotel and Restaurants) Tax Act, 1972. All these taxing statutes, except for certain aspects individual to them, are analogous and the scheme of the legislation is substantially similar. The variations are in the differences in the criteria of classification of the hotels to which the Act is applied and the rates of taxes. The grounds of challenge are substantially the same. The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity as the tax on luxuries does not restrict freedom of trade or intercourse throughout India, and articles 14, 19(1)(g) and 301 of the Constitution are not violated.

Once the legislative competence and the nexus between the taxing power and the subject of taxation is established, the other incidents are matters of fiscal policy behind the taxing law. The measure of tax is not the same thing as, and must be distinguished from, the subject of tax. Mere existence of a tax or that it affects the earnings cannot per se be held to be violative of article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. A provision which is against evasion does not offend article 19(1)(g). The mere absence of the corrective machinery or existence of a provision imparting finality by itself, would not be conclusive so as to render the conferment of power on the authority per se unreasonable and arbitrary, rendering the provision unconstitutional.

Taxes can and do sometimes having regard to their effect and impact on the free flow of trade, constitute restrictions on the freedom under Article 301 of the Constitution. But the restrictions must stem from the provisions of the law imposing the tax which could be said to have the direct and immediate effect of restricting the free flow of “trade, commerce and intercourse”. It is not all taxes that have this effect.

Constitutional validity - The provisions of section 276C are constitutionally valid and does not contravene/violate the provisions of Articles 14 & 21 of the Constitution of India on ground that revenue is compensated with regard to delay in payment of tax or submission of return by making payment of interest [Dr. (Mrs.) M. S. Dhowani v. J. Ranganathan Second ITO[1992] 65 Taxman 541 (Mad.); Sonarome Chemicals (P.) Ltd. v. UOI[2003] 127 Taxman 31 (Kar.)].

Section 276C(1) and section 276C(2) - Section 276C(1) deals with evasion of tax, penalty or interest chargeable or imposable under the Act, which might include wilful suppression in the returns before assessment and completion. But section 276C(2) deals with evading the payment of any tax, penalty or interest under the Act. The words 'chargeable' or 'imposable' are not there. What section 276C(2) says is 'without prejudice to any penalty that may be imposable on him under any other provision of this Act, be punishable...'. Therefore, evidently, section 276C(2) takes in cases of tax evasion after charging or imposition. Evasion after completion of assessment also comes within the operation of section 276C(2). Section 276C(2) is so clear that at any rate it takes in the cases of evasion of tax, penalty or interest after assessments were made. Avoidance of tax is avoidance of tax liability under some manner as distinguished from evasion of tax whether before or after charging or imposition. It is not illegal as distinguished from penal evasion. Section 276C(2) deals with evasion after quantification. It becomes applicable only after income is assessed and the assessee attempts to evade payment [G. Viswanathan v. ITO[1987] 35 Taxman 66 (Ker.)]. Also see, Vinodchandra C. Patel v. In K.P. Varghese v. ITO [1981] 131 ITR 597, the Supreme Court had to interpret section 52(2) of the Act which provided that if in the opinion of the AO, the fair market value of a capital asset transferred by an assessee exceeds the consideration declared by the assessee by at least 15% of the consideration so declared, then such fair market value shall be deemed to be the full value of the consideration for such capital asset. Thus, section 52(2), on literal interpretation permitted substitution of the declared consideration by fair market value. The Supreme Court did not accept the literal interpretation on various grounds based on the language, the context, the Finance Minister's speech, etc., and also on certain general principles of law.

The Supreme Court observed as follows:

"section 52 is not a charging section but is a computation section. It has to be read along with section 48 which provides the mode of computation and under which the starting point of computation is "the full value of the consideration received or accruing". What in fact never accrued or was never received cannot be computed as capital gains under section 48. Therefore, sub-section (2) cannot be considered as bringing within the computation of capital gains an amount which, by no stretch of imagination, can be said to have accrued to the assessee or been received by him".

". . . .It is a well settled rule of interpretation that the Court should as far as possible avoid that construction which attributes irrationality to the Legislature. Besides, under entry 82 in List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, which deals with "Taxes on income other than agricultural income" and under which the Income-tax Act, 1961, has been enacted, Parliament cannot "choose to tax as income an item which in no rational sense can be regarded as a citizen's income or even receipt. Sub-section (2) would, therefore, on the construction of the revenue, go outside the legislative power of Parliament and it would not be possible to justify it even as an incidental or ancillary provision or a provision intended to prevent evasion of tax".

". . . .Sub-section (2) would also be violative of the fundamental right of the assessee under article 19(1)(f) - which fundamental right was in existence at the time when sub-section (2) came to be enacted - since on the construction canvassed on behalf of the revenue, the effect of sub-section (2) would be to penalize the assessee for transferring his capital asset for a consideration lesser by 15% or more than the fair market value and that would constitute unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right of the assessee to dispose of his capital asset at the price of his choice".

". . . .Sub-section (2) has no application in the case of an honest and bona fide transaction where the consideration received by the assessee has been correctly declared or disclosed by him and there is no concealment or suppression of the consideration".

All the aforesaid arguments are applicable in relation to section 50C :

(a)

It attempts to tax what may have never accrued or received.

(b)

It goes outside the legislative power of the Parliament since such fair value cannot in a rational manner be regarded as income/receipt.

(c)

It would hit a bona fide transaction, where there is no concealment or suppression of the consideration.

Having regard to the above it appears that there are strong arguments against the constitutional validity of section 50C.

In other words, the other provisions would not be affected or rather cannot be considered as in conflict with the provision. The inference is based on the following reasoning:

Broadly stated, section 115JB lays down:

◆ Substitution of SPT for income-tax payable [sub-section (1)];

◆ Providing machinery for computation of book profit [sub-section (2)];

◆ Saving determination of unabsorbed losses, etc. [sub-section (3)];

◆ Requires obtaining and furnishing Accountant’s Report [sub-section (4)]; and

◆ Application of the other provisions of the Act [sub-section (5)].

It would be appreciated that the section provides for the levy; machinery for computation; compliance with certain conditions, etc. How-ever, it does not provide for the charge, collection and recovery, assessment, etc. Accordingly, it makes the other provisions of the Act applicable. Accordingly, it’s a complete code. The substantive provision is sub-section (1). Effectively, it seeks to create a fiction, limited to levy of SPT.

The non obstante clause, read with sub-section (5), and in particular, the first limb thereof, namely, ‘save as otherwise provided in this section’ and the limited object of levying SPT, seems to have only a limited overriding effect; but otherwise it relies on the other provisions of the Act, for the effective levy and recovery of tax.

The fiction, thus, has a limited field, namely

◆ Substitution of tax payable by SPT; and

◆ Computation of book profit.

Otherwise, it appears that all the provisions of the Act including the provisions relating to charge, definitions, recovery, payment, assessment, etc., would apply in construing the provisions of section 115JB.

Constitutionality judged by generality of provisions

Law is judged for its constitutionality on the generality of its provisions and not by the freaks and exceptions it martyrs [R.S. Joshi v. Ajit Mills Ltd. [1977] 40 STC 497]. In the matters relating to taxing statutes, courts have conceded a much greater latitude to the Legislature, keeping in view the sensitivity and the complex nature of the economic mechanism and the difficulties inherent in the test providing a near perfect answer to all possible situations. The courts have recognised the need to grant greater play in the joints and greater amount of discretion and choice of the Legislature in matters relating to taxes and statutes imposing the same [Union Home Products Ltd. v. Union of India [1995] 215 ITR 758 (Kar.)]

The validity of the legislation is not dependent on its or the capacity of the Legislature which enacts the same, to cater all conceivable situations and to prevent harsh and undesirable effect. Legislation, otherwise valid, cannot be struck down simply because, in some extreme or freak cases, it would operate so unfairly as to make it look penal or confiscatory. The presumption that the Legislature is supremely wise and informed about the needs of the time notwithstanding it is not expected to envisage and provide for all conceivable situations which may arise in the course of human affairs. Its legislative measures are, therefore, to be judged not by the capacity of the enactment to cater satisfactorily to all imaginable situations, but by the generality of the cases and problems it aims and purports to solve to provide for [Union Home Products Ltd. v. Union of India [1995] 215 ITR 758 (Kar.)]. A law has to be judged for its constitutionality on the generality of its provisions and not by freaks and exceptions it martyrs [R. S. Joshi v. Finance Act, 2015

24.1 Penalty provisions

24.1-1 Penalty for concealment of income [Section 271(1)(c)]

Under the existing provision contained in clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 of the Act penalty for concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income is levied on the "amount of tax sought to be evaded", which has been defined, inter alia, as the difference between the tax due on the income assessed and the tax which would have been chargeable had such total income been reduced by the amount of concealed income. Courts have held that penalty under clause (c) of sub- section (1) of section 271 cannot be levied in cases where the concealment of income occurs under the income computed under general provisions and the tax is paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act.

In CIT v. Nalwa Sons Investment Ltd. [2012] 21 taxmann.com 184 (SC), it was held that when assessment was made on income computed under section 115JB and tax had been paid on income so computed, penalty under section 271(1)(c) would not be imposed with reference to additions that would have been made taking into account concealment made by assessee while making assessment under normal procedure.

In CIT v. Jindal Polyester & Steel Ltd. [2014] 52 taxmann.com 259 (All.) the High Court held that book profit disclosed by assessee for purpose of tax liability under MAT provision was relevant and not income determined under provisions of the Income-tax Act. When concealment of income did not lead to tax evasion under MAT provisions, no penalty would be levied.

In Unison Hotels Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2013] 40 taxmann.com 237 (Delhi) it was held that when taxable income is computed on book profits under section 115JB, there cannot be imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c) for additions made under normal provisions.

Tax paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC over and above the tax liability arising under general provisions is available as credit for set off against future tax liability. Understatement of income and the tax liability thereon under general provisions results in larger amount of such credit becoming available to the assessee for set off in future years. Therefore, where concealment of income, as computed under the general provisions, has taken place, penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 should be leviable even if the tax liability of the assessee for the year has been determined under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act.

Section 271 of the Act has been amended so as to provide that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be the summation of tax sought to be evaded under the general provisions and the tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. However, if an amount of concealment of income on any issue is considered both under the general provisions and provisions of section 115JB or 115JC then such amount shall not be considered in computing tax sought to be evaded under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. Further, in a case where the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC are not applicable, the computation of tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC shall be ignored. This amendment will take effect from 1-4-2016 and will accordingly apply, in relation to the assessment year 2016-17 and subsequent assessment years.

To give effect to the above, Explanation 4 to section 271(1)(c) has been substituted Explanation 4 provides that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be determined in accordance with the following formula—

(A-B) + (C-D)

where,

A = amount of tax on the total income assessed as per the provisions other than the provisions contained in section 115JB or section 115JC (herein called general provisions);

B = amount of tax that would have been chargeable had the total income assessed as per the general provisions been reduced by the amount of income in respect of which particulars have been concealed or inaccurate particulars have been furnished;

C = amount of tax on the total income assessed as per the provisions contained in section 115JB or section 115JC;

D = amount of tax that would have been chargeable had the total income assessed as per the provisions contained in section 115JB or section 115JC been reduced by the amount of income in respect of which particulars have been concealed or inaccurate particulars have been furnished:

1.4-3 The provisions of section 115JB - SPT, as discussed above, substitutes the tax payable. Accordingly, about its constitutional validity, there are two views. As per one view, the provision cannot be considered as valid, since the tax is not on total income. As per the other view, however, the tax is still on total income. The two views are stated hereafter with the reasons therefor.

As per the first view, for the purposes of levy, the total income is disregarded to determine tax payable. In place of that, 7.5 per cent of book profit is considered as tax payable. However, such book profit is not total income. Under the Act, as required by section 4, tax can be levied on total income. However, section 115JB does not levy SPT on total income and, therefore, it does not meet with the requirements. This view can also be supported by a decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Khatau Makanji Spinning & Weaving Co. Limited [1960] 40 ITR 189.

In that case, there was a charge of additional income-tax in respect of excess distribution of dividends under the applicable Finance Act. The Supreme Court held that section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1922 levied tax on income of the previous year and would not cover something which is not the income of the previous year. The Finance Act failed in its purpose - the additional tax was not properly laid upon the total income because what was actually taxed was never a part of the total income of the previous year. The Finance Act did not lay down that it should be taxed as the part of the total income.

The other view is that there is mere substitution of tax payable and therefore the tax is on total income. The reasons are :

The tax can be levied in terms of section 115JB read with section 4 of the Act. The provision reads:

13.3.2a In case of any assessee, where search is initiated on or after 1-7-2012, in respect of the undisclosed income of the specified years, the penalty is larger than provided in case of any assessee, where search was conducted prior to 1-7-2012. Against a penalty of 10% of the undisclosed income, the penalty is payable at different rates depending on the nature and extent of disclosure of the undisclosed income as follows:

13.3.2b It may be noted that for levying the penalty the section imposes an additional condition (when compared with Explanation 5 applicable upto 1-6-2007), namely, substantiation of the manner of deriving income.

'Manner', as explained in the Law Lexicon by P. Ramanatha Aiyar means: 'mode of action, way of performing or effecting anything, method, style the way of managing; the way of doing thing, the method of procedure; method or mode or style... '.

'Substantiates', Webster's New Collegiate Dictionary means:

'1: to impart substance to 2: to put into concrete form 3: to establish by proof or competent evidence'.

Accordingly, in the context of 'deriving income', for claiming concessional penalty, it would be necessary for an assessee to:

♦ Explain the way, mode and method of deriving such income; and

♦ Prove his explanation by proof or competent evidence.

To illustrate, an assessee explains, in the course of search, the cash found represents income derived from speculation. To claim concessional penalty, the assessee will have to:

♦ State the manner of deriving the income (that is, the way, mode and method adopted); and

Courts have consistently held that shares in an unlisted company have to be discounted for restrictions on transferability. The erstwhile Rule 1D of the Wealth-tax Rules provided for a discount of 20% for restrictions on transfer in an unlisted company. No such discounting is provided in rule 11UA. If the rules under section 50CA do not provide for a discounting, it is a moot point as to what extent the computation formula would be intra vires the Act.

Constitutional validity

In K. P. Varghese v. ITO [1981] 7 Taxman 13 (SC), the Supreme Court had to interpret section 52(2) of the Act, which prior to its omission, read as follows:

"(2) Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (1), if in the opinion of the Income-tax Officer the fair market value of a capital asset transferred by an assessee as on the date of the transfer exceeds the full value of the consideration declared by the assessee in respect of the transfer of such capital asset by an amount of not less than fifteen per cent of the value so declared, the full value of the consideration for such capital asset shall, with the previous approval of the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner, be taken to be its fair market value on the date of its transfer:"

On a literal interpretation, the only condition for attracting the applicability of that provision was that the fair market value of the capital asset transferred by the assessee as on the date of the transfer exceeded the full value of the consideration declared by the assessee in respect of the transfer by an amount of not less than 15% of the value so declared. Once the AO was satisfied that this condition existed, he could proceed to invoke the provision in section 52(2) and take the fair market value of the capital asset transferred by the assessee as on the date of the transfer as representing the full value of the consideration for the transfer of the capital asset and compute the capital gains on that basis.

However, the Supreme Court, inter alia, observed as follows:

Moreover, if sub-section (2) is literally construed as applying even to cases where the full value of the consideration in respect of the transfer is correctly declared or disclosed by the assessee and there is no understatement of the consideration, it would result in an amount being taxed which has neither accrued to the assessee nor been received by him and which from no view point can be rationally considered as capital gains or any other type of income. It is a well-settled rule of interpretation that the Court should as far as possible avoid that construction which attributes irrationality to the Legislature. Besides, under entry 82 in List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, which deals with "Taxes on income other than agricultural income" and under which the Income-tax Act, has been enacted, Parliament cannot "choose to tax as income an item which in no rational sense can be regarded as a citizen's income or even receipt. Sub-section (2) would, therefore, on the construction of the revenue, go outside the legislative power of Parliament and it would not be possible to justify it even as an incidental or ancillary provision or a provision intended to prevent evasion of tax.

The Court must obviously prefer a construction which renders the statutory provision constitutionally valid rather than that which makes it void.

We must, therefore, hold that sub-section (2) of section 52 can be invoked only where the consideration for the transfer has been understated by the assessee or, in other words, the consideration actually received by the assessee is more than what is declared or disclosed by him and the burden of proving such understatement or concealment is on the revenue. This burden may be discharged by the revenue by establishing facts and circumstances from which a reasonable inference can be drawn that the assessee has not correctly declared or disclosed the consideration received by him and there is understatement or concealment of consideration in respect of the transfer. Sub-section (2) has no application in case of an honest and bona fide transaction where the consideration received by the assessee has been correctly declared or disclosed by him, and there is no concealment or suppression of the consideration.

This is because, in earlier years a trust was entitled to an exemption, and then on account of some alleged infringement which has taken place subsequently, tax is proposed to be levied on such accumulation which was hitherto exempt. To illustrate, suppose an institution was registered in year 2000. For the years 2000 to 2016, there is no violation of any provision and the institution has built assets of Rs. 25 crores. It is an avowed principle of equitable taxation that the penalty must correspond to the gravity of the offence [UOI v. A. Sanyasi Rao [1996] 85 Taxman 321 (SC)]. It is not clear whether this principle would be satisfied in all cases where tax on accreted income is triggered.

2.1-25 Provision could trigger taxation under section 10(23C)/section 11(2)

The third proviso to section 10(23C) requires an institution to utilize its surplus exceeding 15% of income within next 5 years. Section 11(2) requires a charitable institution which has accumulated income to utilise it in the specified period not exceeding 5 years. If the tax is triggered, then, the institution will suffer dual damage, one in the form of tax under section 10(23C) or 11(2); and another under section 115TD. It is obvious that such dual tax is not intended.

2.1-26 Additional capital gains tax likely

In order to meet the tax liability, an institution may have to dispose of certain assets. This disposal will itself attract capital gains tax. Thus, the accreted tax could result in more than 30% of the funds of an institution be subject to payment of tax.

2.1-27 Provision could trigger violation of FCRA or contractual terms

It is possible that the institution is subject to other laws or contractual terms, which have imposed restrictions on utilisation of the assets. To illustrate, the foreign contribution received by an institution can be utilized only for specified purposes. A grant received by an institution can be utilized only in accordance with the purposes specified by the donor. On a literal reading, all these assets would be subject to the accreted income tax. Further, in order to meet the liability, they may have to be liquidated in violation of the purposes specified under FCRA or under the grant agreement. This would all trigger further penal consequences.

2.1-28 Penalty, waiver of

Section 270AA confers power on the AO to grant immunity from penalty. Section 273A gives discretion to the Commissioner of Income tax to waive any penalty. Both these provisions mitigate hardship caused by penalty even on a serious offence such as concealment. However, no such power is granted in respect of accreted tax.

2.1-29 Constitutional validity and "reading down" of the provisions in Chapter XII-B

Section 115TD(1) states that the accreted income … shall be charged to 'tax'. Tax has been defined in section 2(43) of the Act as income tax chargeable under the provisions of the Act. Further, section 115TD(6) refers to tax 'in respect of the said income' and section 115TD(7) refers to 'income which has been charged'. Thus, the tax on accreted income is clearly purported to be is a tax on income. Hence, the tax on accreted income has to satisfy that it is a tax on income under Entry 82 in List I of the Schedule VII to the Constitution of India. For this purpose, it is now very well settled that while the word 'income' should be construed liberally and in a very wide manner and the power to legislate will take in all incidental and ancillary matters, including the authorisation of to make provision to prevent evasion of tax, in any suitable manner, [UOI v. A. AA, 272B, 273 and the expression” with reasonable cause or excuse” from sections 272A, 276A, 276AB, 276B, 276DD, 276E. New sections 273B, 278AA and 278E, were inserted, shifting the burden on the assessee to prove that the failure or omission or commission is with ‘reasonable cause’ or ‘excuse’ or the absence of the existence of culpable mental state. Explaining reasons for these amendments and insertion of new sections, the Explanatory Memorandum1 states that one of the reasons for the unsatisfactory performance of Income-tax Department in the matter of successfully levying penalty and of prosecuting the defaulters is that invariably appellate authorities and the courts have cast upon the Department the near impossible burden of proving the existence of a culpable state of mind on the part of the defaulters. On a consideration of the relevant factors in this regard, it was announced by the Long Term Fiscal Policy that in order to effectively tackle the problem of tax evasion, the Income-tax Department will implement a strategy consisting, inter alia, of removing weaknesses in the law which hinder effective prosecution of tax evaders and that it was intended to incorporate certain provisions in the direct tax laws similar to those which already exist in the Customs Act and the Gold (Control) Act. For example, under section 123(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, when any gold, diamonds or any other class of specified goods are seized in the reasonable belief that they are smuggled goods, the burden of proving that they are not smuggled goods shall be on the person from whose possession, the goods were seized and any person claiming to be the owner of such seized goods. Similarly, under section 98B of the Gold (Control) Act, 1968 in any prosecution for an offence under that Act which requires a culpable mental state on the part of the accused, the court shall presume the existence of such mental state but it shall be open to the accused to prove the fact that he had no such mental state with respect to the offence. Accordingly, the intention of the Government was announced by the Long Term Fiscal Policy to amend the direct tax laws also to provide similar provisions so that once evasion is proved, the intention to evade need not be proved by the Department.

Apart from the above, in the context of the existing scheme of accepting returns without scrutiny, which is based on trust, it is only logical that the burden should be cast on the assessee to prove his innocence if he has concealed the particulars of his income or to prove the existence of reasonable cause if he has committed any other default under the tax laws.

By omitting the words “without reasonable cause” from penalty provisions, it has been provided that default by itself will attract penalty. At the same time, it has been provided by a new section 273B, inserted by the Amendment Act, that notwithstanding anything contained in these provisions, no penalty shall be imposable on the person or the assessee, as the case may be, for any failure referred to in the said provisions if he proves that there was reasonable cause for the said failure. By this amendment, the onus of proving the existence of reasonable cause for the defaults referred to in these provisions has been cast on the taxpayer. In this context, reference may be made to section 123(1) of the Customs Act, 1962.

Union of India [1995] 215 ITR 758 (Kar.)]. 3.5-2a LACK OF CLASSIFICATION CREATES INEQUALITY AND IS HIT BY ARTICLE 14 - An illustration how lack of classification creates inequality and renders an Act violative of article 14 is found in the decision of the Supreme Court in Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala.1 The Travancore-Cochin Land Tax Act, 1955 was enacted by the Kerala Legislature to provide for the levy of a low and uniform rate of basic tax on all lands in the State of Travancore Cochin. Section 4 of the said Act, the charging section, read thus : “subject to the provisions of this Act, there shall be charged and levied in respect of all lands in the State, of whatever description and held under whatever tenure, a uniform rate of tax to be called the basic tax.” The basic tax, which was prescribed at Rs. 2 per acre, was payable on all lands notwithstanding any other law, contract or agreement. Section 5A provided for a provisional assessment of basic tax in case of unsurveyed lands subject, however, to a regular assessment to be made later. The Act did not contain a provision for issuing notice or opportunity to the concerned land-holder to make his submissions before determining the tax. A uniform tax was imposed on all lands. There was no provision for appeal. Indeed, there was no assessment of tax as such. The tax levied was payable irrespective of the quality of the land, or its productive capacity, and irrespective of the fact whether the land yields any income, or not. The petitioners, who challenged the validity of the Act, were owners of forest areas in certain parts of Kerala which, before the reorganisation of States, formed part of the State of Madras. They were governed by a Madras Act which continued to govern them even after reorganisation, until the impugned Act came into force. The Madras Act provided that the forests shall not be cut, nor the rights in the forest produce sold, or otherwise alienated without the permission of the District Collector. A particular petitioner, whose case was taken as representative of others, was deriving an income of Rs. 3,100 per year by lease of forest. The forest was assessed provisionally under section 5A to a tax of Rs. 50,000 per annum. Since it was an unsurveyed forest, the District Collector conjectured the area of forest at 25,000 acres and on that basis, determined the tax payable at Rs. 50,000. The petitioner’s case was that he was being given permission to cut the forest only in instalments, that his annual income was only Rs. 3,100, whereas he was called upon to pay a tax of Rs. 50,000 per annum. It was also submitted that his forest had large areas of arid rocks, rivulets, and gorges. The Supreme Court observed that ordinarily a tax on land, or land revenue, is assessed on the actual or potential productivity of the land sought to be taxed, and that the tax has reference to the income actually made, or which could have been made with due diligence. But the impugned Act, it was pointed out, makes no such distinction. There may be several types of land; a particular land may be arid desert yielding no income; the second one does not yield any income, but may be capable of yielding an income by raising a crop after a disproportionately large investment of labour and capital; a third type of land yields just enough to pay for the incidental expenses, labour charges, and taxes, while the fourth type of land may be making large profits because it is very fertile and capable of yielding good crops. While the fourth category, it was pointed out, would easily be able to meet the burden of tax and the third one might be just able to bear the tax, the first and second categories would not be able to bear the tax burden. Because the tax is not paid, the very land may be sold for realizing the demand, which would make the Act confiscatory in nature. It was observed, “there is no attempt at classification in the provisions of the Act...It is one of those cases where the lack of classification creates inequality. It is, therefore, clearly hit by the prohibition to deny equality before the law contained in article 14 of the Constitution.....” It was also observed that the Act constitutes an unreasonable restriction upon the right to hold property, guaranteed by article 19(1)(f), and being a disproportionate and unreasonable imposition, was not saved by clause (6) thereof.

10.2 The tax rate on unexplained income is reduced from 60% to 30% [Section 195 of ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 115BBE of ITA 1961)]

10.2-1 Position under the ITA 1961

The unexplained income as referred to in sections 68 to 69D detected by the Assessing Officer or offered by the assessee suo-moto to tax in the Income-tax return shall be taxable at a special rate as provided in Section 115BBE. This provision provides that such an unexplained income shall be taxable at the rate of 60%, which shall be further increased by a surcharge of 25% and health and education cess. The effective tax rate shall be 78% [Tax 60% + 15% Surcharge (at the rate of 25% of 60%) + 3% Health & Education Cess (at the rate of 4% of the aggregate of Tax and Surcharge of 75%)].

The Assessing Officer shall also levy a penalty in respect of unexplained income in accordance with section 271AAC.

10.2-2 Position under the ITA 2025 (as amended by the Finance Act, 2026)

Section 195 of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to section 115BBE of the ITA 1961) specified the same tax rate of 60% (plus surcharge and cess) in respect of the unexplained income.

The Finance Act, 2026, effective from 1-4-2026, makes comprehensive changes in the provisions dealing with the taxation of the unexplained income, which includes the following:

(a)

Section 195 is amended to reduce the tax rate on undisclosed income from 60% to 30%.

(b)

Section 443 (corresponding to section 271AAC of the ITA 1961), which provides for the levy of a penalty in case of unexplained income, is omitted from the Act [see Para 18.2-2].

(c)

Section 439 (corresponding to Section 270A of the ITA 1961), which provides for the levy of a penalty in case of undisclosed income due to under-reporting or mis-reporting, is amended to include the unexplained income within the scope of this provision [see Para 18.3].

(d)

Section 440 (corresponding to section 270AA of the ITA 1961), which provides immunity from the penalty on fulfilment of specified conditions, is amended to grant immunity from the penalty to be imposed under section 439 on the unexplained income on the payment of a fee [see Para 18.4].

Also see Para 18.4-4 for the implications of taxation of unexplained income under ITA 205 vis-à-vis ITA 1961.

10.2-3 Reduction in the tax rate

Section 195 of the ITA 2025 deals with the following two situations:

(a)

If the total income of the assessee as reflected in the Income-tax return includes any unexplained income as referred to in Sections 102 to 106 (corresponding to sections 68 to 69D of ITA 1961).

(b)

If the total income of the assessee determined by the Assessing Officer includes any unexplained income as referred to in sections 102 to 106.

13.3.2b It may be noted that for levying the penalty the section imposes an additional condition (when compared with Explanation 5 applicable upto 1-6-2007), namely, substantiation of the manner of deriving income. 'Manner', as explained in the Law Lexicon by P. Ramanatha Aiyar means: 'mode of action, way of performing or effecting anything, method, style the way of managing; the way of doing thing, the method of procedure; … method or mode or style... '.

'Substantiates', Webster's New Collegiate Dictionary means:

'1: to impart substance to 2: to put into concrete form… 3: to establish by proof or competent evidence'.

Accordingly, in the context of 'deriving income', for claiming concessional penalty, it would be necessary for an assessee to:

Explain the way, mode and method of deriving such income; and

Prove his explanation by proof or competent evidence.

To illustrate, an assessee explains, in the course of search, the cash found represents income derived from speculation. To claim concessional penalty, the assessee will have to:

State the manner of deriving the income (that is, the way, mode and method adopted); and

13.1-8 Exclusions [Sub-section (6)]

It is provided, the unreported income should not include certain specified amount of income under the specified circumstances, like, bona fide explanation; estimation; undisclosed income liable to penalty under section 271AAB etc. and they are discussed hereafter.

Before dealing with different situations, it may be pointed out that the opening language of sub-section (6), reads: 'the under-reported income, for the purposes of this section, shall not include the following …'; and, thereafter, it lists five different situations providing that the amount of income or underreported income referred to in each of them shall not be included.

As said earlier, while providing the circumstances in which it can be said that the income is under-reported and/or quantification thereof, the section compares and/or treats the difference between total income as per return or intimation and total income as per assessment or reassessment as the under-reported income. In other words, it does not add up various different additions made in the course of assessment to quantify the same as underreported income. However, while providing for the exclusions, it does refer to the components of income (added while computing the total income).

ellate Tribunal - Under section 254 prior to its amendment by the Finance Act, 2007, the Appellate Tribunal could pass an order of stay in any proceeding relating to an appeal filed before it. 1-6aAGGREGATION OF PENALTY IN CASE OF THE TOTAL INCOME [115JB/115JC] - To provide for aggregation, in section 271(1), Explanation 4 was inserted by the Finance Act, 2015 and the reasons for the introduction of the same were explained as follows:

'Amount of tax sought to be evaded for the purposes of penalty for concealment of income under clause (iii) of sub-section (1) of section 271 Under the existing provision contained in clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 of the Act penalty for concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income is levied on the "amount of tax sought to be evaded", which has been defined, inter alia, as the difference between the tax due on the income assessed and the tax which would have been chargeable had such total income been reduced by the amount of concealed income. Problems have arisen in the computation of amount of tax sought to be evaded where the concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income occurs in the computation of income under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act and also under the provisions other than the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act (hereafter referred as general provisions). Further, courts have held that penalty under section clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 cannot be levied in cases where the concealment of income occurs under the income computed under general provisions and the tax is paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act. Tax paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC over and above the tax liability arising under general provisions is available as credit for set off against future tax liability. Under-statement of income and the tax liability thereon under general provisions results in larger amount of such credit becoming available to the assessee for set off in future years. Therefore, where concealment of income, as computed under the general provisions, has taken place, penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 should be leviable even if the tax liability of the assessee for the year has been determined under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act. Accordingly, it is proposed to amend section 271 of the Act so as to provide that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be the summation of tax sought to be evaded under the general provisions and the tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. However, if an amount of concealment of income on any issue is considered both under the general provisions and provisions of section 115JB or 115JC then such amount shall not be considered in computing tax sought to be evaded under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. Further, in a case where the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC are not applicable, the computation of tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC shall be ignored. This amendment will take effect from 1st April, 2016 and will accordingly apply, in relation to the assessment year 2016-17 and subsequent assessment years. [Clause 68]'.

It appears, as per the Memorandum, the intention was to identify separately tax sought to be evaded in respect of income as per the general provisions and deemed total income and aggregate the same. However, prima facie, it appears that the section, as such, does not aggregate the under-reported income as per the general provisions and under-reported income as per deemed total income.

In Fakir Mohmed Haji Hasan v. CIT [2002] 120 Taxman 11 (Guj.), the Gujarat High Court laid down the following propositions:

The scheme of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C of the Act would show that in cases where the nature and source of investments made by the assessee or the nature and source of acquisition of money, bullion, etc., owned by the assessee or the source of expenditure incurred by the assessee are not explained at all, or not satisfactorily explained, then the value of such investments and money, or value of articles not recorded in the books of account or the unexplained expenditure may be deemed to be the income of such assessee.

It follows that the moment a satisfactory explanation is given about such nature and source by the assessee, then the source would stand disclosed and will, therefore, be known and the income would be treated under the appropriate head of income for assessment as per the provisions of the Act.

However, when these provisions apply because no source is disclosed at all on the basis of which the income can be classified under one of the heads of income under section 14 of the Act, it would not be possible to classify such deemed income under any of these heads including 'Income from other sources' which have to be sources known or explained.

When the income cannot be so classified under any one of the heads of income under section 14, it follows that the question of giving any deductions under the provisions which correspond to such heads of income will not arise.

If it is possible to peg the income under any one of those heads by virtue of a satisfactory explanation being given, then these provisions of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C will not apply, in which event the provisions regarding deductions, etc., applicable to the relevant head of income under which such income falls will automatically be attracted.

The opening words of section 14 'Save as otherwise provided by this Act' clearly leave scope for 'deemed income' of the nature covered under the scheme of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C being treated separately, because such deemed income is not income from salary, house property, profits and gains of business or profession, or capital gains, nor is it income from 'other sources' because the provisions of sections 69, 69A, 69B, and 69C treat unexplained investments, unexplained money, bullion, etc., and unexplained expenditure as deemed income where the nature and source of investment, acquisition or expenditure, as the case may be, have not been explained or satisfactorily explained. Therefore, in these cases, the source not being known, such deemed income will not fall even under the head 'Income from other sources'.

Therefore, the corresponding deductions, which are applicable to the incomes under any of these various heads, will not be attracted in case of deemed incomes which are covered under the provisions of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C in view of the scheme of those provisions.
