3.6-4 Constitutional validity of the Gujarat Tax Luxuries (Hotels and Lodging Houses) Act, 1977 and other similar Acts - Not violative of Article 19(1)(g) - Writ petitions were filed before the Supreme Court challenging the constitutional validity of legislations of different States, viz., the State of Gujarat, State of Tamil Nadu, the State of Karnataka and the State of West Bengal imposing a tax on ‘luxuries’ under entry 62 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India.

These relate to the challenge to the legislation by the State of Gujarat, viz., the Gujarat Tax on Luxuries (Hotel and Lodging Houses) Act, 1977, to the corresponding legislation of the State of Tamil Nadu, viz., the Tamil Nadu Tax on Luxuries in Hotels and Lodging Houses Act, 1981, to the corresponding Karnataka legislation, viz., the Karnataka Tax on Luxuries (Hotel and Lodging Houses) Act, 1979, to the West Bengal Entertainments and Luxuries (Hotel and Restaurants) Tax Act, 1972. All these taxing statutes, except for certain aspects individual to them, are analogous and the scheme of the legislation is substantially similar. The variations are in the differences in the criteria of classification of the hotels to which the Act is applied and the rates of taxes. The grounds of challenge are substantially the same. The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity as the tax on luxuries does not restrict freedom of trade or intercourse throughout India, and articles 14, 19(1)(g) and 301 of the Constitution are not violated.

Once the legislative competence and the nexus between the taxing power and the subject of taxation is established, the other incidents are matters of fiscal policy behind the taxing law. The measure of tax is not the same thing as, and must be distinguished from, the subject of tax. Mere existence of a tax or that it affects the earnings cannot per se be held to be violative of article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. A provision which is against evasion does not offend article 19(1)(g). The mere absence of the corrective machinery or existence of a provision imparting finality by itself, would not be conclusive so as to render the conferment of power on the authority per se unreasonable and arbitrary, rendering the provision unconstitutional.

Taxes can and do sometimes having regard to their effect and impact on the free flow of trade, constitute restrictions on the freedom under Article 301 of the Constitution. But the restrictions must stem from the provisions of the law imposing the tax which could be said to have the direct and immediate effect of restricting the free flow of “trade, commerce and intercourse”. It is not all taxes that have this effect.

The matter is concluded by the judgment of the Constitution Bench in Jain Brothers v Union of India [1970] 77 ITR 170 (SC) though the observations were made in a different context. The facts of that case may be noticed. The assessment year was 1960-61, the corresponding accounting year ending with October 31,1959. On 26th of May, 1960, a notice under section 22(2) of the Old Act was served on the firm calling upon it of submit a return of its income. The return had to be filed within 36 days of the service of the notice. It was not filed. Further notices were served on two occasions. The firm filed a return on 18th of November, 1961, showing an income of Rs. 3,55,566. The Income-tax Officer completed the assessment on 23rd November, 1964, computing the total income of the firm art Rs. 4,75,368. On the same day the Income-tax Officer issued a notice under section 271 read with section 274 of the Act calling upon the firm to show cause why an order imposing a penalty should not be passed on account of its failure to furnish the return in time. After considering the Explanation submitted by the assessee the Income-tax Officer made an order on November 19,1966, under section 271(c). In that case while the assessment proceeding was pending the assessee challenged the constitutionality of section 297(2)(g) and section 271(2) of the Act. The constitutionality of section 297(2)(g) and section 271(2) was attacked as being hit by article 14 of the Constitution.

Section 297(2)(g) ran thus:

"297. (2) Notwithstanding the repeal of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 (hereafter referred to as "the repealed Act"),—.........

(g) any proceeding for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on the 31st day of March, 1962, or any earlier year, which is completed on or after the 1st day of April, 1962, may be initiated and any such penalty may be imposed under this Act."

It was contended that the section was discriminatory under article 14 inasmuch as assessments already completed before April 1, 1962, were treated on a different footing from assessments made subsequent thereto without any reasonable nexus for the differentia keeping the object in view. Their Lordships repelled this contention and made the following observations Jain Bros. case (Supra):

"There can be no matter of doubt that penalty has to be calculated and imposed according to the tax assessed. It follows that imposition of penalty can take place only after assessment has been completed...........It is obvious that for the imposition of penalty it is not the assessment year or the date of the filing of the return which is important but it is the satisfaction of the income-tax authorities that a default has been committed by the assessee which would attract the provisions relating to penalty. Whatever the stage at which the satisfaction is reached, the scheme of sections 274(1) and 275 of the Act of 1961, is that the order imposing penalty must be made after the completion of the assessment. The crucial date, therefore, for purposes of penalty, is the date of such completion."

The aforesaid observations of their lordships leave absolutely no room for doubt that the penalty proceedings is to be initiated only on the completion of the assessment when the assessing authority would have the satisfaction that the assessee had concealed income which had escaped assessment.

Mr. B.K. Mohanti who argued this case with considerable ability as amicus curiae at our request, contended that the aforesaid Supreme Court decision is not a direct authority that the date of the satisfaction of the appropriate authority is the date for initiation of the proceeding under section 271(1)(c). We find no force in this contention. Enunciation of law by the Supreme Court does not vary according to the context in which it is argued. The exposition was on the legal position and it is on that basis that the question of discrimination under article 14 was examined. An answer could not be given by their Lordships on a wrong exposition of law that the section was not discriminatory. Mr. Mohanti fairly concedes that if this decision is taken as laying down the law on the point in issue, then clearly the amended section 271 after April 1, 1964, would have application to this case and consequently the Tribunal would have invoked the Explanation.

As regards contention regarding hostile discrimination, it is well-settled that while article 14 forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purposes of legislation. In East India Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh AIR 1962 SC 1733 and Twyford Tea Co. v. State of Kerala AIR 1970 SC 1133, the Supreme Court has held that in order to be able to succeed on the charge of discrimination and in order to sustain the attack on the ground of violation of article 14, so far as taxation statutes are concerned, a person challenging the legislation must establish conclusively that persons equally circumstanced have been treated unequally and vice versa. Unless the petitioner succeeds in establishing that there was a clear and hostile discrimination by virtue of the impugned legislation, the challenge on the ground of article 14 cannot be sustained so far as taxation statutes are concerned.

In V.J. Ferreira v. Bombay Municipality AIR 1972 SC 845, the Supreme Court has held that a taxing statute is not invalid on the grounds of discrimination merely because other objects could have been but are not taxed by the legislature. It was held that when a statute divides the objects of tax into groups or categories, so long as there is equality and uniformity within each group, the tax cannot be attacked on the ground of its being discriminatory, although due to fortuitous circumstances or a particular situation some included in a class or group may get some advantage over others, provided of course they are not sought out for special treatment. In view of those provisions it was clear that provisions regarding penal interest set out in clause (iii) of the proviso to section 139(1) which has been put in the statute book as a deterrent measure and to compensate the exchequer for the loss which occurs because of delay in completing the assessments which delay in turn is caused by the respective assessee not filing his return within time, is a supplementary measure enacted with a view to enforce the machinery of tax collection. Therefore, it is not possible to say that there was any such hostile discrimination, when a distinction was made between persons filing delayed returns and persons filing no return at all.

Therefore, the provisions in clause (iii ) of proviso to section 139(1) regarding levying of interest were not violative of article 14 of the Constitution and were not ultra vires and void.

As regards contention regarding charging of penal interest in case of registered firm by treating it as an unregistered firm, the legislation was placed the registered firms in a special category for purpose of payment of tax. That special category has been treated favourably so far as the payment of tax is concerned as compared to other associations of persons and unregistered firms. But there is nothing wrong if the legislature at the same time imposes a condition that the entity enjoying such a privileged position must conform to the provisions of law and abide by the provisions of law in order to continue enjoying such privileges. Therefore, the same reasoning which justifies the creation of such a class amongst the assessees, namely, class of registered firms, also sustains the provision in clause (iii )(a) of the proviso to section 139(1) to the effect that if there is a belated filing of a return by a registered firm, then the penal interest is to be calculated on the total amount of tax which it would have been called upon to pay if it were an unregistered firm. Under these circumstances it cannot be said that in the case of a registered firm penal interest ceases to be an amount of compensation and it cannot be said that there is violation of the object of the Income-tax Act nor does it result in payment of double penalty. The payment of double penalty is out of the question because penal interest is not penalty at all. It is only by way of compensation and since penalty is not being imposed twice over, there cannot be any question of double jeopardy so far as registered firms are concerned.

Therefore, the provisions of clause (iii ) of proviso to section 139(1) were not invalid on ground of double jeopardy.

In view of aforesaid, the writ petition was to be dismissed.

The provision concerned is a provision in a taxing statute. It is open to the Parliament to classify the taxpayers on any rational basis and also treat the different classes of taxpayers differently. It is also permissible for the Parliament to further classify in a rational and non-arbitrary manner the assessees in relation to their conduct. The Parliament can legislate with respect to the assessees who comply with the requirements of law and extend such concessions as it deems fit to such assessees, which concessions it may choose to deny to those who have violated the law and such violations have been established by reason of the action taken by the authorities. It is in that background and with the object of laying down a special procedure for the assessment of the assessees who fail to comply with the law by not disclosing in full their taxable income and by not paying the taxes properly due from them that Chapter XIV-B consisting of sections 158B to 158BH was inserted in the Act.

The assumption made in the Scheme of the Act that a person who comes forward with the return or with further information after a search, does so only on account of the detection already made under the search and the likelihood of further exposure is a reasonable assumption and it can in no way be regarded as arbitrary. The special procedure provided in Chapter XIV-B is meant to apply to all such cases notwithstanding anything contained in any other provisions of the Act as provided in section 158BA(1) and other provisions of the Act, therefore, cannot control the contents of this Chapter except to the extent provided for in Chapter XIV-B.

There is no fundamental right in an assessee to commit breaches of the law. The right that can be asserted by one who has chosen to violate the law is the right to be treated in a manner similar to that in which other similar offenders are treated. Chapter XIV-B accords similar treatment to all persons belonging to the class to whom that Chapter is to apply. There is no discrimination therein among those who suffer such searches.

The petitioner’s argument that in cases where the assessee had paid advance tax, such payment would clearly indicate his intention to disclose his income and it could not be said that such person would not have disclosed his income, cannot be accepted for the payment of advance tax by itself does not establish an intent to disclose the income. The disclosure is to be made by filing the return. Even in search cases, where the time for filing the return under section 139(1) has not expired, income disclosed in the books of account is not treated as undisclosed income. All that is denied to the assessee in search cases is the opportunity to file a return after the period specified in section 139(1) and to claim that the income that he would have disclosed in a belated return is not to be regarded as undisclosed income. The reason for denying such opportunity in search cases is obvious. After having suffered a search, the assessee is not to be enabled to escape the consequences of his failure to disclose all his income by filing a return after the search and after the expiry of the time prescribed under section 139(1) and by disclosing therein income which had remained undisclosed up to the date of the search. Therefore, section 158BB(1)(c ) is not in any way unconstitutional.

As to the other contention raised against the validity of section 34(1A) of 1922 Act, that at the relevant time, section 34(1)(a) of 1922 Act dealt with cases similar to those falling under section 34(1A) of 1922 Act, and yet, whereas in the former category of cases a period of limitation was prescribed as 8 years there was no such limitation in regard to the latter, and that, it was unconstitutional discrimination. It is true that in a broad sense both section 34(1)(a) and section 34(1A) of 1922 Act deal with cases of income which has escaped assessment, and in that sense, the assessees against whom steps are taken in respect of their income which has escaped assessment can be said to form a similar class; but the similarity between the two categories disappears when it is remembered that section 34(1A) of 1922 Act is intended to deal with assessees whose income has escaped assessment during a specified period between 1-9-1939 and 31-3-1946. It is well known that that is the period in which as a result of the war, huge profits were made in business and industry.

Secondly, in regard to the cases falling under section 34(1A) of 1922 Act, action can be taken only where the income which has escaped assessment is likely to amount to Rs. 1 lakh or more. In other words, it is only in regard to cases where the escaped income is of a high magnitude that the restriction of the period of limitation has been removed. It was difficult to accept the argument that the legislature was not justified in treating this smaller class of assessees differently on the ground that the profits made by this class were higher and the income which had escaped assessment was correspondingly of a much larger magnitude. The object of the legislature being to catch income which had escaped assessment, it would be legitimate for the legislature to deal with the class of assessees in whose cases the income which had escaped assessment was much larger, because that would be a basis for rational classification which has an intelligible connection with the object intended to be achieved by the statute.

Therefore, there was no substance in the argument that the absence of the restriction as to period of limitation under section 34(1A) of 1922 Act introduced any infirmity in the said provision. In the result, it was to be held that section 34(1A) of 1922 Act was valid and had not contravened article 14 of the Constitution.

The appeals and petitions were dismissed and judgment of Allahabad High Court was affirmed.

It has also been repeatedly held that the differentia and object are different elements and that the object by itself cannot be the basis of classification. Another principle equally well settled is that article 14 condemns discrimination not by substantive law alone but even by procedural law. The Explanation does not fall in the category of a substantive provision of law but answers the description of procedural law. The Explanation purports to raise a presumption against the assessee if certain facts mentioned therein are proved after assessment has been made, and then shift the burden on the assessee to prove that his case does not fall under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271. According to the Explanation , if the total income returned by any person is less than eighty per cent of the total income as assessed, that person shall, unless he proves that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on his part, be deemed to have concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income for the purpose of clause (c ) of sub-section (1). In other words, if the margin of difference in the case of a particular assessee between the income returned by him and his actual income is more than twenty per cent., then it would be for him to establish that he had not concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of that income by reason of fraud or gross or wilful neglect on his part, while in the case of assessees whose returned income reveals less than twenty per cent departure from the actual income, the burden of proving the ingredients of clause (c) shall rest, as before, on the income-tax authorities. Obviously, the main purpose of the Explanation is to place the burden of establishing want of fraud or gross or wilful neglect in the matter of income-tax return filed by an assessee on him where the difference revealed between the returned income and assessed income is more than twenty per cent. Therefore, although the ultimate object of the Explanation may be to provide effective checks against evasion of income-tax, the immediate object of the Explanation appears to be that if an assessee has been apparently guilty of gross deflation of his income as entered in his return compared to his actual income, it shall be for him to establish that he has not merited imposition of penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271. Briefly put, if the gap between the returned and actual income is more than 20 per cent a presumption of law arises that the assessee's case is covered by clause (c) but that presumption being in rebuttal the assessee is given an opportunity to establish that it is not so.

The classification of the assessees into two varieties as envisaged by the Explanation is founded on intelligible differentia. The two categories of assessee in legislature wisdom are; (1) who, in the opinion of parliament, have been guilty of gross and flagrant violation of ethics benefiting a citizen in the matter of submission of income-tax returns, and (2) the rest of the assessees falling in the category not answering such description. The Explanation is an instance of the legal adage res ipsa loquitur, meaning that the thing speaks for itself. In substance, Parliament wants the income tax authorities to assume if the gap between the returned income and the actual income is so glaring as to the extent of not less than 20 per cent that assessee in question has concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income, but in case the difference is less than twenty per cent., then such assumption would not arise and it shall be for the department to establish that the assessee has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. In allocating the burden of proof in one class of cases on the assessee and in the other on the departmental authority, think Parliament has adopted an intelligible differentia dictated by the experience gathered in administering the Act.

It is not for the courts to tell Parliament what sort of classification it should introduce. The function of the courts is only to find out whether the classification actually introduced by Parliament is hit by article 14 of the Constitution. There may be a variety of classifications which can be introduced for achieving a particular object, but if Parliament in its wisdom adopts one in preference to another, the courts cannot take exception to the classification chosen if it is not proved to be obnoxious to the constitutional provision. The classification introduced by the Explanation to section 271(1) does not offend article 14 of the Constitution.

The ITO is entitled to initiate proceedings under section 34(1A), of the 1922 Act if he in good faith has reason to believe the matters specified in section 34(1A)(i) and (ii ). He is not bound to disclose to the assessee the source of the information upon which he came to entertain that belief. The working of section 34(1A) of the 1922 Act will be wholly impossible if one is to hold that the ITO is bound to disclose the source of his confidential information or the name of the informant. The notice under section 34(1A) of the 1922 Act commences a quasi-judicial enquiry in which the assessee is entitled to appear and produce his evidence. In that enquiry the ITO will be bound to disclose to the assessee the material on the basis of which is seeks to find that the assessee's income to the extent of rupees one lakh or more has escaped assessment during the relevant years. Natural justice demands full disclosure of all the materials which the ITO seeks to use against the assessee in course of that enquiry, so that the assessee has sufficient opportunity to meet the case made against him. That stage of the enquiry will arise in this case after the assessee files its return and produces its account books. It is not desirable that the assessee should be informed of those materials at this stage. If the assessee is dishonest, the disclosure of the materials to this stage will be likely to lead to the manipulation of the books of account and other records. An honest trader who has not concealed his income has nothing to fear by submitting a fresh return and producing his account books pursuant to the notices issued by the ITO. If the assessee is an honest trader, there is no likelihood of its incurring fresh penalties by filing a fresh return and by producing its account books. There had been no violation of natural justice in this case and the proceedings under section 34(1A) of the 1922 Act upto this stage could not be quashed on the ground of any alleged violation of natural justice.

There was no merit in the appeal the same dismissed accordingly.

GENERAL

Constitutional validity - The provisions of section 276C are constitutionally valid and does not contravene/violate the provisions of Articles 14 & 21 of the Constitution of India on ground that revenue is compensated with regard to delay in payment of tax or submission of return by making payment of interest [Dr. (Mrs.) M. S. Dhowani v. J. Ranganathan Second ITO[1992] 65 Taxman 541 (Mad.); Sonarome Chemicals (P.) Ltd. v. UOI[2003] 127 Taxman 31 (Kar.)].

Section 276C(1) and section 276C(2) - Section 276C(1) deals with evasion of tax, penalty or interest chargeable or imposable under the Act, which might include wilful suppression in the returns before assessment and completion. But section 276C(2) deals with evading the payment of any tax, penalty or interest under the Act. The words 'chargeable' or 'imposable' are not there. What section 276C(2) says is 'without prejudice to any penalty that may be imposable on him under any other provision of this Act, be punishable...'. Therefore, evidently, section 276C(2) takes in cases of tax evasion after charging or imposition. Evasion after completion of assessment also comes within the operation of section 276C(2). Section 276C(2) is so clear that at any rate it takes in the cases of evasion of tax, penalty or interest after assessments were made. Avoidance of tax is avoidance of tax liability under some manner as distinguished from evasion of tax whether before or after charging or imposition. It is not illegal as distinguished from penal evasion. Section 276C(2) deals with evasion after quantification. It becomes applicable only after income is assessed and the assessee attempts to evade payment [G. Viswanathan v. ITO[1987] 35 Taxman 66 (Ker.)]. Also see, Vinodchandra C. Patel v. State of Gujarat[2001] 118 Taxman 526 (Guj.).

PROSECUTION PROCEEDINGS

Notice - In order to initiate prosecution proceedings u/s 276C, no notice of demand u/s 156 is required to be issued separately [Kalluri Krishan Pushkar v. DCIT[2015] 63 taxmann.com 150/[2016] 236 Taxman 27 (AP & Telangana)].

For filing a complaint u/s 276C, determination of a principal officer was not necessary and non-issuance of individual notice before filing of compliant would be of no consequence [Mrs. Sujatha Venkateshwaran v. Asstt. CIT[2018] 96 taxmann.com 203/257 Taxman 195 (Mad.)].

'Wilful attempt to evade any tax, penalty or interest chargeable or imposable under this Act or the payment thereof' – The Explanation concerns only section 276C(1) and not section 276C(2). Further the Explanation is only inclusive and not exhaustive. Clause (iv) also makes this position clear [G. Viswanathan v. ITO[1987] 35 Taxman 66 (Ker.)].

The word 'evade' will take in non-disclosure as well, depending upon the facts and the mens rea of the petitioner. The Explanation which deals with examples of wilful attempt to evade any tax is only 'inclusive' and does not catalogue all instances of wilful evasion [K. A. Khaja v. Sixth ITO[1992] 196 ITR 627 (Mad.)].

Where there was a specific allegation that petitioner/accused was in possession of two documents of agreements for construction of a building with different values, as per Explanation to section 276C prima facie material was available against petitioner to frame charge u/s 276C [Vijayalalitha v. State[2010] 327 ITR 261 (Mad.)].

HELD: The question whether a given provision in a status is a penal one or not is sometimes not easy of comprehension. This is because the word "penal" is somewhat ambiguous in its scope and content. A penalty may be the subject-matter of a breach of statutory duty or may be the subject-matter of a complaint. In ordinary parlance the word "penal" may embrace penalties for avoidance of civil liabilities which do not constitute offences against the State. This marked distinction is responsible for any statute intended to protect public revenue, to speak of pecuniary penalties for any violation of its provisions and also specifically provide for prosecutions in an ordinary criminal court as if it is an offence or crime. Thus, "penalty" is a slippery word and has to be understood in the context in which it is used in a given statute. All penalties do not flow from an offence as is commonly understood, but all offences lead to a penalty. Whereas the former is a penalty which flows from a disregard of strict statutory provisions, the latter is entailed when there is mens rea and is made the subject-matter of adjudication in a prosecution launched for the purpose in a criminal court. In fact, the new Act provides for a contemporaneous prosecution for submission of false statement in a declaration. If once, it is clear from the scheme of the New Act and its working that the penalty sought to be imposed under section 297(2)(g) read with section 271 is a penalty imposable by the revenue in exercise of its power derived from the express statutory provisions made for the purpose and in the interests of public revenue, then it ceases to be a penalty imposed on the delinquent as if he has been charged for an offence under one or the other provisions in Chapter XXII of the new Act.

What is due towards tax cannot be said to be the "property" of the assessee since it is a debt due to the State towards tax, even as per his own return. The mere fact that it is not quantified by the department on that date would not make it any the less the tax due under section 140A(1). It is not necessary that every provision conceived in the interest of the revenue, i.e., made to ensure proper payment of taxes should be compensatory only and that no penalties can be provided therefore. Therefore, sub-section (3) of section 140A does not in any manner infringe article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution of India and that it is not an unreasonable restriction upon the said right.

The impugned provisions, therefore, squarely come within the ambit of article 31-C of the Constitution and even if petitioner's contention, that the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property conferred under clause (f) of sub-article (1) of article 19 is affected, was to be accepted, he was not entitled to raise any challenge. These two contentions of the petitioner must, therefore, fail. As to the contention of impugned provision being beyond the legislative competence; Entry 82 of List I of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution authorises legislation relating to taxes on income other than agricultural income. The contention was that it was under this entry that the impugned provisions have been enacted, the true purpose of Chapter XX-A is beyond the purview of the entry and, therefore, Parliament had no legislative competence to enact the Amending Act of 1972. Legislative power has been distributed between the Union and the States and some heads of legislation had been kept in the concurrent list under Schedule VII. The ambit of each entry is of the widest amplitude and law is settled beyond doubt that if by the pith and substance test the legislative entry supports legislation, a statute is not open to attack on the ground of want of competence. Undoubtedly, the Income-tax Act is a legislation in exercise of legislative powers under entry 82. So is the impugned provision. The impugned Chapter makes provision for imposition of penalty and for checking evasion of tax, because such a position is concomitant to the power to raise taxes. Such supplementary provisions are necessary for administering the statute effectively and for meeting the purpose for which the law is made. The scheme under the impugned provision for compulsory buying of the property at the stated consideration together with fifteen per cent thereof in the event of a clandestine deal to evade tax is not foreign to the law of income-tax. Parliament was initially satisfied with levy of penalty. By experience it appeared that that was not sufficient to meet the growing evil. The background of the legislation clearly indicates that as evasion of tax and black money became a growing menace, a high-power commission had to be appointed and, after probing into the matter, some of its recommendations were laid before Parliament and emerged in the shape of the Amending Act of 1972. The Amending Act in these circumstances cannot be held to be beyond the range of legislative competence.

The writ application failed and was accordingly dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

If in a particular case any mala fide action is taken that can always be challenged by an assessee in appropriate proceedings but the mere possibility that some officer may intentionally delay the disposal of a case can hardly be a ground for striking down clause (g) as discriminatory under article 14.

The classification made is based on intelligible differentia having reasonable relation to the object intended to be achieved. The object essentially was to prevent the evasion of tax. It is true that clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 271 mentions the corresponding provisions of the Act of 1961 and does not mention provisions of Act of 1922 but that will not make the part relating to payment of penalty inapplicable once it is held that section 297(2)(g ) governs the case. Both sections 271(1) and 297(2)(g) have to be read together and in harmony and so read the only conclusion possible is that for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year which is completed after first day of April, 1962, the proceedings have to be initiated and the penalty imposed in accordance with the provisions of section 271 of the Act of 1961. Thus the assessee would be liable to a penalty as provided by section 271(1) for the default mentioned in section 28(1) of the Act of 1922 if his case falls within the terms of section 297(2)(g).

The provision of section 271 of the Act of 1961 will apply mutatis mutandis to proceedings relating to penalty initiated in accordance with section 297(2)(g) of that Act.

As regards challenge to section 271(2) of the Act of 1961 on the ground of contravention of article 14 of the Constitution, it was open to the legislature to say that once a registered firm committed a default attracting penalty, it should be deemed or considered to be an unregistered firm for the purpose of its imposition. No question of discrimination under article 14 can arise in such a situation. There was nothing to prevent the legislature from giving the benefit of a reduced rate to a registered firm for the purpose of tax but withhold the same when it committed a default and became liable to imposition of penalty.

The appeal was dismissed.

The provision of clause (c ) of sub-section (1) of section 271, which deals with imposition of penalty for concealment of particulars of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income by the assessee, has remained untouched since the 1922 Act was enacted, except for a brief interval in 1987 when the Direct Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 1987 was passed. However, the same was not brought into force and the original position was reverted to, with the enactment of the Direct Tax (Amendment) Act, 1989. The gap, if any, in the interregnum was sought to be filled up by insertion of sub-section (5) in section 271. [Para 8]

What was sought to be achieved by the Direct Tax Law (Amendment) Act, 1987 was restored by the Direct Tax Law (Amendment) Act, 1989, insofar as clause (c) of section 271(1) was concerned. Therefore, there was no cogent reason articulated as to why retrospectivity to the impugned provision of section 271(1B) was also with effect from 1-4-1989. It was not the case of the revenue that this had been done keeping in mind its administrative convenience or for the reason that it did not want to continue with penalty proceedings in respect of stale cases. [Para 8.1]

But would the cut off date of 1-4-1989 create an invidious discrimination or result in a class legislation vis-a-vis those whose case is to be considered on the basis of law obtaining prior to 1-4-1989. There would be no violation of the equality clause under article 14 of the Constitution on this ground alone, for the reason that if an assessee has fallen foul of the law, that is, penalty provisions are otherwise applicable to him, he cannot be heard to say that rigours of law ought not to apply to him because another person similarly placed has not been exposed to such a rigour. There is no equality in illegality. This is not the case where a more onerous procedure is applied to him as against an assessee to whom pre-amendment law is applied. While considering a challenge to the vires of a statute, the Court is required to lean in favour of its validity, preferring an interpretation that would preserve its constitutionality, as the Legislature, it is presumed, does not exceed its jurisdiction. The onus is squarely on the person challenging the constitutional vires of the statute. The exception to the rule is that where a challenge is made on the ground of infraction of fundamental rights, then the State must justify its action. In ascertaining the intention of the Parliament, the Court is required to come to its own view based on the language of the statute and not to be governed by affidavits filed in the Court by parties to justify and sustain the legislation. [Para 8.2]

A bare reading of section 271(1)(c ) would show that to initiate penalty proceedings following prerequisites should obtain :—

(i )

The Assessing Officer should be satisfied that:—

(a )

the assessee has either concealed particulars of his income; or

(b )

furnished inaccurate particulars of his income; or

(c )

infracted both, (a) and (b) above.

(ii )

This satisfaction should be arrived at during the course of any proceeding. These could be assessment, reassessment or rectification proceedings, but not penalty proceedings.

(iii )

If ingredients contained in (i) and (ii) are present, a notice to show cause under section 274 shall be issued setting out therein the infraction the assessee is said to have committed. The notice under section 274 can be issued both, during or after, the completion of assessment proceedings; however, the satisfaction of the Assessing Officer that there has been an infraction of clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 should precede conclusion of the proceedings pending before the Assessing Officer.

(iv )

The order imposing penalty can be passed only after assessment proceedings are completed. The time-frame for passing the order is contained in section 275. [Para 10]

The provisions of section 271(1)(c ) remain insulated from the amendment brought about by the Finance Act, 2008 whereby the impugned provision, that is, section 271(1B) was inserted. [Para 11]

Where such concealed income is already detected, it cannot be said that there is concealed income, and hence, excluding them from the benefit of the scheme is clearly reasonable and appropriate to the object of the scheme. The contention that persons equally placed are not treated equally arises from an assumption that the section applies to the persons but in fact, the section applies only to incomes. Consequently, the classification of the income as concealed income and discovered income is certainly a valid classification appropriate to the purpose of the Scheme. The contention that a search made during the Scheme period is an arbitrary exercise of power to deprive the petitioner of the benefit of the Scheme also fails on three grounds. Firstly, as held by the Supreme Court in Tribhovandas Bhimji Zaveri v. Union of India [1993] 204 ITR 368/ 71 Taxman 309, the income-tax authorities are not debarred from conducting a search. Secondly, the person whose premises are searched is also not debarred from making a disclosure of income which was not discovered. Thirdly, on a proper construction of sub-section(2)(ii) as relating only to the income detected, it has no relevance to the Scheme period and applies equally to all the assessees whatever be the previous year in which the search is conducted as it would be confined to the income detected.

The contention that the classification of the cases of search as a separate class ignores the case where nothing is discovered, also falls to the ground in view of the proper construction of the section inasmuch as, if nothing is found, there would be no bar to the declaration of income which remained concealed.

In conclusion, it is declared that—

(A) Section 64 of the Finance Act, 1997 grants concession of tax and immunity to the undisclosed income which is declared in the Scheme period.

(B) The income that is not returned within the time prescribed in the notice issued under section 142 or 148 and which expires before the commence-ment of the scheme, would be ineligible under section 64(2)(i) for the benefit under section 64(1).

(C) That benefit is denied to the income which is detected in a search under section 132, on a requisition under section 132A or in a survey under section 133A, whichever be the previous year to which the detected income relates.

(D) Any undisclosed income other than such detected income in relation to any previous year can still be declared and would be eligible for the benefit under section 64(1).

(E) If subsequently it is found that the income disclosed under VDIS, 1997 is to be assessed as part of the total income of any previous year and is, thus, ineligible to be declared under section 64(1), the tax paid under section 64(1) would be adjusted against the assessed tax.

Therefore, it is held that on a proper construction of section 64, there is no discrimination or infirmity in that section and it is constitutionally valid.

In the circumstances, the respondents were directed to entertain voluntary disclosures falling within the above parameters as falling under section 64(1) of the Finance Act, 1997.

As per section 297(2)(g) the proceedings for imposition of penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year which is completed on or after the 1-4-1962, shall be under the Act. As the assessment was for the assessment year 1954-55, and as it was completed after April, 1962, the proceeding for imposition of penalty under the Act was perfectly competent. Therefore, the proceedings for the imposition of penalty under section 271 of the Act were not open to attack.

As regards violation of article 20(1) of the Constitution, the argument was that as this article prohibited the imposition of a penalty greater than that which might have been imposed upon the petitioner under the law in force on the date of the commission of the offence, she was not liable to be prosecuted, as a penalty had already been imposed upon her on the same facts, and that the petitioner stood in danger of being prosecuted for an offence under section 277 of the Act of 1961.

From section 277 it is clear that, unless a person makes a statement in any verification under the Act or under any rules made thereunder or delivers an account or statement which is false and which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true, he shall not be punishable. The act of the petitioner was not an offence under the Act. Therefore, a prosecution on the basis that she committed an offence under the provisions of section 277 would not lie. Hence the apprehension of the petitioner that she would be prosecuted under the new Act was an idle one.

The maximum penalty being the same in both the enactments, there was no substance in the contention that the petitioner was being subjected to a greater penalty under the new Act because a minimum is specified in section 271 of the 1961 Act, Penalty is nothing but compensation for damages collected by the State for attempting to evade the provisions of the Act. No conviction for any offence is involved in the imposition of a penalty. Article 20(1) of the Constitution will have application only when a person is subjected to a penalty greater than that which might to have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. This would indicate that commission of an offence and a conviction thereof are necessary in order that the provisions of the Article may be attracted.

Although the concealment of the particulars of the income was made an offence under section 52 of the 1922 Act and is also made an offence under section 277 of the new Act, it couldnot be said that the penalty imposed under section 28 of the 1922 Act or under section 271 of the 1961 Act was or is imposed on the basis that it was or is an offence. For the offence punishment was or is prescribed such as imprisonment, fine or both. The imposition of penalty on the basis of an act or omission by an assessee is not because the act or omission constitutes an offence, but because that act or omission would constitute an attempt at evasion. Therefore penalty is exacted not because an act or omission is an offence but because it is an attempt at evasion of tax on the part of the assessee. Article 20(1) of the Constitution can have no application to a case where a penalty is imposed not as punishment for an offence but for some other collateral purpose.

So, even assuming that the penalty has been enhanced under the new Act, that would not attract the constitutional inhibition of article 20(1) of the Constitution because the penalty is imposed not as punishment for the commission of an offence, even though the act for which the penalty is imposed is an offence liable to be punished.

In view of above, the instant petition failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : The decision was in favour of revenue.

In K.P. Varghese v. ITO [1981] 131 ITR 597, the Supreme Court had to interpret section 52(2) of the Act which provided that if in the opinion of the AO, the fair market value of a capital asset transferred by an assessee exceeds the consideration declared by the assessee by at least 15% of the consideration so declared, then such fair market value shall be deemed to be the full value of the consideration for such capital asset. Thus, section 52(2), on literal interpretation permitted substitution of the declared consideration by fair market value. The Supreme Court did not accept the literal interpretation on various grounds based on the language, the context, the Finance Minister's speech, etc., and also on certain general principles of law.

The Supreme Court observed as follows:

"section 52 is not a charging section but is a computation section. It has to be read along with section 48 which provides the mode of computation and under which the starting point of computation is "the full value of the consideration received or accruing". What in fact never accrued or was never received cannot be computed as capital gains under section 48. Therefore, sub-section (2) cannot be considered as bringing within the computation of capital gains an amount which, by no stretch of imagination, can be said to have accrued to the assessee or been received by him".

". . . .It is a well settled rule of interpretation that the Court should as far as possible avoid that construction which attributes irrationality to the Legislature. Besides, under entry 82 in List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, which deals with "Taxes on income other than agricultural income" and under which the Income-tax Act, 1961, has been enacted, Parliament cannot "choose to tax as income an item which in no rational sense can be regarded as a citizen's income or even receipt. Sub-section (2) would, therefore, on the construction of the revenue, go outside the legislative power of Parliament and it would not be possible to justify it even as an incidental or ancillary provision or a provision intended to prevent evasion of tax".

". . . .Sub-section (2) would also be violative of the fundamental right of the assessee under article 19(1)(f) - which fundamental right was in existence at the time when sub-section (2) came to be enacted - since on the construction canvassed on behalf of the revenue, the effect of sub-section (2) would be to penalize the assessee for transferring his capital asset for a consideration lesser by 15% or more than the fair market value and that would constitute unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right of the assessee to dispose of his capital asset at the price of his choice".

". . . .Sub-section (2) has no application in the case of an honest and bona fide transaction where the consideration received by the assessee has been correctly declared or disclosed by him and there is no concealment or suppression of the consideration".

All the aforesaid arguments are applicable in relation to section 50C :

(a)

It attempts to tax what may have never accrued or received.

(b)

It goes outside the legislative power of the Parliament since such fair value cannot in a rational manner be regarded as income/receipt.

(c)

It would hit a bona fide transaction, where there is no concealment or suppression of the consideration.

Having regard to the above it appears that there are strong arguments against the constitutional validity of section 50C.

Further, different stamp duty statutes have different basis or valuation. To illustrate, in Andhra Pradesh, the stamp duty is payable on the market value of the property. In Punjab, the stamp duty is payable on the value or amount of consideration (Article 23). In Delhi, it is payable on the consideration amount set forth in the instrument (Article 23). In Maharashtra, it is payable on the 'true market value' of the property (Article 25). Thus, the section puts different entities in different States in different position vis-a-vis section 50C.

It may be noted that the section refers to stamp duty valuation by a State Government and is silent about a property in a Union Territory.

Constitutional validity of section 143(1A)(a )(B) was challenged in Sanctus Drugs Pharmaceuticals (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [1997] 225 ITR 252/ 91 Taxman 246 (MP). The Division Bench held that Entry 82, List-1, of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India, empowers the Parliament to enact the law on income-tax and when the Parliament is competent to enact the law prospectively, it can also lay down the law retrospectively. Under section 143(1A), prior to amendment by the Finance Act, 1993 with effect from 1-4-1989, what was being taxed was the difference between the income determined as a result of adjustments under section 143(1)(a ). But after the amendment, the actual reduction in the loss had been directly made taxable at 20 per cent of the tax payable as if such difference was the total income, as additional tax. The levy of tax was not on the loss. This device was to check evasion of tax by clever taxpayers. Hence, it was of a compensatory nature. Thus, there was no unconstitutionality in section 143(1A)(a)(B). [Para 10]

A close look at the statutory provision under challenge demonstrated that it was not penal in nature. It was the device to check evasion of tax. It is no doubt true that a power under a taxing statute can be assailed if it is found to be arbitrary or lays down unreasonable restriction upon the freedom of trade, but in the instant matter, the restriction had been made for a justifiable reason in order to check the evasion of tax. By the insertion of that provision in the Act, the assessee might not be able to evade tax by resorting to the method of showing loss first and then by reducing the loss. Thus, the provision was compensatory in nature. [Para 12]

Consequently, appeal of the revenue was to be allowed and impugned judgment dated 19-1-1993 would stand as set aside. The writ petition of the assessee was to be dismissed as there was no unconstitutionality in section 143(1A)(a)(B). [Para 13]

Subsequently, regular assessments were completed and the tax payable thereon were determined. On appeal, the AAC had reduced the quantum of penalty, while the Writ Petitiions were pending.

FACT: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of section 18(1)( a), as it stood for the assessment year 1969-70, on the following grounds: (i) that this provision permitted the levy of minimum penalty of ½ per cent of the net wealth assessed per month for each month of delay in filing the return and, therefore, it was in contravention of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution as in ah appropriate case the penalty may be equal to the value of total wealth assessed, that is, the maximum limit of the penalty permissible, and was, therefore, confiscatory; (ii) that section 18(1)(a)( i) permitted the imposition of penalty for delay of each month whereas the wealth-tax was assessed on the net wealth per year and this was in contravention of article 19(1)(f); (iii )that the penalty should be co-related with the duty and not with the net wealth assessed and, thus, the penalty being leviable at ½per cent of the net wealth was unreasonable and was hit by article 19(1)(f); (iv)that as this provision conferred jurisdiction on the WTO to impose minimum penalty which was 2 per cent of the assessed wealth up to the maximum which was equal to the total value of the assessed wealth and thereby gave a wide discretion to the WTO without any guidelines, this discretion violated article 14 of the Constitution; and (v) that levy of penalty at the rate of ½ per cent was discriminatory because the assessee, who was a smaller assessee and whose wealth-tax was assessed at ½ per cent. also will suffer a penalty of ½ per cent whereas the other who may be a substantial assessee and paid wealth-tax at a higher rate still the penalty which could be imposed was only ½ per cent and in this manner so far as a smaller assessee was concerned it was harsh, whereas for a substantial assessee it was rather lenient and, thus, was discriminatory and, therefore, contrary to the provisions contained in article 14 of the Constitution.

HELD: So far as the question of confiscatory nature of the provision was concerned, it was clear that the penalty had been provided at the rate of ½ per cent of the net assessed wealth per month or each month's delay. It was, therefore, clear that for a month's delay in filing the return the only penalty which could be imposed was ½ per cent of the total wealth. The contention that if this delay went on to the extent that the penalty will be equal to the wealth as that was the maximum limit permissible it was confiscatory and, therefore, contravened article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution, was purely based on a hypothesis consideration of which was nothing but an academic exercise as admittedly the penalty imposed on the petitioner was only for four months' delay which will come to only two per cent of the total wealth assessed and it could, therefore, not be contended that the penalty imposed against the petitioner was confiscatory in nature. Such a situation can never arise, as admittedly, the provision has then been amended and there is no question of such a situation now. In this view of the matter this contention could not be accepted as it was just a mere imagination and was not based on facts of this case. The imposition of penalty at the rate of ½ per cent {of the total assessed wealth) for each month's delay could not be said to be confiscatory in nature.

So far as contention No. ( iii) was concerned, the levy of penalty of ½ per cent of the total wealth assessed could not be said to be unreasonable for any reason on the basis of which it could be said that it will be in contravention of article 19(1)(f).

HELD: Section 140A, is a new section introduced with effect from 1-4-1964. As per sub-section (1), the moment a return is furnished the tax due, on the basis of the return as reduced by the tax already paid, becomes payable. With reference to the legal position prior to the introduction of section 140A, the Supreme Court in Kesoram Industries and Cotton Mills Ltd. v. CWT [1966] 59 ITR 767; [1966] 2 SCR 688 (SC) held that a liability to pay income-tax was a present liability, though the tax became payable after it was quantified in accordance with the ascertainable data and that there was a perfected debt at any rate on the last date of the accounting year and not a contingent liability. Again, in CWT v. Standard Vacuum Oil Co. Ltd., [1966] 59 ITR 569; [1966] 2 SCR_317 (SC) approving the decision of the Gujarat High Court in CWT v. Raipur Manufacturing Co., [1964] 52 ITR 482 (Guj.), the Supreme Court observed that a condition subsequent, the fulfilment of which may result in the reduction or even extinction of liability, would not have the effect of converting the liability which attaches into a contingent liability. This tax which was a present liability and a perfected ‘debt’ on the last date of the accounting year and which would become payable after it was quantified in accordance with the provisions of the Act, has now been made payable on furnishing of the return itself without waiting for the quantification in the assessment proceedings. After the tax became payable the relationship between the Government and the assessee is that of a creditor and debtor. In this respect there is no distinction between the tax payable under section 140A and one payable under a demand notice made after a provisional assessment under section 141 or a regular assessment under section 143 or 144. The only difference is that no demand notice under section 156 could be issued in respect of the liability under section 140A. Section 140A speaks of self-assessment and no order is made by any assessing authority under that section. The consequences of non-applicability of section 156 may result in the non-applicability of the tax recovery provisions under sections 220 and 221. But section 232 saves the right of the Government to recover the same under the provisions of any other law for the time being in force relating to the recovery of debts due to the Government or the right of the Government to institute a suit for recovery of arrears due from the assessee. Thus, the tax payable under section 140A(1), if not voluntarily paid, is recoverable as any other debt due to the Government.

Any provision intended to enforce payment or recovery of tax payable could also provide for inclusion and recovery of anything compensatory for delayed payment or retention of the amount of tax payable. It is also the ordinary rule in actions for recovery of money only, that the creditor recovers beyond the amount of the debt the interest on the money withheld or the value of the use of the money while he is kept out of it provided the agreement, express or implied, between the parties provided for it or there exists an express statutory provision to the effect that the interest may be allowed. The Act itself has in various pro-visions imposed liability to pay interest on delayed payment of taxes. But the question is whether Parliament could not provide for levy of a penalty of the nature stated in section 140A(3) for failure to pay in time the tax payable.

Every citizen is entitled to retain his income ascertained after deduction of the taxes payable under the Act. The Government is entitled for payment of only the taxes. Any provision which authorises the taking by the Government of the retained income of the citizen would be confiscatory unless it is saved under article 19(5). It is now well-settled that tax laws also are subject to fundamental rights under articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court has also held that, in order to decide whether a particular legislative measure contravenes any of the fundamental rights, it is necessary to examine with some strictness the substance of the legislation in order to see what the legislation has really done. The legislation cannot bypass a constitutional prohibition by employing indirect methods and, therefore, the court has to look behind the form and appearance to discover the true character and nature of legislation: vide Dwarkadas Shrinivas v. Sholapur Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd. [1954] 24 Comp. Cas 103; [1954] SCR 674; AIR 1954 SC 119 and Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India AIR 1960 SC 554.

By virtue of section 44AC inserted by the Finance Act, 1988, a person dealing in alcohol meant for human consumption, timber, and forest produce, who obtained such goods by way of auction, tender or any other mode from specified sellers such as the Central or State Government, local authority, etc., was deemed to earn profits thereon at the rate of specified percentage of the purchase price and tax was to be collected from him by the seller at the time of sale and credited to the Government in terms of section 206C, also inserted by the Finance Act, 1988. These two provisions were enacted with a view to curbing tax evasion. By way of writ petitions this presumptive and pre-emptive levy of tax had been challenged by the petitioners on the grounds, (i) that what was sought to be taxed by force of section 44AC was not income and as such, the Parliament lacked legislative competence to enact it as well as section 206C, (ii)that section 44AC was discriminatory and arbitrary and hence violative of article 14, and (iii) that the rates fixed by section 44AC were confiscatory and the same had imposed unreasonable restrictions on the freedom to carry on trade or business and as such this section was violative of article 19(1)(g).

133A under the Income-tax Act’ was inserted before the phrase "or in respect of any earlier previous year" which has led to a situation where a reference to the earlier previous years gets attached to the survey operation which can only refer to the current or specific year and not all earlier years, whereas both sections 132 and 132A refer to the special procedure for assessment of search cases involving a block of 10 previous years, thus, giving rise to a certain absurdity unless properly construed. The real scope of the ban in respect of ‘any earlier previous years’ must, therefore, be clearly understood. Since the main section grants a concession in respect of concealed income which is declared, the ban under sub-section (2)(ii) can only refer to the concealed income which has been detected and which can no longer be the concealed income. In other words, the income referred to in sub-section (2)(ii) must be that income which could otherwise be declared under sub-section (1). Construed in this way income which was a subject of an assessment under Chapter XIV-B would not be eligible for the benefit and the ban would operate for the block of 10 previous years preceding the previous year in which a search was conducted because that would be the block period for which assessment would be made under Chapter XIV-B of the Income-tax Act. In the case of a survey, only such income which is concealed from the books but detected, would be ineligible for the benefit. Since that income would be confined to the year of survey of specific year to which the data related, it would follow that the ban cannot operate in respect of any or all other earlier previous years. The revenue submitted that the ban was with reference to the assessee and not the income. It is not possible to accept this interpretation because of two reasons. Firstly, sub-section (2) of section 64 stated that nothing in sub-section (1) shall apply in relation to the cases mentioned in that sub-section. Since sub-section (1) only relates to the income eligible for concessional rate of tax and immunity, income referred to in sub-section (2) could also relate only to that income and not the assessee. Secondly, section 78 specifically lists the persons to whom the scheme would not apply and since the assessees who are subject to search or survey, are not listed under section 78, it underlines the position that section 64 (ii ) refers only to income and not to persons. This construction removes the internal contradictions in the section about the application to the earlier previous years with reference to the search and survey operations. It also saves those persons where nothing is detected in the search and enables them to make a disclosure of the concealed income which will go to effectuate the main objective of the VDIS.

The meaning of the word "income" in section 64(2)(ii) could only refer to the kind that would otherwise be governed by sub-section (1). If it is to refer to the total income of the previous year, it would prohibit the disclosure of undetected income contrary to the very object of the scheme which is to harness black money for productive purposes. Therefore, undisclosed income duly declared is eligible for the concession. But if the interpretation that income referred to the entire income of the previous year is adopted, it would discriminate against concealed income left undiscovered in a search without any rational basis. On a true construction of the section, any concealed income declared is eligible for concessional rate of tax and immunities. The question of discrimination arises only if the section is read in the way in which the revenue wants to read it so as to deny the benefit to income concealed in spite of a search, In the context of section 64(1), the word "income" in section 64(2)(ii) can refer only to undisclosed income eligible for concessional tax becoming ineligible by detection before declaration. This meaning is in consonance with the object of the Scheme as stated in the memorandum. Thus, reading all the sections together and on a true construction of sub-section 2(ii) only the income which is the subject-matter of the assessment would be ineligible for disclosure and the assessee is free to disclose the income of any previous year as long as it has not been detected.

Regarding the question of discrimination, the contention that the classification of tax evaders has no nexus with the object of the scheme is untenable. On a true construction of the Scheme, the object is to give a concessional rate of tax and immunity in respect of the disclosure of concealed income. Where such concealed income is already detected, it cannot be said that there is concealed income, and hence, excluding them from the benefit of the scheme is clearly reasonable and appropriate to the object of the scheme. The contention that persons equally placed are not treated equally arises from an assumption that the section applies to the persons but in fact, the section applies only to incomes. Consequently, the classification of the income as concealed income and discovered income is certainly a valid classification appropriate to the purpose of the Scheme.

the courts is only to find out whether the classification actually introduced by Parliament is hit by article 14 of the Constitution. There may be a variety of classifications which can be introduced for achieving a particular object, but if Parliament in its wisdom adopts one in preference to another, the courts cannot take exception to the classification chosen if it is not proved to be obnoxious to the constitutional provision. The classification introduced by the Explanation to section 271(1) does not offend article 14 of the Constitution. Intelligible differentia deductible from the wording of the Explanation to section 271(1) has a rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved by the Explanation. If the assessees commit the excess of showing their incomes at figures so short as to attract the applicability of the Explanation, they shall be presumed to be guilty within the meaning of clause (c) and liable to penalty to the extent mentioned in sub-section (1)(iii ) of section 271 if they cannot prove that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on their part. The allocation of burden on the assessees in the circumstances mentioned in the Explanation will surely have a deterrent effect in the matter of submitting under-estimated or false returns with the consequence that the prospects of submitting true returns of the income or returns which are more close to actuality shall brighten up. Hence there is a rational nexus between the differentia introduced by the Explanation and the object which Parliament had in view in enacting that Explanation.

In the result, the writ petition failed and was dismissed.

to say that in spite of the provisions of the Act mentioned in the non obstante clause, enactment following it will have its full operation;

◆ Non obstante clause is to be understood as operating to set aside as no longer valid anything contained in relevant existing law which is inconsistent with the new enactment; and

◆ The enacting parts of the statute must, where it is clear, be taken to control the non obstante clause, where both cannot be read harmoniously. As discussed above, section 115JB(1) only seeks to substitute the income-tax payable by SPT. This is the only and limited objective. Thus, the non obstante clause will override only those provisions which are in conflict with the objective of providing for the payment of SPT. In other words, the other provisions would not be affected or rather cannot be considered as in conflict with the provision. The inference is based on the following reasoning:

Broadly stated, section 115JB lays down:

◆ Substitution of SPT for income-tax payable [sub-section (1)];

◆ Providing machinery for computation of book profit [sub-section (2)];

◆ Saving determination of unabsorbed losses, etc. [sub-section (3)];

◆ Requires obtaining and furnishing Accountant’s Report [sub-section (4)]; and

◆ Application of the other provisions of the Act [sub-section (5)].

It would be appreciated that the section provides for the levy; machinery for computation; compliance with certain conditions, etc. How-ever, it does not provide for the charge, collection and recovery, assessment, etc. Accordingly, it makes the other provisions of the Act applicable. Accordingly, it’s a complete code. The substantive provision is sub-section (1). Effectively, it seeks to create a fiction, limited to levy of SPT.

The non obstante clause, read with sub-section (5), and in particular, the first limb thereof, namely, ‘save as otherwise provided in this section’ and the limited object of levying SPT, seems to have only a limited overriding effect; but otherwise it relies on the other provisions of the Act, for the effective levy and recovery of tax.

The fiction, thus, has a limited field, namely

◆ Substitution of tax payable by SPT; and

◆ Computation of book profit.

Otherwise, it appears that all the provisions of the Act including the provisions relating to charge, definitions, recovery, payment, assessment, etc., would apply in construing the provisions of section 115JB.

Constitutional validity of section 115JB

1.4 It is examined having regard to:

◆ Decisions in respect of section 115J;

◆ Principle of Promissory Estoppel; and

◆ The provisions of section 115JB.

Constitutional validity of section 115J under articles 14 and 19 was considered and upheld by Delhi High Court in National Thermal Power Corporation Limited v. Union of India[1991] 192 ITR 187.

1.4-1 Decisions in respect of section 115J - The Supreme Court has granted special leave to the petitioner in the above case to appeal against the said judgment [1991] 192 ITR 3 (St.) Andhra Pradesh High Court in Suryalatha Spinning Mills Ltd. v. Union of India [1997] 223 ITR 713 inter alia, considered constitutional validity of section 115J and, following Supreme Court decision in Jain Brothers v. Union of India[1970] 77 ITR 107 and ITO v. N. Takin Roy Rymbai[1976] 103 ITR 82, it upheld the validity and, inter alia, relied on the following extracts from the decision of the Supreme Court in N. Takin Roy Rymbai’s case (supra).

“In taxation laws the State has, in view of the intrinsic complexity of fiscal adjustments of diverse elements, a considerably wide discretion in the matter of the classifications for taxation purposes. Legislature has ample freedom to select and classify persons, districts, goods, properties, incomes and objects which it could tax and which it would not tax. So long as the classification made within this wide and flexible range by a taxing statute does not transgress the doctrine of equality it is not vulnerable to attack on the ground of discrimination merely because it taxes or exempts from taxation, some incomes or objects and not others. Nor is the mere fact that a tax falls more heavily on some in the same category, by itself a ground to render the law invalid.”

It also relied on Delhi High Court decision in National Thermal Power Corporation Ltd. v. Union of India[1991] 192 ITR 187 upholding the validity of section 115J.

It also rejected the contention about Double Taxation for two reasons:

◆ What is taxed, on the basis prescribed, does not result into re-tax of the same income; and

◆ Double Taxation per se would not render an otherwise valid provisions, invalid, following Supreme Court decision in Jain Brothers v. Union of India [1970] 77 ITR 107.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c), read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1986-87 - Assessee, a wholesale dealer of cigarettes, confessed that it was charging ‘on-money’ on certain brands under directions of manufacturer-principal - On basis of assessee’s confession, Assessing Officer imposed penalty for concealment of income - Tribunal quashed penalty holding that though facts disclosed concealment of income, assessee was forced to charge ‘on-money’ for benefit of principal and business interest - Whether a referable question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was a dealer of cigarettes manufactured by GPIL. During search of GPIL’s premises, certain circulars were collected which instructed its dealers to charge ‘on-money’ on certain brands and to remit major portion of it to GPIL. The assessee-firm confessed that such ‘on-money’ charged so far was not accounted for in their books of account and they confirmed additional income. The Assessing Officer imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelled the penalty. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that though the dealers like the assessee concealed income, penalty could not be imposed as they were forced to charge ‘on-money’ for the benefit of the principal and other purposes in the interest of business. As a result, the Tribunal affirmed the deletion of penalty. The Tribunal refused to refer the issue to the High Court on the ground that the finding recorded by it was based on appreciation of materials available on record which gave rise to no question of law.

On an application under section 256(2) :

HELD: The Tribunal had clearly erred in considering the question arising out of its order to be a question of fact. Undoubtedly, the question of facts or inference of facts drawn from other established facts also becomes question of fact and, thus, cannot be said to be a question of law. The established facts as per the Tribunal’s order were that the assessee had concealed particulars of his income which he was required to disclose. The penalty had been held not liable to be imposed solely on the ground that though the facts disclosed concealment of income by the wholesale dealers of GPIL, yet such dealers could not be successfully visited with penalty under section 271(1)(c) in view of the circumstances that they were forced to charge ‘on-money’ for the benefit of the principal and promotion of sale and other bona fide conduct. The question, therefore, which required consideration was whether under the provisions of the Act, the assessee could legitimately claim justification for not disclosing income which was alleged to have been earned involuntarily by him or retained by him. It also gave rise to the question, whether such a finding was a finding to which any person instructed in law could reasonably reach. These were not questions of fact but rather questions of law or at any rate mixed questions of facts and law. Therefore, a referable question of law arose from the Tribunal’s order deleting the penalty.

Substitution of SPT for income-tax payable [sub-section (1)];

Application of the other provisions of the Act [sub-section (5)].

1.4-1 Decisions in respect of section 115J - The Supreme Court has granted special leave to the petitioner in the above case to appeal against the said judgment [1991] 192 ITR 3 (St.) Andhra Pradesh High Court in Suryalatha Spinning Mills Ltd. v. Union of India [1997] 223 ITR 713 inter alia, considered constitutional validity of section 115J and, following Supreme Court decision in Jain Brothers v. Union of India[1970] 77 ITR 107 and ITO v. N. Takin Roy Rymbai[1976] 103 ITR 82, it upheld the validity and, inter alia, relied on the following extracts from the decision of the Supreme Court in N. Takin Roy Rymbai's case (supra).

"In taxation laws the State has, in view of the intrinsic complexity of fiscal adjustments of diverse elements, a considerably wide discretion in the matter of the classifications for taxation purposes. Legislature has ample freedom to select and classify persons, districts, goods, properties, incomes and objects which it could tax and which it would not tax. So long as the classification made within this wide and flexible range by a taxing statute does not transgress the doctrine of equality it is not vulnerable to attack on the ground of discrimination merely because it taxes or exempts from taxation, some incomes or objects and not others. It also relied on Delhi High Court decision in National Thermal Power Corporation Ltd. v. Union of India[1991] 192 ITR 187 upholding the validity of section 115J.

It also rejected the contention about Double Taxation for two reasons:

What is taxed, on the basis prescribed, does not result into re-tax of the same income; and
