Union of India [1995] 215 ITR 758 (Kar.)]. 3.5-2a LACK OF CLASSIFICATION CREATES INEQUALITY AND IS HIT BY ARTICLE 14 - An illustration how lack of classification creates inequality and renders an Act violative of article 14 is found in the decision of the Supreme Court in Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala.1 The Travancore-Cochin Land Tax Act, 1955 was enacted by the Kerala Legislature to provide for the levy of a low and uniform rate of basic tax on all lands in the State of Travancore Cochin. Section 4 of the said Act, the charging section, read thus : “subject to the provisions of this Act, there shall be charged and levied in respect of all lands in the State, of whatever description and held under whatever tenure, a uniform rate of tax to be called the basic tax.” The basic tax, which was prescribed at Rs. 2 per acre, was payable on all lands notwithstanding any other law, contract or agreement. Section 5A provided for a provisional assessment of basic tax in case of unsurveyed lands subject, however, to a regular assessment to be made later. The Act did not contain a provision for issuing notice or opportunity to the concerned land-holder to make his submissions before determining the tax. A uniform tax was imposed on all lands. There was no provision for appeal. Indeed, there was no assessment of tax as such. The tax levied was payable irrespective of the quality of the land, or its productive capacity, and irrespective of the fact whether the land yields any income, or not. The petitioners, who challenged the validity of the Act, were owners of forest areas in certain parts of Kerala which, before the reorganisation of States, formed part of the State of Madras. They were governed by a Madras Act which continued to govern them even after reorganisation, until the impugned Act came into force. The Madras Act provided that the forests shall not be cut, nor the rights in the forest produce sold, or otherwise alienated without the permission of the District Collector. A particular petitioner, whose case was taken as representative of others, was deriving an income of Rs. 3,100 per year by lease of forest. The forest was assessed provisionally under section 5A to a tax of Rs. 50,000 per annum. Since it was an unsurveyed forest, the District Collector conjectured the area of forest at 25,000 acres and on that basis, determined the tax payable at Rs. 50,000. The petitioner’s case was that he was being given permission to cut the forest only in instalments, that his annual income was only Rs. 3,100, whereas he was called upon to pay a tax of Rs. 50,000 per annum. It was also submitted that his forest had large areas of arid rocks, rivulets, and gorges. The Supreme Court observed that ordinarily a tax on land, or land revenue, is assessed on the actual or potential productivity of the land sought to be taxed, and that the tax has reference to the income actually made, or which could have been made with due diligence. But the impugned Act, it was pointed out, makes no such distinction. There may be several types of land; a particular land may be arid desert yielding no income; the second one does not yield any income, but may be capable of yielding an income by raising a crop after a disproportionately large investment of labour and capital; a third type of land yields just enough to pay for the incidental expenses, labour charges, and taxes, while the fourth type of land may be making large profits because it is very fertile and capable of yielding good crops. While the fourth category, it was pointed out, would easily be able to meet the burden of tax and the third one might be just able to bear the tax, the first and second categories would not be able to bear the tax burden. Because the tax is not paid, the very land may be sold for realizing the demand, which would make the Act confiscatory in nature. It was observed, “there is no attempt at classification in the provisions of the Act...It is one of those cases where the lack of classification creates inequality. It is, therefore, clearly hit by the prohibition to deny equality before the law contained in article 14 of the Constitution.....” It was also observed that the Act constitutes an unreasonable restriction upon the right to hold property, guaranteed by article 19(1)(f), and being a disproportionate and unreasonable imposition, was not saved by clause (6) thereof.

10.2 The tax rate on unexplained income is reduced from 60% to 30% [Section 195 of ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 115BBE of ITA 1961)]

10.2-1 Position under the ITA 1961

The unexplained income as referred to in sections 68 to 69D detected by the Assessing Officer or offered by the assessee suo-moto to tax in the Income-tax return shall be taxable at a special rate as provided in Section 115BBE. This provision provides that such an unexplained income shall be taxable at the rate of 60%, which shall be further increased by a surcharge of 25% and health and education cess. The effective tax rate shall be 78% [Tax 60% + 15% Surcharge (at the rate of 25% of 60%) + 3% Health & Education Cess (at the rate of 4% of the aggregate of Tax and Surcharge of 75%)].

The Assessing Officer shall also levy a penalty in respect of unexplained income in accordance with section 271AAC.

10.2-2 Position under the ITA 2025 (as amended by the Finance Act, 2026)

Section 195 of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to section 115BBE of the ITA 1961) specified the same tax rate of 60% (plus surcharge and cess) in respect of the unexplained income.

The Finance Act, 2026, effective from 1-4-2026, makes comprehensive changes in the provisions dealing with the taxation of the unexplained income, which includes the following:

(a)

Section 195 is amended to reduce the tax rate on undisclosed income from 60% to 30%.

(b)

Section 443 (corresponding to section 271AAC of the ITA 1961), which provides for the levy of a penalty in case of unexplained income, is omitted from the Act [see Para 18.2-2].

(c)

Section 439 (corresponding to Section 270A of the ITA 1961), which provides for the levy of a penalty in case of undisclosed income due to under-reporting or mis-reporting, is amended to include the unexplained income within the scope of this provision [see Para 18.3].

(d)

Section 440 (corresponding to section 270AA of the ITA 1961), which provides immunity from the penalty on fulfilment of specified conditions, is amended to grant immunity from the penalty to be imposed under section 439 on the unexplained income on the payment of a fee [see Para 18.4].

Also see Para 18.4-4 for the implications of taxation of unexplained income under ITA 205 vis-à-vis ITA 1961.

10.2-3 Reduction in the tax rate

Section 195 of the ITA 2025 deals with the following two situations:

(a)

If the total income of the assessee as reflected in the Income-tax return includes any unexplained income as referred to in Sections 102 to 106 (corresponding to sections 68 to 69D of ITA 1961).

(b)

If the total income of the assessee determined by the Assessing Officer includes any unexplained income as referred to in sections 102 to 106.

The Finance Act, 2026, reduces the tax rate on unexplained income under section 195 from 60% to 30% in both situations.

Unexplained income declared by the assessee in the return of income, which was previously taxed at an effective rate of 78%, is now taxable at a reduced effective rate of 39%. This amendment offers a significant reduction in the tax burden for taxpayers who voluntarily declare their unexplained income. However, the effective tax rate will differ in these situations if a penalty is imposed under Section 439 or if the assessee pays the immunity fee under section 440. 13.3.2b It may be noted that for levying the penalty the section imposes an additional condition (when compared with Explanation 5 applicable upto 1-6-2007), namely, substantiation of the manner of deriving income. 'Substantiates', Webster's New Collegiate Dictionary means:

'1: to impart substance to 2: to put into concrete form… 3: to establish by proof or competent evidence'.

Accordingly, in the context of 'deriving income', for claiming concessional penalty, it would be necessary for an assessee to:

Explain the way, mode and method of deriving such income; and

Prove his explanation by proof or competent evidence.

To illustrate, an assessee explains, in the course of search, the cash found represents income derived from speculation. To claim concessional penalty, the assessee will have to:

State the manner of deriving the income (that is, the way, mode and method adopted); and

In Calicut Trading Co. v. CIT [1989] 178 ITR 430 (Ker.), special leave petition dismissed by the Supreme Court: (1989) 180 ITR (St.) 40 (SC), the petitioner firm filed a return for the assessment year 1983-84 on April 28, 1984, disclosing a total income of Rs. 274510. The Income- tax officer wrote to the assessee pointing out certain cash credits and other credit balances not accounted for and, therefore, the assessee was asked to furnish evidence to prove the source of the said credits. The assessee then filed a return on December 22, 1984, which, according to the assessee, was to purchase peace. The assessment order was passed by the Income-tax Officer, accepting the return, on December 28, 1984, on a total income of Rs. 524510 which included Rs. 250000 the enhanced income returned by the assessee. Subsequently, in the course of the assessment for the assessment year 1984-85, the income-tax officer found that the accounts of the partners were credited with a total sum of Rs. 250000 in proportion to their profit sharing ratio along with a narration that these credit represented additional income offered for assessment in the assessment year 1983-84. 1-6aAGGREGATION OF PENALTY IN CASE OF THE TOTAL INCOME [115JB/115JC] - To provide for aggregation, in section 271(1), Explanation 4 was inserted by the Finance Act, 2015 and the reasons for the introduction of the same were explained as follows:

'Amount of tax sought to be evaded for the purposes of penalty for concealment of income under clause (iii) of sub-section (1) of section 271 Under the existing provision contained in clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 of the Act penalty for concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income is levied on the "amount of tax sought to be evaded", which has been defined, inter alia, as the difference between the tax due on the income assessed and the tax which would have been chargeable had such total income been reduced by the amount of concealed income. Problems have arisen in the computation of amount of tax sought to be evaded where the concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income occurs in the computation of income under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act and also under the provisions other than the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act (hereafter referred as general provisions). Further, courts have held that penalty under section clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 cannot be levied in cases where the concealment of income occurs under the income computed under general provisions and the tax is paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act. Tax paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC over and above the tax liability arising under general provisions is available as credit for set off against future tax liability. Under-statement of income and the tax liability thereon under general provisions results in larger amount of such credit becoming available to the assessee for set off in future years. Therefore, where concealment of income, as computed under the general provisions, has taken place, penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 should be leviable even if the tax liability of the assessee for the year has been determined under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act. Accordingly, it is proposed to amend section 271 of the Act so as to provide that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be the summation of tax sought to be evaded under the general provisions and the tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. However, if an amount of concealment of income on any issue is considered both under the general provisions and provisions of section 115JB or 115JC then such amount shall not be considered in computing tax sought to be evaded under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. Further, in a case where the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC are not applicable, the computation of tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC shall be ignored. This amendment will take effect from 1st April, 2016 and will accordingly apply, in relation to the assessment year 2016-17 and subsequent assessment years. [Clause 68]'.

In Fakir Mohmed Haji Hasan v. CIT [2002] 120 Taxman 11 (Guj.), the Gujarat High Court laid down the following propositions:

The scheme of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C of the Act would show that in cases where the nature and source of investments made by the assessee or the nature and source of acquisition of money, bullion, etc., owned by the assessee or the source of expenditure incurred by the assessee are not explained at all, or not satisfactorily explained, then the value of such investments and money, or value of articles not recorded in the books of account or the unexplained expenditure may be deemed to be the income of such assessee.

It follows that the moment a satisfactory explanation is given about such nature and source by the assessee, then the source would stand disclosed and will, therefore, be known and the income would be treated under the appropriate head of income for assessment as per the provisions of the Act.

However, when these provisions apply because no source is disclosed at all on the basis of which the income can be classified under one of the heads of income under section 14 of the Act, it would not be possible to classify such deemed income under any of these heads including 'Income from other sources' which have to be sources known or explained.

When the income cannot be so classified under any one of the heads of income under section 14, it follows that the question of giving any deductions under the provisions which correspond to such heads of income will not arise.

If it is possible to peg the income under any one of those heads by virtue of a satisfactory explanation being given, then these provisions of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C will not apply, in which event the provisions regarding deductions, etc., applicable to the relevant head of income under which such income falls will automatically be attracted.

The opening words of section 14 'Save as otherwise provided by this Act' clearly leave scope for 'deemed income' of the nature covered under the scheme of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C being treated separately, because such deemed income is not income from salary, house property, profits and gains of business or profession, or capital gains, nor is it income from 'other sources' because the provisions of sections 69, 69A, 69B, and 69C treat unexplained investments, unexplained money, bullion, etc., and unexplained expenditure as deemed income where the nature and source of investment, acquisition or expenditure, as the case may be, have not been explained or satisfactorily explained. Therefore, in these cases, the source not being known, such deemed income will not fall even under the head 'Income from other sources'.

Therefore, the corresponding deductions, which are applicable to the incomes under any of these various heads, will not be attracted in case of deemed incomes which are covered under the provisions of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C in view of the scheme of those provisions.

18.3-1aPenalty for under-reporting and misreporting of income - Section 270A of the ITA 1961 provides that a penalty is levied if a person has under-reported income (except unexplained income). The penalty may be levied at a rate of 50% of the tax payable on under-reported income, or at 200% where under-reported income is in consequence of misreporting. The following cases will be considered as misreporting of income:

(a)

Misrepresentation or suppression of facts,

(b)

Failure to record investments in the books of account,

(c)

Claim of expenditure not substantiated by any evidence,

(d)

Recording of any false entry in the books of account,

(e)

Failure to record any receipt in books of account having a bearing on total income, and

(f)

Failure to report any international transaction or any transaction deemed to be an international transaction or any specified domestic transaction.

18.3-1b Penalty in case of unexplained income - Section 271AAC of the ITA 1961 states that a penalty is imposed if the income determined for the assessee includes unexplained income for which the assessee has not provided any explanation about its nature and source, or if the explanation given is unsatisfactory. The penalty is imposed at the rate of 10% of the tax payable on such unexplained income.

The ITA 1961 provides for the taxation of unexplained income under Sections 68 to 69D. Unexplained income includes all incomes, investments, or expenditures for which the assessee does not have any satisfactory explanation. The Assessing Officer may identify the unexplained income, or the assessee can voluntarily declare it in the Income-tax return. In both cases, the unexplained income will be taxed at the special rate specified in Section 115BBE. No penalty will be imposed under this provision if the assessee has included the unexplained income in the return of income and has paid the tax thereon under Section 115BBE on or before the end of the relevant previous year.

13.1-8 Exclusions [Sub-section (6)]

It is provided, the unreported income should not include certain specified amount of income under the specified circumstances, like, bona fide explanation; estimation; undisclosed income liable to penalty under section 271AAB etc. and they are discussed here after.

Before dealing with different situations, it may be pointed out that the opening language of sub-section (6), reads: 'the under-reported income, for the purposes of this section, shall not include the following …'; and, thereafter, it lists five different situations providing that the amount of income or underreported income referred to in each of them shall not be included.

As said earlier, while providing the circumstances in which it can be said that the income is under-reported and/or quantification thereof, the section compares and/or treats the difference between total income as per return or intimation and total income as per assessment or reassessment as the under-reported income. In other words, it does not add up various different additions made in the course of assessment to quantify the same as underreported income. However, while providing for the exclusions, it does refer to the components of income (added while computing the total income).

◆ Non obstante clause is to be understood as operating to set-aside as no longer valid anything contained in relevant existing law which is inconsistent with the new enactment; and

◆ The enacting parts of the statute must, where it is clear, be taken to control the non obstante clause, where both cannot be read harmoniously. Section 115JC(1) has a limited objective to substitute regular income tax payable by AMT. Thus the non obstante clause will override only those provisions which are inconsistent with or in conflict with the objective of providing for the payment of AMT. In other words, the other provisions would not be affected or rather cannot be considered as inconsistent with or in conflict with the provision. The inference is based on the following reasoning:

Broadly stated, the section lays down:

◆ substitution of AMT for regular income tax [sub-section (1)];

◆ providing machinery for computation of adjusted total income [sub-section (2)];

◆ obtaining and furnishing Accountant’s Report [sub-section (3)]; and

◆ application of the other provisions of the Act [section 115JE].

It would be appreciated that the section provides for the levy; machinery for computation; compliance with certain conditions, etc. However, it does not provide for the charge, collection and recovery, assessment, etc. Accordingly, to make it a complete code, the non obstante clause, read with section 115JE, and, in particular, the first limb thereof, namely, ‘save as otherwise provided in this section’ and the limited object of levying AMT, seems to have only a limited overriding effect; but otherwise it relies on the other provisions of the Act, for the effective levy and recovery of tax.

The fiction, thus, has a limited field, namely:

◆ Substitution of regular income tax payable by AMT; and

◆ Computation of adjusted total income.

Thus, it appears that all the provisions of the Act including the provisions relating to charge, definitions, recovery, payment, assessment, etc., would apply in construing the provisions of section 115JC.

33 Penalties

No amendment has been made in section 271 dealing with concealment penalty. Hence, it appears that the general provisions for penalty would apply to any IAA and its consequences as determined by the tax authorities. In other words, the principles for determining whether an assessee has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of his income within the meaning of section 271(1)(c) read with the Explanations to it have remained the same. Thus,

(a) assessment proceedings and penalty proceedings are two separate and distinct proceedings and the fact that certain additions are made in assessment proceedings would not automatically justify the Revenue to impose penalty under section 271(1)(c) [CIT v. Dharamchand L. Shah [1993] 70 Taxman 414/204 ITR 462 (Bom.);]

(b)

findings given in assessment proceedings, though relevant and admissible material in penalty proceedings, cannot operate as res judicata [CIT v. Gurudayalram Mukhlal [1991] 190 ITR 39/[1992] 60 Taxman 313 (Gau.); CIT v. Azad Bharat Finance Co. [1970] 75 ITR 40 (Delhi); Dwarka Prasad Sheokaran Das v. CIT [1953] 24 ITR 410 (All.); CIT v. Anwar Ali [1967] 65 ITR 95 (Cal.) affirmed in CIT v. Anwar Ali [1970] 76 ITR 696 (SC)].

(c)

The plain meaning of the expression 'furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income' implies furnishing of details or information about income which are not in conformity with the facts or truth. The details or information about income deal with the factual details of income and this cannot be extended to areas which are subjective such as the status of taxability of an income, admissibility of a deduction and interpretation of law. The furnishing of inaccurate information hence relates to furnishing of factually incorrect details and information about income [Kanbay Software India (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2009] 31 SOT 153 (Pune - Trib.)].

(d)

The meaning of the word 'particulars' used in section 271(1)(c) would embrace the details of the claim made. Where no information given in the return is found to be incorrect or inaccurate, the assessee cannot be held guilty of furnishing inaccurate 'particulars'. By no stretch of imagination can making an incorrect claim tantamount to furnishing inaccurate 'particulars' [CIT v. Reliance Petroproducts Pvt. Ltd. [2010] 189 Taxman 322/322 ITR 158 (SC)].

Hence merely because an arrangement is declared as an IAA, it would not necessarily be subject to concealment penalty under section 271(1)(c).

The contention was that the tax is fixed at a percentage of the purchase price of the commodities and, therefore, the tax really is not on income but on purchase price. It may be noted that this section provides immunity to 'the declarant'. Thus, in case a company is a declarant under the Scheme and if under any law (including those listed above), penalty is leviable or prosecution is liable to be launched on a principal officer or any officer of the company (which may include a director or an auditor or a company secretary, etc.) this section provides no immunity to such an officer.

Secrecy of the declaration

1.8 Section 72 lays down that all particulars contained in the declarations made under VDS-1997 shall be treated as 'confidential'. It further lays down that the declarant cannot be required by any Court or any other authority to :

(a) produce before it any such declaration or any part thereof; or

(b) give any evidence before it in respect thereof.

Similarly, no public servant could be required by any Court or any authority to produce declaration or give evidence in respect of a declaration filed by an assessee.

However, the particulars of the declaration could be disclosed to :

(a) any officer employed in the execution of the Income-tax Act or the Wealth- tax Act; or

(b) any officer appointed by the Comptroller & Auditor General of India or the Board to audit the income-tax receipts or refunds.

Levy of interest under the Income-tax Act

1.9 The scheme does not specifically provide for any immunity from payment of interest leviable under sections 234A, 234B and 234C or under any of their predecessor sections of the Income-tax Act.

However, all calculations of interest under all the aforesaid sections are based, inter alia, on one or more of the following variables :

(i) 'tax on total income';

(ii) 'assessed tax';

(iii) 'tax due on returned income'; etc.

Now, as seen above, the VDS does not contemplate filing any return of income. Secondly, the VDS does not provide for any assessment. Thirdly, section 68 grants an immunity from the VDI being included in the total income of any assessment year. As such, none of the variables required for computation of mandatory interest is present. As such, the Assessing Officer will not be in a position to levy any interest in respect of income disclosed under the VDS-1997.

(i) declared VDI;

(iii) paid tax on the VDI;

then, the assets representing such VDI (like cash, bank deposits, shares, debts commodities, bullion or any other assets) which were hereto not disclosed for the purpose of wealth-tax, shall not be liable for levy of wealth-tax in respect of any of the years prior to and including assessment year 1997-98. However, if such assets were disclosed but were undervalued, then such undervaluation will not be liable for wealth-tax only to the extent of VDI utilised for acquiring such assets.

In order to enjoy this exemption, it appears that the nature and value of the asset should be 'specified in the declaration' made under section 64(1) [refer Section 73(1) - Opening sentence].

Clarification on amendment to section 271 by Finance Bill, 2008 - In view of the apprehension raised on the retrospective amendment to section 271 of the Income-tax Act, proposed in the Finance Bill, 2008, empowering the Assessing Officer to, inter alia, levy penalty in case of concealment of income, the Ministry of Finance has issued the following clarification:

In the context of levy of penalty under section 271, there has been an ongoing dispute between the Income-tax department and taxpayers on whether an Assessing Officer is required to record his satisfaction before initiating penalty proceedings. The Income-tax department has held the view that no separate satisfaction is required to be recorded before initiating penalty proceedings. In the case of Commissioner of Income-tax v. S.V. Angidi Chettiar [1962] 44 ITR 739, the Supreme Court has, while dealing with penalty under section 28 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, held that "satisfaction before conclusion of proceeding under the Act, and not the issue of a notice or initiation of any step for imposing penalty is a condition for the exercise of the jurisdiction". The same matter came up once again before the Calcutta High Court in the case of Becker Gray and Company (1930) Ltd. v. ITO, Central Circle-I, Calcutta [1977] 112 ITR 503. Relying on the Supreme Court decision in the above case, the Calcutta High Court held that "It is true that the Income-tax Officer should be prima facie satisfied before the penalty notice is issued, but it does not mean that he is required to record such satisfaction in writing in every case." Following these decisions, wherever additions are made, Assessing Officers have, without separately recording any satisfaction, been issuing directions for initiating penalty proceedings.

However, interpreting the aforesaid Supreme Court decision, the Delhi High Court has, in the case of CIT v. Ram Commercial Enterprises Ltd. [2000] 246 ITR 568/[2002] 122 Taxman 620 held that "It is the assessing authority which has to form its own opinion and record its satisfaction before initiating penalty proceedings."

Subsequently, the Allahabad High Court went into this issue in the case of Shyam Biri Works Pvt. Ltd. v. CIT [2003] 259 ITR 625/131 Taxman 253. After considering the above Calcutta High Court decision and the Delhi High Court decision, it has held that "With profound respect to the Delhi High Court decision, we are unable to agree…. We are, therefore, of the opinion that although the Assessing Officer must have satisfaction as required under section 273 of the Act, it is not necessary for him to record that satisfaction in writing before initiating penalty proceedings under section 273 of the Act.".

In view of conflicting judicial opinion on this issue, it was necessary to make legislative intervention and settle the matter. Therefore, clause 48 of the Finance Bill, 2008 proposes to insert a new sub-section (1B) in section 271 so as to unambiguously provide that where any amount is added or disallowed in computing the total income or loss of an assessee in any order of assessment or reassessment, and such order contains a direction for initiating of penalty proceedings under sub-section (1) of section 271, such an order of assessment or reassessment shall be deemed to constitute satisfaction of the Assessing Officer for initiating penalty proceedings under sub-section (1) of that section.

The provisions are explained in the table given below: 4.2-1 Constitutional validity - The aforesaid amendment seeks to tax income which might have never been received. Hence doubts have arisen as to the constitutional validity of the amendment.

In K.P. Varghese v. ITO[1981] 131 ITR 597, the Supreme Court had to interpret section 52(2) of the Act which provided that if in the opinion of the AO, the fair market value of a capital asset transferred by an assessee exceeds the consideration declared by the assessee by at least 15% of the consideration so declared, then such fair market value shall be deemed to be the full value of the consideration for such capital asset. Thus, section 52(2), on literal interpretation permitted substitution of the declared consideration by fair market value. The Supreme Court did not accept the literal interpretation on various grounds based on the language, the context, the Finance Minister’s speech, etc., and also on certain general principles of law.

The Supreme Court observed as follows:

“section 52 is not a charging section but is a computation section. It has to be read along with section 48 which provides the mode of computation and under which the starting point of computation is “the full value of the consideration received or accruing”. What in fact never accrued or was never received cannot be computed as capital gains under section 48. Therefore, sub-section (2) cannot be considered as bringing within the computation of capital gains an amount which, by no stretch of imagination, can be said to have accrued to the assessee or been received by him”.

“. . . .It is a well settled rule of interpretation that the Court should as far as possible avoid that construction which attributes irrationality to the Legislature. Besides, under entry 82 in List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, which deals with “Taxes on income other than agricultural income” and under which the Income-tax Act, 1961, has been enacted, Parliament cannot “choose to tax as income an item which in no rational sense can be regarded as a citizen’s income or even receipt. Sub-section (2) would, therefore, on the construction of the revenue, go outside the legislative power of Parliament and it would not be possible to justify it even as an incidental or ancillary provision or a provision intended to prevent evasion of tax”.

“. . . .Sub-section (2) would also be violative of the fundamental right of the assessee under article 19(1)(f) - which fundamental right was in existence at the time when sub-section (2) came to be enacted - since on the construction canvassed on behalf of the revenue, the effect of sub-section (2) would be to penalize the assessee for transferring his capital asset for a consideration lesser by 15% or more than the fair market value and that would constitute unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right of the assessee to dispose of his capital asset at the price of his choice”.

“. . . .Sub-section (2) has no application in the case of an honest and bona fide transaction where the consideration received by the assessee has been correctly declared or disclosed by him and there is no concealment or suppression of the consideration”.

All the aforesaid arguments are applicable in relation to section 50C :

(a) It attempts to tax what may have never accrued or received.

(b) It goes outside the legislative power of the Parliament since such fair value cannot in a rational manner be regarded as income/receipt.

(c) It would hit a bona fide transaction, where there is no concealment or suppression of the consideration.

Having regard to the above it appears that there are strong arguments against the constitutional validity of section 50C.

Further, different stamp duty statutes have different basis or valuation. To illustrate, in Andhra Pradesh, the stamp duty is payable on the market value of the property. In Punjab, the stamp duty is payable on the value or amount of consideration (Article 23). In Delhi, it is payable on the consideration amount set forth in the instrument (Article 23). In Maharashtra, it is payable on the ‘true market value’ of the property (Article 25). Thus, the section puts different entities in different States in different position vis-a-vis section 50C.

It may be noted that the section refers to stamp duty valuation by a State Government and is silent about a property in a Union Territory.

Administrative convenience is a valid ground for classification in a taxation measure.5 Differentiation made to check evasion or avoidance of tax is also a valid ground.6 3.5-3f Service tax on chartered accountants not discriminatory - In All Kerala Chartered Accountants’ Association v. Union of India [2002] 258 ITR 679 (Ker.), it was contended that levy of service tax as provided by the Finance Act, 1994 and amended by the Finance Act, 1998, on chartered accountants is discriminatory and hit by article 14 of the Constitution. It was urged that there are several persons practising different professions and there is no rationale or reason why several other professionals are kept out of the tax net, and only certain professionals like practising chartered accountants, practising cost accountants, etc., are subjected to levy of service tax and that there is no intelligible differentia on which some professionals are in the tax net, while some are left out and that the levy is discriminative and hit by article 14. Repelling the argument, the Court held that although tax laws are not really outside the purview of article 14, the Legislature is permitted to exercise extremely wide discretion in classifying items for tax purposes, so long as it refrains from clear and hostile discrimination against particular persons or classes. It is not obligatory on Parliament to tax all professionals. As far as levy on practising chartered accountants is concerned, the Court observed that those falling within the definition are treated uniformly. Because some categories are given exemption (may be for the time being) by reason of exercise of power to exempt vested in the Government, it does not mean that they are not covered by the statute. In effect, the power to exempt can arise only in a situation where the liability under the statute exists but is protem exempted from the implementation. The court held that the imposition of service tax on practising chartered accountants is not hit by article 14 of the Constitution.

3.5-3 Specific instances of discrimination - Some of the illustrative examples are given below where the courts applied article 14.

3.5-3a SECTION 10(26) OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961 IS NOT DISCRIMINATORY - Taxation Laws have to pass the test of article 14. The State does not have to tax everything in order to tax something and it is allowed to pick and choose districts, objects, persons, methods and even rates for taxation, if it does so reasonably. The Supreme Court applied this principle in considering a question whether exclusion of Government servants from the exemption given under section 4(3)(xxi) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 and under section 10(26) of the 1961 Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that since the exemption has been given on the basis of the persons being members of a particular tribe, some of the members of a particular tribe could not be excluded unless they belonged to a well defined class for the purpose of income-tax. The Court came to the conclusion that there would be no distinction between income earned by a Government servant and that earned by a person serving in a company or under a private individual or professional income. Consequently it struck down the severable clause “who is not in the service of Government”.1 Subsequently, these words were retrospectively deleted from section 10(26) of the Act of 1961.

The Gauhati High Court2 had the occasion to consider constitutional validity of section 10(26) as to whether it is discriminatory as it made a difference between persons belonging to the same scheduled tribe without any rational basis whatsoever as the assessee was held liable to income-tax for earning the particular income outside the notified area, which if he had earned in Garo Hills, he would have been exempted. The argument before the Court was that section 10(26) treats unequally persons equally circumstanced and placed.

had the occasion to consider constitutional validity of section 10(26) as to whether it is discriminatory as it made a difference between persons belonging to the same scheduled tribe without any rational basis whatsoever as the assessee was held liable to income-tax for earning the particular income outside the notified area, which if he had earned in Garo Hills, he would have been exempted. The argument before the Court was that section 10(26) treats unequally persons equally circumstanced and placed. The Court held that the scheme and pattern of the Income-tax Act is to give relevance to a territorial nexus with the assessable income. The clear object of section 10(26) is in the interest of the scheduled tribe, as also in the interest of the area which that tribe makes the lot to live in. By exempting the scheduled tribe in this behalf for earning income which accrues or arises in the area, not only the members of the tribe are helped but also the interest of the area is adequately furthered. The members of the scheduled tribe, earning income which accrues in the tribal area specified, are well-defined class and there is a reasonable nexus for exempting that class from other members of the scheduled tribe who may have income accruing to them in a place or area outside the tribal areas. In view of the object of the provision the classification is well defined. The classification is founded on an intelligible differentia and that differentia has a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved by the exemption clause. The provision was, therefore, held to be valid, and not violative of article 14.

In ITO v. N. Takin Roy Rymbai3, the Supreme Court upheld the validity of sub-clause (a) of clause (26) of section 10 by holding that classification of sources of income is integral to the basic scheme of the Act, that classification made in section 10(26)(a) for purposes of exemption is now well recognised pattern and is based on intelligible differentia. The Supreme Court again held that section 10(26) is not discriminatory.4

3.5-3b SeCTION 214 OF THE Income-tax Act IS NOT DISCRIMINATIVE - Before the Kerala High Court, in Lord Krishna Bank Ltd. v. ITO5, the validity of section 214 of the Income-tax Act was challenged on the ground of discrimination and arbitrariness. The High Court held that the provision for payment of interest of the difference between the aggregate of the instalments of advance tax paid and the amount determined on regular assessment has sufficient justification, because such payments are made on income yet to arise. Refusal to pay interest on excess amount of tax deducted at source after the income had actually arisen and was earned, but before the taxable income was determined and the rate was applied, is not discriminatory or arbitrary. Both payments are made in advance of actual assessment but the vital distinction that the former is tax paid on income yet to arise and the latter on income already accrued, marks out one from the other.

3.5-3c Hotel receipts tax Act, 1980 is not discriminatory - Writ petitions under article 32 of the Constitution of India were filed before the Supreme Court challenging article 19(1)(g), the constitutional validity of the Hotel Receipts Tax Act, 1980 which imposed a special tax on the gross receipts of certain categories of hotels. Section 3 of the Act limits the application of the Act to those hotels where the ‘room charges’ for residential accommodation provided to any person during the previous year are Rs. 75 or more per day per individual. If a hotel is within this class, then, section 5 brings to charge the hotel’s ‘chargeable receipts’ as defined under section 6 of the Act. The Act was passed on December 4, 1980, and came into force on December 9, 1980 when it received the assent of the President of India. The levy under the Act commences from the assessment year 1981-82 and brings to tax the chargeable receipts of the corresponding previous year. The rate of tax is a flat rate of 15 per cent of the ‘chargeable receipts’ defined in section 6 as the total amount of all charges, by whatever name called, received by, or accruing or arising to, the assessee in the previous year in connection with the provision of residential accommodation, food, drink and other services in the course of carrying on the business of a hotel. But such charges received from persons within the purview of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961, or Vienna Convention on Consular Relations are exempt from the tax. The machinery under the Income-tax Act, 1961 is engrafted for purposes of assessment, levy and collection of tax under the Act. It is, however, relevant to note that though the Act is put into force from the assessment year 1981-82, the levy was discontinued from February 27, 1982. view to reduce the tax liability, the Court observed ‘when the Legislature of this country which is assumed to know the conditions of the people and their requirements, with the awareness of this particular wide-spread fraudulent device in the matter of evasion of tax, made a law to prevent the said fraud, it is difficult for this Court, in the absence of any counter-balancing circumstances, to hold, on the analogy drawn from American decisions, that the need for such a law is not in existence...’ Thus, while upholding the constitutional validity of section 16(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, corresponding to section 64(1), the Supreme Court in Balaji v. ITO1 pointed out that the object of the legislation was to prevent evasion of tax and to put an end to the perpetration of fraud and taxation. The section should be interpreted in such a manner as to prevent the mischief and to advance the remedy according to the true intentions of the makers of the statute.2 The section has, therefore, to receive strict construction.3 Before an income can be held to come within the ambit of section 64(1), it must be proved to have arisen - directly or indirectly from a transfer of assets made by the assessee in favour of his wife or minor children. The connection between the transfer of assets and the income must be proximate.The income in question must arise as a result of the transfer and not in some manner connected with it.4 Income sought to be taxed and transfer of asset must be connected with each other by proximity in every respect.That would take in the time limit also.5 The two must be so near to each other that it would form one chain of causation. What has to be considered is whether the income in question can be linked with the transfer of assets as a direct or indirect consequence. The facts of a case should be scanned for the purpose of finding out the aforesaid connection with the object of the section in the background. If, on the facts of the case, it is possible to discover the inner thread whereby the tax liability is sought to be evaded or reduced, it is to be held in such cases that there is a nexus between the transfer of assets and the income in question.6 Income may not always mean taxable income and income arising from a transfer of assets yielding non-taxable income, e.g., agricultural land, will not always be outside the purview of section 64.1 An asset yielding non-taxable income is transferred by the assessee to his or her spouse with the object of converting it into another asset which would yield taxable income and by evading payment of tax by keeping it in the name of the transferee, the assessee cannot escape the net cast by section 64.

Before the Madras High Court in K. Krishnaveni v. AAC2, the constitutional validity of section 64(1)(iii) as amended by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1975, was challenged on the ground that there is no legislative competence for the Parliament to enact a law so as to tax the income earned by one person in the hands of another. It was argued before the High Court that the amended provision of section 64(1)(viii) was constitutionally invalid for the parent is forced to pay the tax due by the minor child arising out of his being admitted to the benefits of the partnership with which the parent has no connection and that the Constitution does not permit the State to levy income-tax on an individual on income of another person, and that provision infringes the doctrine of equality before law guaranteed under Article 14 of the Constitution as there is a hostile discrimination between an individual who has earned income by having been admitted to the benefits of a partnership and who earned income otherwise than by being admitted to the benefits of the partnership. While upholding the constitutional validity of the provision, the learned Judges observed :

“...As already stated, the income of the minor from a partnership has been taken as the income of the parent as the Legislature found that the creation of partnerships or admitting minors to the benefits of the partnership is one of the methods adopted to evade tax and as pointed out by the Wanchoo Committee normally it is possible for a parent in one family to admit a minor from another family to the benefits of the partnership in his firm in consideration of the parent of the minor admitting to the benefits of the partnership, the son of the former so that there will be cross or mutual advantage got by both the parents. It is only to plug the said loophole, the Legislature came forward to say that if any minor has been admitted to the benefits of a partnership, the minor’s income from that partnership should be taken to be the income of the parent. It is not, therefore, possible to say that the provision is ultra vires.” (p. 91)

6.4 Proceedings were initiated against the assessees for non-payment and short-payment of excise duty. The demand for duty was confirmed on the assessees and penalty under section 11AC was also imposed. However, the Tribunal in its impugned orders had taken a view that there was no warrant for levy of penalty since the assessees had deposited the duty even before the show-cause notice was issued. In the instant appeal, the revenue relying upon the decision in Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2008] 306 ITR 277/174 Taxman 571 (SC), contended that mere non-payment or short payment of duty would inevitably lead to imposition of penalty equal to the amount by which duty was short paid.

The Hon’ble Supreme Court held that payment of differential duty, whether before or after the show-cause notice is issued, cannot alter liability for penalty, the conditions for which are clearly spelled out in section 11AC. From section 11A(1) read with its proviso, it is clear that in case the short-payment, non-payment or erroneous refund of duty is unintended and not attributable to fraud, collusion or any wilful mis-statement or suppression of facts, or contravention of any of the provisions of the Act or of the rules made under it, with an intent to evade payment of duty then the revenue can give notice for recovery of the duty to the person in default within one year from the relevant date. In other words, in the absence of any element of deception or malpractice, the recovery of duty can only be for a period not exceeding one year but in case the non-payment, etc., of duty is intentional and by adopting any means as indicated in the proviso, then the period of notice and the period for which duty can be demanded, gets extended to five years.

The Supreme Court further held that sub-section (2B) of section 11A provides that in case the person-in-default makes payment of the escaped amount of duty before the service of notice, then the revenue will not give him the notice under sub-section (1). This, perhaps, is the basis of the common, though erroneous view that no penalty would be leviable if the escaped amount of duty is paid before the service of notice. It, however, overlooks the two Explanations qualifying the main provision. Explanation 1 makes it clear that the payment would, nevertheless, be subject to imposition of interest under section 11AB. Explanation 2 makes it further clear that in case the escapement of duty is intentional and by reason of deception, the main provision of sub-section (2B) will have no application.

19. Excess share premium not taxable in hands of closely held co. if its shareholders are relatives: ITAT

[Vaani Estates (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2018] 98 taxmann.com 92 (Chennai - Trib.)] The assessee-company had only two shareholders 'S' and her husband. On passing away of husband, his shares devolved on their daughter 'V'. The assessee proposed to acquire an immovable property at approximately Rs. 23.09 crores. 'S' brought in money into the company in lieu of allotment of fresh 10,100 shares with a share premium of Rs. 23.31 crores.

The Assessing Officer opined that company had received excess price/share premium for the shares allotted to 'S' over and above the face value of shares. Accordingly, he brought Rs. 23.31 crores to tax in the hands of the company under Section 56(2)(viib).

The ITAT held in favour of assessee as under:

When 'S' introduced money into the company for allotment of shares at an exorbitant premium in contrast to its intrinsic value of just Rs. 10 per share, the benefit of such investment had only passed on to her daughter because there were only two shareholders in the company at that point of time. Had 'S' gifted the money to her daughter 'V' and thereafter if daughter had brought the same into the company for allotment of equity shares at face value, question of invoking of the provisions of section 56(2)(viib) would not have arisen.

Provisions of section 56(2)(viib) couldn't be invoked in the case of the assessee-co. because by virtue of introducing cash in the company by 'S' for allotment of equity shares with unrealistic premium the benefit had only passed on to her daughter 'V' and there was no scope in the Act to tax when cash or asset was transferred by a mother to her daughter.

21. Australia has taxing rights under Australia-India DTAA even if there is no provision in its domestic law: Australian Court

[Satyam Computer Services Ltd. (Now Tech Mahindra Limited) v. Commissioner of Taxation [2018] 98 taxmann.com 358 (FC-Australia)]

The Applicant, Tech Mahindra, had offices in Sydney and Melbourne through which it provided software products and information technology services to entities in Australia. Payments received by applicant for the services provided in Australia by the employees located in India were treated as 'Royalties' as per Article 12(3)(g) of the Australia-India DTAA .

Applicant argued that, though Australia was allocated the right to tax the 'Royalties' by the Indian Agreement but it could only exercise that right if it had the right to impose tax on those amounts under Australia's domestic law. As of now, the domestic law does not give any right to Australia to tax such income.

The Federal Court of Australia held as under:

The language of Article 23 should be given effect to according to its terms and the context. Article 23 provides that that income derived by a resident of one contracting States may be deemed to be income from sources in other contracting state for purpose of law of that other State. Therefore, royalty income was to be included in the applicant's assessable income because it was income from an Australian source by reason of Article 23 of the Australia-India DTAA. The Court rejected the argument that the tax treaties can only be used as shields not swords. It held that the tax treaties also provide standalone taxing power and independent imposing of tax to a particular income.

Constitutional validity of this provision was challenged in C.B. Gautam v. Union of India [1993] 199 ITR 530/[1992] 65 Taxman 440. The Honour-able Supreme Court gave well reasoned decision. In my submission, the ratio of that decision is as under: 1.Where there is an attempt at tax evasion, it should be curbed.

2.Law does not confer arbitrary or unfettered discretion to the authorities.

3.Where a provision in law causes natural injustice, Courts would read down the provision causing injustice; and read in provisions granting justice. Where this is not possible, the law has to be held to be invalid.

Now apply this ratio to TP provisions and see whether the TP provisions would pass the test of natural justice!

We may consider following steps for improving the quality of justice under TP. These are only brief outlines. Each thought can invite full length discussion.

Just as we have Double Tax Avoidance Agreements; there should be TP Adjustment agreements.

Corresponding adjustments

10. Present Indian law does not permit "Corresponding Adjustments". These adjustments can be of two kinds.

1. Where the Indian AE as well as the foreign AE - both are taxable in India. For example, interest or royalty payment. If there is an allegation of payment at prices other than ALP; adjustment in price for both the assessees should be allowed. Indian law permits the adjustment where Indian tax revenue is increased; and not the corresponding adjustment where tax revenue is reduced.

Is it natural justice? Is it decency and dignity that one expects from such a large and prominent Government like the Indian Government?

2. In an international transaction, one Government alleges under pricing by its assessee - AE. Consequently it collects higher tax.

Natural Justice demands that the AE of the other country should get a higher price as deductible expenditure. Its tax should be reduced.

Just as we have Double Tax Avoidance Agreements; there should be TP Adjustment agreements. These may look ‘absurd’ today; and "essential good tax law practice" tomorrow.

‘Corresponding adjustment’ is a different term from the ‘Subjective adjustments’ required to compensate for differences between the circumstances of two different companies.

Safe harbours

11. It is well known that TP compliance imposes a very heavy cost on the assessee. Not imposing all procedures for small assessees is one kind of safe harbour.

When both AEs are residents of normal tax countries - like say India and USA; the incidence to transfer taxable profits may be rare. (If one of the AEs has substantial losses; or if it is entitled to tax exemption; there is room for suspicion) When two normal assessees from two normal tax countries are AEs doing international transaction; much greater discretion may be used in making ‘Subjective adjustments’ in prices. In other words, there may be less scrutiny of the assessee and more liberties to him.

Red signals

12. When we call for ‘safe harbours’, it is equally justifiable to have ‘Red Signals’. For example, when an AE is dealing with another AE situated in a tax haven, the tax Commissioner would be justified in more investigative scrutiny. Here also, he may not draw any conclusions before investigation. But deep investigation may be justified.

Penalty - Three Levels

13. There can be a full paper on the concept that: ‘The adjustments between the price charged by the assessee and the market price is subjective. By definition there can be no final word on something that is subjective. Each person is entitled to his own view. And yet frauds cannot be tolerated.’

If we accept the above statement; on TP assessment, where the Assessing Officer makes an addition, there can be three alternative situations.

1. In genuine cases like Gillette and Pepsi in the initial years - where one established AE is subsidising another AE; the TP provisions should not be applied. No additional tax and no penalty.

2. There is no cause for subsidy. And there is a genuine difference of opinion between: (i) Assessee on one side - whose opinion is approved by the TP auditor; and (ii) The Assessing Officer on the other side.

The assessee recognises that he may be wrong; and pays up additional tax. The Assessing Officer recognises that he may be wrong. So no penalty. This position is accepted in some countries like Spain. No penalty under TP.

3. The assessee has committed an outright fraud. Deterrent penalty may be levied.

Such approach calls for discretion. And it should be allowed in TP. The present Indian legal provisions on TP fall short of natural justice. Introduction of adequate ‘Safe Harbours’; ‘Red Signals’ and reasonableness in penalty provisions can bring more justice in the Indian Law.

It is hoped that the Indian tax department and professional will sit together and evolve a TP code which in letter and in administration passes the test of natural justice.

CASE PILOTS

1. CHAMBER OF TAX CONSULTANTS V. UNION OF INDIA . (2017) 6

FACTS

The writ petition was filed in the high court of Delhi by the petitioner. The petitioner challenged the section 145(2) of the income tax Act which notify us to follow the ICDS, empowered by the central government for computing the income chargeable using mercantile system of accounting under the head "Profit and gains of business or profession" or "income from other sources". The petitioner challenged the notification no. 87/2016 and circular no. 10/2017 demanding to follow 10 ICDS.

ISSUSE

Is part of ICDS which override the laws as mentioned in judicial precedents are need to be struck down or not?

HELD

The Delhi High Court held the updated ICDS and its specific provisions and also CBDT for issuing clarification as to be ultra vires the Act. And the section 145(2) has been read down by restricting the central government powers to only notify if the provisions made do not contradict the judicial precedents. The court also held that, under Articles 141 and 1447 of the Constitution, when there is a binding judicial precedent, the executive cannot supersede it unless the Act is amended by way of a validation statute.

ANALYSIS

As ICDS is mandatory to follow it was no longer possible for an Assessee to measure taxable income in accordance with the Act, as elucidated by Supreme Court and High Court judgments. Also many provisions in the ICDS were in conflict with the act or judicial precedents which in result becomes prevailing over the judicial precedents. So, accordingly there is a need to resist the powers of central government in notifying the ICDS in such a way that no override situation occurs. The decision taken by Delhi High Court to read down the section 145(2) of the Act is in accordance with the constitution. Further, CBDT clarified that in the event of a conflict between the provisions of the ICDS and the Act, the provisions of the act will take precedence.

2. HERCULES PIGMENT INDUSTRY V. ITO 8

FACTS

The assessee is in business of manufacturing and marketing of pigments and following inclusive method of accounting. The excise duty paid or received were taken into unutilized CENVAT credit (UCC) account by assessee. During assessment the AO disallowed the unutilized CENVAT of Rs. 1.39 million under the section 145A of the Act. On appeal the order of AO was confirmed by the CIT(A) although relief of Rs. 0.339 million was allowed to the assessee. The aggrieved assessee is in appeal before tribunal.

ISSUES

Is the profit determined by the assessee for the stated assessment year is applicable irrespective of inclusive or exclusive method of accounting followed?

DECISION

Appeal of the assessee was dismissed as the assessee doesn't carefully followed the provisions of section 145A of the income tax Act for valuation to determine correct taxable value.

ANALYSIS

The UCC account maintained by the assessee is a measure of excise liability on removal of goods but it does not represent the unutilized credit available on the goods that were held as stock in trade. So, the UCC account cannot be taken as correct measure of excise duty on inventories. PART II - TRANSFER PRICING

Need for transfer pricing provisions

7. At the outset it may be stated that Indian direct tax laws as a package are much better than most packages in similar countries.’ We cannot talk of ‘city countries’ or tax havens. For a proper industrial country, the Indian tax package is good. As stated in the beginning of this article - Part I; ‘good’ can always be improved. Our legal system is in the process of continuous evolution. Some specific attention needs to be paid to transfer pricing.

It is known that multinational corporations (MNCs) and even small business enterprises would like to reduce their tax liabilities by transferring their taxable income out of India to a country where they would face lower or ‘nil’ tax. This may be easily accomplished by under pricing taxable exports & over pricing imports of goods & services. This is called transfer pricing. Income earned in India is Indian tax base. Transfer of income to another jurisdiction is erosion of the tax base. Hence it is the right of Indian tax department to prevent erosion of its tax base through proper transfer pricing provisions.

India is following OECD and scores of other countries who have already introduced similar provisions. We are learning from the experiences of all these countries and making a better law.

However, the very system of transfer pricing presents severe complications.

The essence of transfer pricing (TP) is that:

‘whenever ‘Associated Enterprises’ (AE) enter into ‘International Transactions’, they have to justify that the price charged is an Arm’s Length Price (ALP). The concept of ALP involves a comparison with price charged by others. Now the Indian Income-tax Act and Rules made for TP have a built-in mechanism for adjustment of differences between the assessee and the other enterprises. This is a fundamental requirement. Every assessee is different from the others. Every assessee will have his own reasons to charge a higher or a lower price. These reasons may be bona fide reasons not involving any concealment of income.’

Each assessee will claim that there is no concealment of income. And yet there will be some assessees who have actually transferred their taxable profits out of the country purely with a view to avoiding Indian tax.

‘How to find out the difference between the two! How to deter the fraudulent and how not to harass the honest’ - is the issue.

The adjustment process involves considerable subjectivity. Let us see some illustrations.

When an Indian AE sells goods to another AE it knows that there is no risk of non-payment of price. It also has a perfect relationship and understanding. There is no sales and marketing cost involved. The demand is assured for a long period; ensuring capacity utilisation. Hence the seller will be prepared to charge a lower price. What should be the adjustment for all these factors! Whatever figures or percentages one person may give, can be challenged by another.

Pepsi & Gillette opened up subsidiaries in India. Their subsidiaries incurred continuous losses for the initial years. Throughout this period, the holding companies subsidised the Indian subsidiaries in several different ways. By its very nature, several products and services were either not charged or were under charged. And yet there was no question of an intention to conceal income. Legitimately, neither the U.S. nor the Indian Government can allege concealment of income.

Implementation of transfer pricing provisions - Need for discretion

8. It is essential that the Commissioner making the TP assessment recognises that he is dealing with several subjective factors. In subjective business matters, the business decision by the businessman cannot be challenged. A person who is not a businessman (This phrase includes auditor as well as tax Commissioner) is not competent to challenge the business decision of the businessman. Hence the TP provisions should be implemented with a lot of discretion and restrain.

Does our law permit non-application of TP provisions in the bona fide cases of Pepsi, Gillette and several similar cases? The Indian tax administration does not give room for discretion. In fact, the profession, the department and even corporate institutions are all unanimous that discretion should be removed and flat provision should be made in the law. Most of the penalties which were discretionary have now been made compulsory and flat with little discretion for the tax Commissioners. We have gone to the extreme where in somecases we do not even trust our judges. Even the Courts’ discretion has been done away with.

Constitutional validity of this provision was challenged in C.B. Gautam v. Union of India [1993] 199 ITR 530/[1992] 65 Taxman 440. The Honour-able Supreme Court gave well reasoned decision. In my submission, the ratio of that decision is as under:

Act disallows a FEO from putting forward or defending any civil claim. Further, any individual filing a claim on behalf of a company or LLP among other things, wherein the FEO has a controlling interest shall also be disallowed from filing or defending claims. Section 14 violates the right of access to justice under Article 21 as there is no rational nexus between the offence and the punishment, as some corporate interests of the FEO may not have any connection to the economic offences in question.8 Proportionality: The declaration of an individual as a FEO entitles the authorities to confiscate the properties owned by the individual even if the property owned by the FEO is not the proceeds from criminal activity, and has been legitimately acquired. It allows the authorities to confiscate property belonging to the perpetrator which is not directly or factually linked with the commission of a particular offence under investigation.9 Furthermore, the Act also allows the appropriate authorities to confiscate the property of a FEO in excess of the amount owed by them. For example, it has been claimed by Vijay Mallaya that the assets confiscated from his firm under the Act amount to Rs. 14000 crores, as opposed to the Rs. 9000 crores that he actually owes.10

Generally, such due process safeguards act as a balancing mediator between the excesses of State power, and the rights of the individual. In the case of FEOs, these safeguards have been put aside to enable the prosecution of individuals who cannot be brought before the justice system. That being said, how far is too far? Rights of an individual may be curtailed by a statute if they are proportionate to the goals sought by it. Therefore, there is a need for proportionality tests to ensure that such confiscation down not interfere with the rights of individuals thereby addressing the risks that the punishment meted out on the accused through the statute is not too harsh as compared to their crimes.11

Draconian Measures as a Deterrent: One of the primary objectives of the Act is to have a deterrent effect on economic offenders by imposing harsh penalties as a consequence of becoming a FEO. The act relies upon the reasoning that if the punishment for absconding is high, then the deterrent effect would also be higher. Consequently, instead of attaching the property of the fugitive economic offenders like other the PMLA act, or the attachment of benami property, the Act contemplates the confiscation of the property of the person after they are declared to be a fugitive economic offender. Furthermore, the Act also does not make a distinction between the properties of the fugitive economic offender, and contemplates the confiscation of their property irrespective of the fact that it may not be proceeds of the crime or benami property. The goal of providing for such excessive punishment is the maximization of the deterrent effect.12

However, this justification is not adequate due to the fact that an individual who is orchestrating economic offences that are above INR 100 crores in value is a legally literate person who knows how to circumvent the law. Therefore, if there is a possibility that the properties of a FEO will be confiscated without following due process safeguards, then they may try to commit a crime that yields higher value to offset the cost of the assets that would be lost through confiscation. Alternatively, a fugitive economic offender could liquidate their assets before absconding in order to take those assets with them.

In such cases, the draconian measures of the Act are economically inefficient because they do not deter a FEO from committing economic offences, while also justifying the commission of said offences in a more damaging manner which puts a lot more revenue on the black market and out of the reach of the confiscating authorities.13

In light of the above, it is contended that the present Act is a prime example of the excesses of state power, wherein the safeguards protecting individuals from wrongful prosecution have been set aside, and the constitutional validity of the provisions of the Act is bound to be challenged. Therefore, a different approach is the call of the hour, which does not infringe upon basic constitutional safeguards.

A mechanism that shifts the focus from the individual to the properties of the FEO would be a more justifiable method for implementing the objective of the Act. Generally, this is how pre-confiscation conviction models sidestep procedural safeguards. In the UK, Part V of the Proceeds of Crime Act, 2002 deal with the confiscation of properties that have been obtained through criminal activity. However, as discussed earlier, the Act follows a 'property centric'14 approach rather than an 'individual centric' approach. In such cases, when a particular property has been proved to be 'proceeds of crime', then the government may confiscate such properties after giving a reasonable opportunity to the 'owner' of the property to defend their claim. In this scenario, an ex parte order would only be against the property and its legitimacy as opposed to a determination of the guilt of the accused. Consequently, a higher quantum of procedural safeguards would not be necessary as it would be a 'civil forfeiture'.

Constitutionality of the levy

7. The constitutionality of the imposition of service tax on the services provided by the practising chartered accountants was challenged by the Chartered Accountants Association of Gujarat before the Gujarat High Court in Chartered Accountants’ Association v. Union of India [2001] 115 Taxman 543 = 252 ITR 53 on the following grounds—

(a)The levy of service tax is a ‘tax on profession’ within the meaning of entry 60 of List II (State List) in the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. Since profession is nothing but rendering services in the respective professional field, therefore, service tax on services rendered by professionals lacks legislative competence, as ‘tax on profession’ is a matter assigned to the States.

(b)The levy of service tax on services provided by ‘professionals’ and not on the similar services provided by ‘non-qualified accountants’ is discriminatory and, thus, violative of article 14 of the Constitution.

(c)The levy will cost the clients 5 per cent (now 10 per cent and 12 per cent after enactment of the Finance Bill, 2006) more than what it would cost when the same services are rendered by a non-qualified person who is not covered by the levy. As such the client would prefer such non-qualified persons. Therefore, the service tax levy violates the freedom of profession guaranteed under article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.

After evaluating the arguments of the petitioner-association in light of the various decisions of the Supreme Court and High Courts, the Gujarat High Court upheld the constitutionality of the levy of service tax, replying the contentions raised by the petitioner-association in the following manner—

(i)Tax on services rendered by a professional is different from the tax on profession itself. The former is a tax payable each time the professional renders services for remuneration, but the latter is payable even if no service is provided. In fact the professional tax is required to be paid for the privilege of having the right to exercise the profession whether or not the person chooses to exercise such profession. Thus, the two taxes being separate, the contention that ‘tax on services of professional’ is a ‘tax on profession’ is unsustainable.

[Note : After the enactment of the Constitution (88th Amendment) Act, 2003, still to come into force) there is no reason for doubting the Parliament’s legislative competence regarding levy of taxes on services. The said Act has inserted an entry 92C in List I (Union List) to the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution which reads as ’92C. Taxes on services.’ Thus, the said entry confers on the Parliament the exclusive power with regard to imposition of taxes on services.]

(ii)Professionals rendering services are not at par with non-qualified persons rendering similar services, the quality of services rendered by the two being different. Further, it is easier for the State to identify the qualified professional and tax services rendered by them as against the difficulty in tracing non-qualified persons rendering services in similar fields. There the classification between qualified professionals and non-qualified persons is not violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
