DR. YOGENDRA KR. VERMA*

SERVICE TAX - ITS CONSTITUTIONALITY AND ADMINISTRATIVE CHALLENGES

Each country evolved a taxation system on services adopting either comprehensive approach or selective approach, depending upon socio-economic compulsion. While most of the developed countries tax all the services with very few and limited exemption, some of the developing countries tax selected services only and India has also adopted a selective approach to taxation of services. The Finance Act, 1994 imposed service tax only on three subjects, but as on date almost hundred subjects have come under the net of service tax. Through this write-up, the author has explained constitutional validity of service tax and administrative challenges faced by it. He is of view that as service tax is important from the viewpoint of neutrality in taxation, well synchronized taxation on manufacturing, trade (domestic and international) and service without giving rise to cascading effect of taxation would be an ideal approach worth pursuing in the immediate future. He has also given a list of suggestions which according to him should be attended urgently to improve the administration of service tax in the country.

Introduction

1. The object of monetary policy is to establish equilibrium between the available resources and the Government expenditure by framing of fiscal policy that aims at growth of the economy and social prosperity, such an ideal condition, however, unfortunately, is hard to achieve. The countries that gained independence after the end of Second World War were poor and undeveloped countries. India also fell into this category. The priorities thrown open to our nation centered around faster and balanced growth of economy directed towards narrowing the gap in social and economic imbalance plaguing our country for centuries.

Services constitute a very heterogeneous spectrum of economic activities. The share of services sector in real GDP (Gross Domestic Product) in India has surpassed that of agriculture and industry at a relatively faster pace as compared to other industrialized nations. Service sector has become the main contributor to the GDP not merely in the developed economies like USA (71%), Japan (60%), UK (67%), but also in developing economies like China (33%), Indonesia (41%), Pakistan (50%) and Brazil (56%). Service sector not only occupies major chunk of the GDP that is around 52 per cent in India, but also the growth rate of economic activities in the service sector is faster. In any welfare State, it is the prime responsibility of the Government to fulfil the increasing developmental needs of the country and its people by way of public expenditure. India being developing economy is striving to fulfil the obligation of a welfare State within its limited resources. In developed economies, consumption of goods and services is treated alike. The Government’s prime sources of revenue are direct and indirect taxes. Collection of revenue through direct taxes is a problem in developing nations due to a narrow tax base with individual income disparities being high. Further, there is a persisting tendency to evade the direct taxes in India. On the other hand, indirect taxes are hidden in the cost of goods and services and it is more convenient to collect indirect taxes and the cost of collection is also comparatively less. Central excise duties on the goods manufactured in India and custom duties on imported goods constitute the two major sources of indirect taxes in India. But revenue receipt from custom and excise are on the decline due to WTO commitments and rationalization of commodities duty. This is one of the reasons of extending the tax base to the service sector to improve the revenue productivity and efficiency of our domestic tax system. It is also necessary from the point of view of evolving a coordinated system of domestic indirect taxation on goods and services.

It is also well-known that services institute a larger proportion of the consumption of rich rather than of the poor as the demand for services is income elastic. Each country evolved a taxation system on services adopting either a comprehensive approach or selective approach, depending upon the socio-economic compulsion. While most of the developed countries tax all the services with very few and limited exemption, some of the developing countries tax selected services only and India has also adopted a selective approach to taxation of services.

Legislative history

2. Dr. Manmohan Singh, the then Union Finance Minister, in his Budget speech for the year 1994-95 introduced the new concept of service tax and stated that "there is no sound reason for exempting services from taxation, therefore, I propose to make a modest effort in this direction by imposing a tax on services of telephones, non-life insurance and stock brokers." In Budget speech 1994, the Finance Minister, giving the reason behind imposition of service tax, said:

"87. Over the years, while attempts have been made to widen the base for domestic indirect taxes, the service sector has not been subjected to taxation. Yet this sector accounts for about 40 per cent of our GDP and is showing strong growth. There is no sound reason for exempting services from taxation, when goods are taxed and many countries treat good and services alike for tax purposes...."1

3. Quantifying under-reported income: Where income is assessed for the first time and ITR was furnished by the assessee the difference between the income assessed and income determined under section 143(1)(a) would be the under-reported income.

Where no ITR is furnished or where it is furnished in response to notice under section 148 then (i) the amount of income assessed would be treated as under-reported income in the case of company, firm or local authority; and (ii) the difference between the income assessed and the basic exemption limit would be the under-reported income for other taxpayers.

Where it is not a case of the income being assessed for the first time the difference between the income reassessed or recomputed less the amount of income assessed or reassessed or recomputed previously would be the quantum of under-reported income.

4. Instances where it is not under-reporting of income: Section 270A(6) says that the following shall not be treated as under-reported income:

(i)

Where the assessee offers an explanation and the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Commissioner or the Principal Commissioner, as the case may be, is satisfied that the explanation is bona fide and the assessee has disclosed all material facts to substantiate the explanation offered by him, the income so enhanced shall not be treated as under-reporting of income.

(ii)

The amount of under-reported income determined on the basis of an estimate shall not be treated as under-reported income if the accounts are correct and complete to the satisfaction of the Assessing Officer or Commissioner (Appeals) or the Commissioner or the Principal Commissioner provided the method employed is such that the income cannot properly be deduced therefrom.

(iii)

The amount of under-reported income determined on the basis of estimate and the assessee on his own estimated a lower amount of addition or disallowance of the same but has included such amount in the computation of his income and has disclosed all the facts material to the addition or disallowance.

(iv)

The amount of under-reported income represented by any addition made with reference to ALP determined by the TPO in case where the assessee has maintained information and documents prescribed under section 92E and declared the international transaction under Chapter X and disclosed all the material facts relating to the transaction.

(v)

The amount of undisclosed income which is dealt with in section 271AAB.

2. This change is more from an administrative perspective. A proviso is proposed to be introduced after section 92CA(3A), requiring extension of the period of limitation for passing an order by a Transfer Pricing Officer ('TPO'), where assessment proceedings are stayed by any court or where a reference for exchange of information has been made by the competent authority. In such cases, if the time available with the TPO to pass an order after excluding, the time for which the assessment proceedings were stayed or the time taken for receipt of information, as the case may be, is less than sixty days, then the period remaining with the TPO shall be extended to sixty days.

The proposed amendment will be applicable from 1st June, 2016.

Rationalization of the provisions relating to Appellate Tribunal

3. As a part of the rationalization measure, it has been proposed to omit section 253(2A) and section 253(3A), to do away with the filing of appeal by the Assessing Officer, before the Appellate Tribunal, against the directions of the dispute resolution panel ('DRP').

This is seen as a welcome step, however as a result of this amendment, one needs to wait and watch whether the DRP would be as judicious as it has been in the past, when its orders were appealable by the tax department before the Appellate Tribunal.

The proposed amendment will be applicable from 1st June, 2016.

Introduction of patent box regime in India

4. In light of OECD BEPS report on Action Plan 5, requiring taxation of income arising from exploitation of intellectual property ('IP') in the jurisdiction, where substantial research and development ('R&D') activities are undertaken, section 115BBF is proposed to be introduced. As per section 115BBF, royalty income in respect of a patent developed and registered in India would be taxable at a concessional rate of ten per cent (plus applicable surcharge and cess) on the gross amount of royalty. Further no expenditure or allowance in respect of such royalty income shall be allowed under the Act.

For the purpose of this concessional tax regime, the taxpayer engaged in development of IP should be a resident in India and also required to be a true and first inventor of the invention, whose name is entered on the patent register as the patentee in accordance with Patents Act, 1970.

Though this amendment does not precisely relates to transfer pricing, but would impact the IP structures in India, going forward. Historically, India has been an importer of technology/IP. The Indian service industry too is engaged in R&D activities on behalf of the foreign principals. Consequently, patents are registered outside India. As a result of this amendment, one could expect that more Indian companies, would start holding IP in their name resulting in dismantling of existing IP structures or creation of new IP structures, specifically in view of the requirement of being first inventor. However the success of this change would to a large extent depend upon the IP protection norms in India, which are required to be very stringent.

The aforesaid proposed amendment is applicable from 1st April, 2017 and shall apply for Assessment Year 2017-18 and onwards.

The primary change to the Indian Transfer Pricing Regime is in line with the global change brought in by the BEPS action plans. However, to what extent, India would be able to implement the changes in an efficient manner would depend upon the quality of administration and the effectiveness of cross-border exchange of information.

7. The mooting of an amnesty scheme for service-tax evaders is totally misconceived one and a wrong strategy. Amnesties cannot be solutions to the problems of non-compliance. The deleterious impacts of VDISs in the report on the study on 'Aspects of the Black Economy in India', carried out by the National Institute of Public Finance & Policy in 1984-85 have been mentioned in the following words in this report:- "Basically, these schemes seek to coax errant tax evaders to disclose their concealed income and wealth in return for taxation at concessional rates and immunity from penalties and prosecution."

By offering de facto amnesty for tax evasion, such schemes blunt the deterrent provisions of the tax laws, including the provisions for prosecution. Voluntary disclosure schemes have been severely criticized in a number of reports of the Lok Sabha's Public Accounts Committee and the Wanchoo Committee. The main points are as follows:-

i.

The quantitative results have been disappointing in relation to even the lowest estimates of tax evasion;

ii.

The view that such schemes permit errant taxpayers to continue on their wayward paths is not supported by the large number of "repeat" beneficiaries of these schemes;

iii.

When such schemes are launched after a few years, they reduce the incentives for voluntary compliance in the first place and weaken the morale of both, honest taxpayers and the tax administration.

The amnesty schemes blunts the impact of deterrent provisions. Deterrence in a firm way, not indiscriminately, is a sine qua non for successful voluntary compliance of tax laws - for that matter, any laws. Serious actions are necessary in the case of recalcitrant assessees. Reports show that debt-ridden Greece came down heavily on tax evaders, who owed money to the State. These included companies (nearly 6,000 in number), a railway undertaking and a host of individuals and other entities. Such concerted action is bound to have deterrent impact. Amnesty cannot be an answer to non-compliance to tax-laws.

The FM needs to appreciate that tax gets collected by governance and not by surrender to the tax evaders.

CASE PILOTS

1. CHAMBER OF TAX CONSULTANTS V. UNION OF INDIA . (2017) 6

FACTS

The writ petition was filed in the high court of Delhi by the petitioner. The petitioner challenged the section 145(2) of the income tax Act which notify us to follow the ICDS, empowered by the central government for computing the income chargeable using mercantile system of accounting under the head "Profit and gains of business or profession" or "income from other sources". The petitioner challenged the notification no. 87/2016 and circular no. 10/2017 demanding to follow 10 ICDS.

ISSUSE

Is part of ICDS which override the laws as mentioned in judicial precedents are need to be struck down or not?

HELD

The Delhi High Court held the updated ICDS and its specific provisions and also CBDT for issuing clarification as to be ultra vires the Act. And the section 145(2) has been read down by restricting the central government powers to only notify if the provisions made do not contradict the judicial precedents. The court also held that, under Articles 141 and 1447 of the Constitution, when there is a binding judicial precedent, the executive cannot supersede it unless the Act is amended by way of a validation statute.

ANALYSIS

As ICDS is mandatory to follow it was no longer possible for an Assessee to measure taxable income in accordance with the Act, as elucidated by Supreme Court and High Court judgments. Also many provisions in the ICDS were in conflict with the act or judicial precedents which in result becomes prevailing over the judicial precedents. So, accordingly there is a need to resist the powers of central government in notifying the ICDS in such a way that no override situation occurs. The decision taken by Delhi High Court to read down the section 145(2) of the Act is in accordance with the constitution. Further, CBDT clarified that in the event of a conflict between the provisions of the ICDS and the Act, the provisions of the act will take precedence.

2. HERCULES PIGMENT INDUSTRY V. ITO 8

FACTS

The assessee is in business of manufacturing and marketing of pigments and following inclusive method of accounting. The excise duty paid or received were taken into unutilized CENVAT credit (UCC) account by assessee. During assessment the AO disallowed the unutilized CENVAT of Rs. 1.39 million under the section 145A of the Act. On appeal the order of AO was confirmed by the CIT(A) although relief of Rs. 0.339 million was allowed to the assessee. The aggrieved assessee is in appeal before tribunal.

ISSUES

Is the profit determined by the assessee for the stated assessment year is applicable irrespective of inclusive or exclusive method of accounting followed?

DECISION

Appeal of the assessee was dismissed as the assessee doesn't carefully followed the provisions of section 145A of the income tax Act for valuation to determine correct taxable value.

ANALYSIS

The UCC account maintained by the assessee is a measure of excise liability on removal of goods but it does not represent the unutilized credit available on the goods that were held as stock in trade. So, the UCC account cannot be taken as correct measure of excise duty on inventories. Therefore, to determine the correct profit the assessee needs to make a correct profit and loss statement including the excise duty in opening stock, closing stock and purchases in a way that the CENVAT credit in integrated within it.

The Government has tabled 'The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2019' in the parliament to make some amendments in the Income-tax Act and also to modify the amendments made by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019 as promulgated by the President on 20-09-2019. Here is the analysis of the major changes in the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2019 viz-a-viz Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance.

1. CHANGES PROPOSED IN SECTION 115BAB

1.1. Concessional rate of tax restricted to income derived from manufacturing activity

A new Section 115BAB has been inserted in Income-tax Act by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019. This provision provided an option to pay tax at the concessional rate of 15% to the newly incorporated domestic manufacturing companies. As a manufacturing company can earn income under the 4 heads of income, the Ordinance did not give any clarity on the nature of income which shall be subject to concessional tax rate. Thus, there was an ambiguity whether the reduced tax rate shall apply on total income of the company or only income derived from the manufacturing activities.

To bring clarity on the issue, the Amendment Bill proposes that the income which is neither derived from nor incidental to manufacturing or production of an article or thing shall be taxed at the rate of 22%. This higher rate of tax shall be applicable only in respect of those income for which no specific rate of tax has been provided seperately in Chapter XII and such tax shall be charged on the gross receipt without claiming any deduction or allowance in respect of any expenditure or allowance.

However, an exception has been proposed in the third proviso to Section 115BAB(1) that the short-term capital gain arising from transfer of a capital asset on which no depreciation is allowable shall be charged to tax at the rate of 22%. Thus, assessee would be able to claim deduction of expenditure or allowance while computing the short-term capital gain arising from non-depreciable assets.

The short-term capital gain from transfer of depreciable asset would continue to be taxed at normal rate of 15% if use of such depreciable assets was incidental to manufacturing or production of any article or thing.

The Single-Bench’s Decision was challenged by the Government of Assam. The Division Bench on August 30, 2007, agreed that there is no violation of article 304(a) since the definition of ‘local area’ had been changed in the Act to remove the discrimination effect. But the violation of article 301 read with article 304(b) was found in the Act and, accordingly, the High Court gave the decision to abolish the Act and asked the Government to refund the tax collected by way of entry tax which amounted to about Rs. 300 crores.

Now in order to comply with article 301 read with article 304(b ), the State Government has decided to create a compensatory fund out of the revenue collected by way of entry tax, namely, ‘Trade Development Fund’ and after making necessary amendment in this regard, the new Assam Entry Tax Act, 2008 had been legislated and published in the Assam Gazette Extraordinary No. 114, dated April 17, 2008 (Notification No. LGL 3/2007/101) which came into force with effect from June 1, 2008.

Findings of the survey

7. The responses gathered from the targeted dealers and manufacturers have been analysed and discussed hereunder. This will reflect the implication of entry tax on trade and commerce.

7.1 Implication of entry tax on the registered dealers and manufacturers - Survey conducted over hundred registered dealers and manufacturers in respect of six selected commodities, namely, cement, marble, biscuits, gamocha (handmade Towels), plant and machinery and ENA (Extra Natural Alcohol) reveals, some positive and some negative aspects of entry tax which are discussed below :

u Entry tax - some positive aspects :

(i )Purchase of commodities directly from other States for consumption like cement from Meghalaya, marble form Rajasthan, gamocha from Tamilnadu and Kerala at comparatively cheaper rate results in trade diversion. When cement is directly purchased from Meghalaya for final consumption in Assam or as an input for construction purpose in Assam, the eventual VAT on cement goes to the exchequer of Meghalaya State. Further, the local dealers in Assam lose their market share. In this place when entry tax is levied on entry of cement from Meghalaya into Assam, perhaps the consumers would not feel encouraged to buy cement from Maghalaya. Thus, the consumer would be forced to buy cement from a local dealer within Assam. This way entry tax can be a counter-veiling measure to check this trade diversion and can protect the local dealers of the State.

(ii )Purchase of commodities from outside the State directly for consumption and not for re-sale, does not attract VAT. So the State Government does not get any revenue on such commodities. Entry tax on such imports can become a source of revenue to the State Government.

(iii )The dealers from other States may open their new branches in Assam if people stop buying from them directly and this may expand the trade and business of the region.

(iv )The trade development fund created out of the revenue collection by way of entry tax, if utilized for infrastructural development and other developmental activities in connection with trade, commerce and industry of the State, as announced by the State Government, will definitely pave the way for farther industrialization of the State.

u Entry tax — Some negative aspects - Entry tax does not only have the positive side, it has some negative aspects as well which are discussed below :—

(i )An analysis of the responses reveals that entry tax on raw-materials purchased from outside the State for manufacturing purpose will definitely have harsh impact on manufacturing units of the State. The raw-materials required like chemicals and wrappers for biscuit manufacturing units, ENA (Extra Natural Alcohol) for the manufacturing of alchohol, etc. are either not available in the State or if available, then they are comparatively costlier or not of good quality. Entry tax on these raw-materials is going to increase the cost of production of the local manufacturers and so they may not be able to compete with the prices of the finished products imported from outside for re-sale.

(ii )Entry tax on plant and machinery may affect the local manufacturing units adversely as all the plant and machineries required for manufacturing purpose are imported from outside the State. This may increase the capital expenditure of the manufacturing units.

(iii )Manner of levy and collection of tax is also not simple for the small consumers. Even small purchasers need to obtain road-permit from transport department which is not practically feasible.

(iv )The commodities carried through buses, passenger trains, etc., are hardly checked. Hence, improper entry of good through buses and trains may increase in number.

(v )The number of check gates and officials required for tax administration are not sufficient in number.

(vi )All the abovesaid negative aspects may pave the way for evasion of tax to a great extent.

Supreme Court of India in its Judgment in Chief Controlling Revenue Authority v. Costal Gujarat Power Ltd. [Civil Appeal No. 6054 of 2015, dated 11-8-2015] held that a mortgage executed by a borrower in favour of a security trustee would not be treated as a single document for determining the liability under the Gujarat Stamp Act, in the event the Security Trustee holds the security for the benefit of multiple lenders. This judgment is a marked departure from the position that only the form of the instrument would be looked at for determination of stamp duty. The Supreme Court has also looked at collateral evidences such as inter-se agreements between the security trustee and the lenders. This article highlights the important provisions of the stamp duty, the implication and consequences of the Supreme Court's Judgment.

Introduction

1. Stamp duty is a State subject and each State Government has its own set of provisions relating to payment of stamp duty payable on various registered as well as on certain unregistered documents. Further, certain State Government Departments, Institutions of Local Self-Government, Semi-Government Organisations, Banks, Non-Banking Institutions etc. which have been notified by the State Government shall ensure that proper stamp duty is paid on the various instruments which are executed in the State. Change is the only constant in life and the law-makers of India are also following the said maxim especially when it comes to Fiscal Statutes like the Stamp Duty Act. Every year certain State Government would amend or change certain provisions of their State Stamp Act. But here is a case due to Supreme Court's landmark judgment and its interpretation of the provisions of the Act and taking into account the collateral documents on the transaction, the stamp duty payable on an instrument increases.

Usually, stamp duty is payable on the instrument and not on the transaction. And in case an instrument e.g. a Mortgage Deed is executed between a borrower (Mortgager) and a Security Trustee (Mortgagee) then the stamp duty is payable only on the instrument. Syndicated loans are very common in lending transactions and in case of large loans consortium of lenders (various bankers) lend the money. But the entire syndicate loan transaction is governed through a single agreement between all the parties. This article highlights the position of law whether in a mortgage deed with security trustee to secure loans of multiple banks would be treated as distinct transactions and would be liable for stamp duty as if separate mortgage deeds were recorded for each bank but in reality only one Mortgage Deed is to be executed covering the entire transaction. The article will also analyse the implication of the latest Supreme Court Judgment on the transaction as it will impact the cost of borrowing and will have far reaching consequences on the settled principle of not going beyond the corporate veil.

Facts of the case

2. A company named Coastal Gujarat Power Ltd [CGPL] secured assistance from few lenders for setting up an ultra mega power project in the area of Kutch-Bhuj in the State of Gujarat. The lenders, i.e., the financial institutions totalling to thirteen in number formed a consortium as a Trust and executed a Security Trustee Agreement [STA] inter se appointing one Banker viz., the State Bank of India [SBI] as the Lead Trustee, called the Security Trustee. CGPL executed an Indenture of Mortgage for Delayed After Assets Deed with SBI, being the Security Trustee, mortgaging its assets as mentioned in the Deed itself. The said document was presented for registration before the Sub-Registrar, Mudra, by paying stamp duty of Rs. 4,21,000 and the Deed was registered.

In Model GST Law, where a person, after any tax has become due from him, creates a charge on or parts with the property belonging to him or in his possession by way of sale, mortgage, exchange, or any other mode of transfer whatsoever of any of his properties in favour of any other person with the intention of defrauding the Government revenue, such charge or transfer shall be void as against any claim in respect of any tax or any other sum payable by the said person.

Income Tax Act says if any proceeding due or any service of notice due after completion of such proceedings, but GST laws are differentiating from it and it covers almost all tax payers whether any proceeding is pending against taxpayer or not. With reference tax due in erstwhile sales tax act, the Calcutta High Court in case of Recols (India) Ltd., In re [1953] 4 STC 371, has held that as soon as there is a taxable turnover, the tax is due.

In case of CST v. Sri Jagatbandhu Mohanty, [1961] 12 STC 706, the Orissa High Court said that there are two important points of difference between the Bihar Sales Tax Act and the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. (1) Whereas income-tax for the assessment year is assessed on the income of the previous year, sales tax becomes liable to be paid immediately after each sale is effected though, for facility of computation and payment of tax, provision has been made for the filing of returns at the. expiry of each quarter. (2) Whereas rates of income-tax vary in accordance with the amount of income and therefore no one can be certain of what income-tax he has to pay at least until the accounting year expires, the rate of sales tax does not vary on the amount of taxable turnover and a dealer, therefore, can always be certain of what sales tax he has to pay as soon as he effects a sale. In other words, sales tax becomes payable immediately after a sale is transacted. It said further that the words 'due' and 'payable' are separate. Eventually, honourable high court came to the conclusion that it is, therefore, clear that to the extent of liability admitted in a return the amount of tax is payable before the dealer submits that return. Thus, there is no doubt that the tax is payable since the sale is transacted and it is incumbent upon the registered dealer to state that amount in the return when submitted.

9. The nomenclature of this dispute resolution scheme i.e. 'Vivad se Vishwaas Scheme' suggests the 'trust-centric' philosophy and intent of the Law Makers behind bringing out this Tax Amnesty Scheme.

It has been asserted that this dispute resolution scheme would benefit primarily in the disputes concerning cash deposit cases in demonetisation period and penny stock cases.

In all such cases, the provisions of section 115BBE have been pressed into service by the Revenue Authorities and an effective tax rate of almost 78% (Basic Rate u/s 115BBE @ 60% plus surcharge @ 25%), has been levied on the additions.

Therefore, in all such cases, even the 'disputed tax' @ 78%, is very high and may not be persuasive enough to motivate the assessee to opt for this scheme.

Therefore, in order to bring fruitful results in such cases, under this scheme, the amount of 'disputed tax' to be paid by the appellant, should be reduced to the maximum marginal rate of tax of approximately 33.66% and not at the high rate of 78%. If at all, some differentiation is to be made between normal cases and such cases, then a higher rate of say 40% may be prescribed, so as to ensure fruitful tax realisation, in such cases, under the scheme.

Introduction

1. GST is the flavour of the season in India. All and sundry have been holding forth on how the introduction of GST would add 1 -2% to the GDP and that it is the panacea for all our economic problems. Political parties and Governments of all hues have largely backed the introduction of GST – the differences between them being only in the details. The industry in particular has been a consistent supporter of GST, although they may demur on some of the specifics. It is only the consumer who ultimately bears the tax, whose voice is not heard – but that is another story.

In this piece, we attempt to address a couple of fundamental questions that many of us may be asking ourselves:

1.

Why did taxing jurisdictions including India allow the Indirect Tax landscape to be littered with a whole host of taxes in the first place?

2.

How GST is going to be the Panacea which addresses the concerns and challenges that led to the litany of indirect taxes?

To arrive at the answers to above questions, the tax, the basic premises on which taxes are levied and the reasons for having Direct and Indirect Taxes1, have to be analysed.

Tax, Multiple Tax and its justification

2. Well, then, what is tax? To put it simply, tax is the price that we pay for 'public goods'. And, what are 'public goods'? Public goods are those goods/services which emanate from the collective wants of the populace and are enjoyed by them collectively – typical examples are preservation of internal order and protection from external aggression and in modern times, it extends to such facilities as roads, dams, sanitation, water, healthcare, education etc; as against this: 'private goods' are goods/services that are rendered by one or more private parties to other private parties in pursuance to a contract. The crucial aspects which distinguish 'public goods' from 'private goods' are:

Public goods being unsolicited, its price cannot be collected contractually and hence the need for a legislation to extract the same by authority of law; and

The distribution of the price of public goods on the populace who are the consumers of such public goods would have to be based on some formula/proposition which is fair and equitable and thereby acceptable to such consumers.

The process of seeking answers or rather addressing the questions posed by the above mentioned distinguishing features of public goods and the need to minimize the risk of default by the consumers of public goods, has formed the bedrock of the theory of taxation over the centuries.

Without getting into the nitty-gritties of the reasons wherefore the assumptions underlying the framing of tax laws have come to be accepted, we outline the same below:

Consumption of public goods is directly proportional to the income earned by the citizen/user of public goods – in other words, more the income earned, more the amount of public goods consumed; and therefore the need to adopt a progressive form of taxation whereby a person with a higher income/earning pays tax which is proportionately more than the tax payable by a person with a lower income. Herein lies the reason why high income individuals are taxed at rates higher than those imposed on lesser earning folks.

The risk of evasion of collecting tax at source/on income is significant, given the nature of human beings especially the more resourceful amongst them; and therefore the risk of evasion has to be mitigated by taxing multiple events such as expenditure, property, consumption of luxury goods etc, rather than attempting to collect all the taxes due at source/income. The underlying assumption being: no person can successfully avoid/evade all events of taxation; and therefore, at least some of the taxes that are due to the government would get paid.

The reader may very well ask, shouldn't we then do away with Income Tax and resort only to transaction taxes as transaction taxes are much less prone to evasion? The answer to that is yes we can, but that would lead to a regressive form of taxation and would result in a poorer person paying more tax as a proportion of his income as against a richer/high income person, simply because a poorer person tends to spend more of his income vis-à-vis a richer/higher income earning person and thereby ends up paying a higher percentage of his income as tax as compared to a richer person. And, therefore the need to spread the taxes due on income as well as expenses – it may be noted that taxing income and expenses together is not double taxation; it is just that the total tax due is spread between the two streams and has proved to be more efficient and equitable in practice.

These then are reasons why we have multiple taxes – in India the need to have multiple taxing events also arises because of the federal structure which divides the taxing powers between the centre, the states and the local government.

In sum, taxes on multiple events were imposed to spread the risks posed to government revenue from the very real threat of evasion. This answers the first of the two questions that we posed.

ization of public-revenue. The possible reasons for re-introduction of entry tax are as follows:

(a)The tax revenue collected under VAT system does not contribute much to the public exchequer as was anticipated as compared to the former sales tax contribution to public revenue.

(b)Purchase of commodities directly from other States at comparatively cheaper rate results in trade-diversion. Hence, to check this trade-diversion and to protect the domestic indigenous industries, the consuming States reintroduce entry tax along with VAT. (c)According to the terms of agreement of the State Finance Ministers duly recommended by the High Powered Committee, the Central Government gradually agreed to phase out Central Sales Tax (CST) to be reduced from 4 per cent in 2006 to 3 per cent in 2007, to 2 per cent in 2008, to 1 per cent in 2009 and to 0 rate by April, 2010. Under this proposition, the States lose their revenue by way of CST. The States put forward their demand through the High Powered Committee to the Central Government seeking a package of compensation for them on account of loss of revenue from CST which was roughly estimated at Rs. 13,000 crores in June, 2008. The States were left with no alternative to mobilize at least the existing level of public revenue they need for governance of the affairs of the State. Unlike the Central Government, in our federal structure, the States have very little options for levy of taxes. All these matters cumulatively prompted the States to go for introduction of entry tax.

(d)Additional Duties of Excise (A.D.E.) items like sugar and textile are not vatable in Assam and so the State Government is getting a share of additional duties of excise from the Centre. If entry tax is levied on these items, the State Government can get additional revenue without losing its share of excise from the Centre.

Rationality of the study

5. As a part of reform of the indirect tax structure in India, VAT (Value Added Tax) system has been introduced replacing the age-old sales tax system of the country. Para-2.16 of the white paper circulated by the Empowered Committee of Finance Ministers suggesting to introduce VAT system was as follows:

"As mentioned earlier, all other existing taxes such as turnover tax, surcharge, additional surcharge and Special Additional Tax (SAT) would be abolished. There will not be any reference these taxes in the VAT Bills. The States that have already introduced entry tax and intend to continue with this tax should make it vatable. If not made vatable, entry tax will need to be abolished."

But entry tax has not been abolished in many States even after the implementation of VAT system specially in the consuming States like Assam, Orissa, Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh, etc.

The Assam Entry Tax Act, 2001 came into force with effect from October 1, 2001 but later on it was declared null and void in the judgment given by the High Court on November 16, 2006. Now with necessary amendments, the new Assam Entry Tax Act, 2008, has again came into force on and from June 1, 2008.

Imposition of entry tax in Assam when the talks are going on to reform the existing indirect tax structure making it more simple and transparent, is a matter of great concern. The taxing authority claims the entry tax as a measure to protect the local dealers and to check the diversion of trade whereas the manufacturers protest it on the ground that this will lead to an increase in their cost of production. Again lack of proper checking at check gates may pave the way for tax evasion to a great extent.

Hence, it is necessary to conduct a research investigation to ascertain the factual position and to see the genesis and rationality of introducing entry tax in Assam and also to see its impact on manufacturers, dealers, consumers and public at large.

Genesis of Entry Tax in Assam

6. Article 265 of the Indian Constitution has empowered the States to levy tax and as per article 267(2) the State Legislature by making a law can establish a new Act levying tax in the State.

The Assam Entry Tax Act came into force with effect from October 1, 2001 vide Notification No. FTX/146/2001/3, dated September 28, 2001. At the beginning the entry tax was levied only on 8 items. But later on, the No. of items on which the entry tax was levied gradually increased and reached up to 58 by December, 2005. No Presidential assent was taken for the levy of entry tax on these subsequent items. The aggrieved dealers and manufacturers filed a law suit in the Gauhati High Court. On this, the Single Bench Decision given on November 16, 2006 by the Hon’ble Gauhati High Court Judge, Mr. Anshari declared the Assam Entry Tax Act, 2001 as ultra vires since the original Act was in violation of article 304(a) of the Indian Constitution and further it amounted to violation of article 301 read with article 304(b) which says that no bill or amendment shall be introduced or moved in the Legislature of a State without the previous sanction of the President.

ARTICLE 25 : MUTUAL AGREEMENT PROCEDURE - 1. Where a resident of a Contracting State considers that the actions of one or both of the Contracting States result or will result for him in taxation not in accordance with this Agreement, he may, notwithstanding the remedies provided by the taxation laws of those States, present his case to the competent authority of the State of which he is a resident or, if his case comes under paragraph 1 of article 24, to that of the State of which he is a national. ARTICLE 26 : EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION - 1. The competent authorities of the Contracting States shall exchange such information including documents as is necessary for carrying out the provisions of this Agreement or of the domestic laws of the Contracting States concerning taxes covered by this Agreement, or for the prevention or detection of evasion or avoidance of taxes covered by this Agreement. LETTER [F.NO.292/62/2012-IT (INV.III)/26]., DATED 23-4-2018

The undersigned is directed to say that the reward scheme for informants, named 'Guidelines for grant of rewards to Informants, 2007', as was issued in 2007 vide Board's letter referred above, has been revised and "Income Tax Informants Rewards Scheme, 2018" has been issued in supersession of it with effect from date of issue. Further, guidelines containing procedure to be followed by Departmental officers for implementation of the Reward Scheme is issued separately. While the "Income Tax Informants Rewards Scheme, 2018" is for public circulation, the "Guidelines for Departmental officers" is for departmental use. Copy of the revised reward scheme is enclosed herewith.

Introduction

1. In supersession of the 'Guidelines for grant of rewards to Informants, 2007' and other existing guidelines on the subject, the following new reward scheme is hereby introduced for regulating grant and payment of reward to a person who is an informant under this scheme. A person can get reward up to Rs. Five crore by giving specific information about evasion of Income tax on income and assets in India and abroad. Identity of the informant shall be kept confidential.

Short Title

1.1. This scheme shall be called "Income Tax Informants Reward Scheme 2018".

Commencement

1.2. This scheme comes into effect on the date of issue.

Scope

1.3.This scheme shall regulate the grant and payment of reward to informants in cases where information is received by a JDIT (Inv) from the informant on or after the date of issue of this Scheme that leads to detection of substantial tax evasion under the provisions of Income Tax Act, 1961 and/or the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income & Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015. This scheme shall not be applicable to information regarding recovery of irrecoverable taxes as the Central Board of Direct Taxes has issued separate Guidelines for the same vide F. No. 385/21/2015-IT (B) dated 26-8-2015.

1.3.1. However, the 'Guidelines for grant of rewards to Informants, 2007' shall continue to be applicable in cases where information was received before the date of issue of this Scheme.

both at the Union and State levels albeit covering different events of taxation, which in theory at least should already have ensured that the bulk of the intermediaries are within the tax fold. The increase in revenues would therefore, have to flow in on account of reduction in the threshold limits; and on account of non-VAT taxes such as Octroi, CST, Entry Tax, Luxury Tax etc being subsumed into GST. The extent of increase in collections on these counts though, remains to be seen. We would like to note that the productivity and efficiency of GST, varies widely, across taxing jurisdictions/countries. One of the measures used to evaluate the efficiency of a GST system is the ratio of actual receipts vs projected receipts computed based on consumption data. Research relating to 2009 for OECD countries reveals a high ratio of around 100% for New Zealand and Luxembourg and a low ratio of around 30% for countries such as Mexico, Turkey and Spain3. The IMF report4 reflects a similar picture– from a high ratio of 95% for Sweden to a low ratio of 60% to Romania and Paraguay. However, it is not quite clear whether the gaps are on account of difference in policies such as threshold limits, exemptions, zero rating or due to fraud/evasion. Whilst New Zealand which practically taxes all goods and services has a high ratio of 100%, Mexico which has a ratio as low as 30% does provide a fair amount of exemptions – but do exemptions alone lead to a ratio as low as 30% or is it also on account of evasion and if so, what is the contribution of evasion to the low ratio, remains to be further investigated. There is not enough information on this front, as of now. Moreover, in a federal polity like India there will be other factors which decides the success and effectiveness of a wholesome tax like GST.

From the aforesaid discussion it follows that:

"Input Tax Credit" is not just a procedural detail in the superstructure of GST, instead, it is the pivot on which GST rests. It is the single biggest innovation that seeks to address the challenge of evasion, structurally, and thereby lends governments/revenue administrations the option to move to a simpler single indirect tax regime;

And, the success of any GST regime would amongst other things hinge on the following two factors:

A liberal and expansive input tax credit regime – this would ensure that the intermediaries have sufficient incentive to stay logged in the system and pay the taxes due.

An effective mechanism to check the misuse of input tax credit, be it on the strength of fake invoices, fictitious purchases or any other stratagem.

Tail Piece

4. GST is viewed to least impact/retard growth, while at the same time generate revenue for the state. In India too, a successful GST would be expected to do the same. However, in a country where an abysmally low percentage of citizens pay Income Taxes and in the context of the stated policy of the Union Government to reduce Corporate Tax from 30% to 25% over the next 5 years, a successful GST could turnout to be regressive and therefore, inequitable. Has this issue been flagged off? If so, how does the Government attempt to address the challenge? As of now, we have no answers to these questions.

1. Argentina enhances the scope of levying tax on the acquisition of 'Foreign Currency'

In 2019, the Argentina Government introduced a new law,the "law of social solidarity and productive reactivation in the framework of the public emergency", that will apply for 5 years.

Chapter 6 of such law provides a levy of "Tax for an Inclusive and Supportive Argentina". Said chapter levied a tax on the purchase of foreign currency without a specific purpose, purchases of goods or services from abroad,purchases made through portals or virtual sites in foreign currency, etc.

These transactions are taxed at the rate of 30%. However, the purchase of digital services was subject to tax at 8%.

Further, in a bid to protect Argentina's dollar reserve, the Govt. tightened controls on buying and spending in foreign currencies and introduced an additional tax of35% computed on the existing 30% tax. The new 35% tax acts as a surcharge, subsequently increasing to 45% for certain transactions.

On 13th October 2022, videDecree 682/2022, the Argentina Government enhanced the scope of transactions in foreign currency that are subject to tax,which includes:

(a)

The acquisition abroad of personal, cultural, and recreational services (does not include educational teaching), or its acquisition in the country when they are provided by non-residents;

(b)

Import of luxury goods mentioned in Annex I of the Decree by the respective tariff code.

Further, the Govt. has also released General Resolution 5272/2022,which provides that the acquisition of personal, cultural, and recreational services is not subject to additional tax. However, the additional tax at the rate of 25% shall be imposed on:

(a)

Purchases of goods with debit or credit cards and other payment systems if the amount exceeds US$ 300 per month;

(b)

Purchases of travel tickets and tours acquired in foreign currency;

(c)

Imports of luxury goods mentioned in Annex I of the Decree by the respective tariff code.

2. Netherlands launches online Consultation Paper on 'Minimum Tax Rate'

On 24th October 2022, the Dutch government published a draft bill for the proposed Minimum Tax Rate Act, 2024. The bill was introduced for the domestic implementation of the OECD Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) 2.0 Pillar Two agreement.

In 2021, the first draft ofthe proposed directive setting out a model for EU member states was declared by European Commission, and in June 2022, almost all member states voted in favour of the directive scheme. In pursuance of this scheme, the Dutch government launched the draft bill.

The proposed bill has been drafted in accordance with the Global Anti-Base Erosion (GloBE) Rules, including Income Inclusion Rule (IIR) and Undertaxed Payment Rule (UTPR)

The draft bill provides a minimum corporation tax rate of at least 15%. This measure will prevent the companies from shifting profits to low-tax jurisdictions to minimize the tax they pay.

Interested parties and stakeholders can submit their comments until 5thDecember 2022 via www.internetconsultatie.nl

8. Taxation of non-residents

8.1. No Significant Economic Presence on the export of goods

Section 9 of the ITA specifies the income deemed to accrue or arise in India. Section 9(1)(i) states that all income accruing or arising, whether directly or indirectly, through or from any business connection in India shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India. Clause (b) of Explanation 1 Section 9(1) clarifies that, in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India if it is derived solely from operations confined to the purchase of goods in India for export.

It is proposed that Explanation 2A of Section 9 be amended so that the transactions or activities of a non-resident in India, which are confined to the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export, shall not constitute a significant economic presence of such non-resident in India. This amendment will align it with Explanation 1 to Section 9(1)(i) concerning business connections.

8.2. Sovereign Wealth Funds and Pension Fund

The deadline for investing by foreign Sovereign Wealth Funds, Pension Funds, and the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority in Indian infrastructure entities for exemption under section 10(23FE) has been proposed to be extended from 31-03-2025 to 31-03-2030. Further, the long-term capital gains arising from investments made by foreign Sovereign Wealth Funds, Pension Funds, and the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority in Indian infrastructure entities are proposed to be exempt under Section 10(23FE) even if they are deemed short-term capital gains under section 50AA.

8.3. Presumptive Tax Scheme

A new presumptive tax scheme has been proposed in Section 44BBD, which would apply to non-residents providing services or technology to a resident company in India to set up an electronics manufacturing facility or manufacture/produce electronic goods. Under this scheme, 25% of the total amount paid or payable to the non-resident for such services or technology would be deemed presumptive income.

8.4. Tonnage Tax Scheme

The benefits of the tonnage tax scheme are proposed to be extended to Inland Vessels registered under the Inland Vessels Act of 2021.

Further, the time limit for the Joint Commissioner to pass an order under Section 115VP(4) has been proposed to be increased to three months from the end of the quarter in which a qualifying company makes an application to opt for a tonnage tax scheme. Presently, the time limit is expiry of one month from the end of the month in which the application was made.

9. Proposals for block assessments

9.1. Undisclosed income arising from the Virtual Digital Assets

Section 158B(b) provides an inclusive meaning of "undisclosed income" for the block assessment scheme. It provides that the following assets shall be considered undisclosed income if such assets represent, wholly or partly, income or property that has not been or would not have been disclosed for the purposes of this Act:

(a)

Money,

(b)

Bullion,

(c)

Jewellery,

(d)

Other valuable articles or things, and

(e)

Income based on any entry in books of account, other documents, and transactions.

The Finance Bill 2025 proposes to include virtual digital assets in the scope of undisclosed income. This amendment is applicable with effect from 01-02-2025.
